articles.title: Knovum 0.0.2: Building an Open-Source Local-First AI Canvas with Tauri 2, Vue 3, and Rust
articles.description:
Like many developers and researchers, I've spent the past two years experimenting with local LLMs (via Ollama) and local RAG. But existing desktop frontends repeatedly hit two frustrating walls:
The 1D Chat Trap: Linear chat streams work well for simple Q&A, but break down during deep research synthesis. Earlier reasoning turns scroll off the top, and you cannot visually compare multiple document excerpts side-by-side.
The Electron Memory Tax: Most desktop AI wrappers idle at 700MB–1GB RAM before you even load model weights into VRAM.
To solve this, we built Knovum — an open-source, local-first desktop AI knowledge workspace built on an infinite 2D canvas with Tauri 2, Rust, and Vue 3. 
Today we just shipped v0.0.2, so I wanted to share the engineering decisions behind the architecture, what we learned building it, and what's new.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             Vue 3 Spatial Frontend                     │
│  (Konva Infinite 2D Canvas + JSON Canvas Specification) │
└───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                            │ Tauri 2 IPC (Channels)
┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
│                    Rust Backend Core                   │
│   ┌────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────┐   │
│   │   SQLite Storage   │      │ Embedded LanceDB   │   │
│   │  (Notes, Boards,   │      │ (In-Process Vector │   │
│   │   Numbered Migr.)  │      │   Search Engine)   │   │
│   └────────────────────┘      └────────────────────┘   │
│   ┌────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────┐   │
│   │    Ollama API      │      │ Embedded Whisper   │   │
│   │ (Local LLM Router) │      │ (Speech-to-Text)   │   │
│   └────────────────────┘      └────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

By leveraging native OS WebViews (WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows) orchestrated by a compiled Rust backend, Knovum cold-boots in sub-second time and idles around 45MB of RAM. This leaves virtually all of your machine's physical memory dedicated to loading model weights.
SQLite: The canonical single source of truth for notes, cards, and relations, guarded by strict numbered migrations.
Embedded LanceDB: Runs in-process on disk for fast vector similarity search without requiring Docker, external daemons, or Python runtimes.
Every visual workspace is stored directly on your local filesystem using the open JSON Canvas (.canvas) specification. You can open, edit, and inspect any Knovum board directly in Obsidian Canvas or parse it with custom scripts.
Here are the key improvements shipped in our 0.0.2 release:
In traditional vector RAG setups, updating a document collection often triggers expensive full re-indexes. In 0.0.2:
Rebuilding a space indexes only the gap (delta) instead of re-processing the entire space.
The live index stays fully readable and searchable while the background rebuild runs.
Indexing is managed as a first-class, cancellable job in the unified Task Center.
Streaming LLM answers now respect clear block boundaries instead of erasing or slicing through previous turns. Concurrency is strictly owned by a single writer per execution run.
Knovum includes an on-device Whisper transcription engine. In 0.0.2, the voice library can be audited and heard before selection, and visualizes the active speaker in real time.
Ships an opaque window with the WebView2 bootstrapper directly embedded.
Startup failures fail visibly instead of leaving hidden zombie windows.
The main window is revealed safely from the async runtime, eliminating white flashes on launch.
Local model memory verification admits memory the OS can dynamically allocate rather than hard-failing.
When an LLM synthesizes an insight from your notes, the citation anchors to exact sentence-level character spans in the source note. If you edit or mutate the source note later, the citation badge automatically flags that the source has evolved—preventing silent hallucination decay.
Knovum is 100% free and open-source under the Apache-2.0 license.
GitHub Repository: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum


v0.0.2 Release Downloads: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/releases/tag/v0.0.2


macOS (Apple Silicon .dmg & Intel .dmg)
Windows (x64-setup.exe)
If you're interested in local-first software, spatial computing, or running LLMs on your own hardware, give the repository a ⭐ on GitHub and let us know your feedback!

articles.title: Where your Codex usage actually goes (and how to make the window last longer)
articles.description:
If you use Codex every day, you know the moment. The plan is clear, half the feature is written, the tests are almost green, and the usage window closes. You didn't do anything unusual. You just did a normal afternoon of AI coding.
The frustrating part is that most of us don't really know which part of the work used the allowance. So let's break that down, look at how to check where you stand, and then talk about a workflow change that made the biggest difference for us.
Quick disclosure before we start: I work on XCR, the plugin I mention later in this post. The habits in the first half work with or without it.
Codex comes with ChatGPT plans, and each plan has usage limits. OpenAI's Codex help article lists what drives usage: the model, where the task runs, task complexity, context size, reasoning effort, speed and tools. A long-running agentic task can use a lot more than a short request.
Two details trip people up:
Usage is tracked in two windows: a five-hour window and a weekly window.
On plans with shared allowances, Codex draws from the same pool as other agent features in ChatGPT.
The exact numbers change by plan and over time, so check the current ChatGPT plans page for yours rather than trusting a screenshot from a forum thread.
When you look at a session after the fact, the expensive parts are pretty predictable.
1. Implementation loops. Write code, run tests, read the failure, patch, run again. Every round re-reads the context. A feature with three or four rounds of test fixes is where most of the window goes.
2. Long threads. Everything Codex has read and written in the thread rides along with each new turn. A thread that started as "add an endpoint" and wandered into "also refactor auth" is carrying a lot of baggage.
3. Repository exploration. Opening file after file to understand a codebase before writing the first line. Useful, but heavy.
4. Heavy reasoning on routine work. The strongest models with high reasoning effort use the allowance fastest. Using them to rename a prop is overkill.
Compare that to planning a change or reviewing a diff. Those are light. Codex reads your request, thinks about the approach, or reads a diff and comments on it. It's the build (multi-file edits plus the test-fix loop) that's heavy.
Keep that split in mind, because the rest of this post depends on it.
Don't guess. Before starting something large:
Open Settings or the usage dashboard in ChatGPT or the Codex app to see which allowance you've used and when it resets.
In an active Codex CLI session, run:




/status

And one myth to kill: starting a new chat does not reset your limits. A fresh thread makes each turn lighter because old context stops riding along, but the windows reset on their own schedule.
Before any tooling, these habits do help:
One task per thread. Switch threads when you switch topics.
Front-load the requirement. Goal, constraints and how to verify it, all in the first message. Drip-fed requirements mean rework.
Name the files. "Look at orders/service.ts and orders/export.test.ts" is far cheaper than "find where orders are handled."
Keep AGENTS.md lean. Codex reads it on every task, so every extra paragraph costs you on every task.
Match model and effort to the task. Lighter settings for routine edits; save the heavy settings for design questions and nasty bugs.
These all help. But they're still optimizing the heavy part, not moving it.
Here's the idea that changed the math for us. If planning and review are cheap and the build is expensive, then the build is what you want off your Codex window. Codex is great at understanding what you want, choosing an approach and catching problems in a diff. That's the part that needs Codex.
My team built a plugin for exactly this split. It's called XCR, and it works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and Grok Build.
The flow looks like this:
Codex hands the task over. Anything bigger than a small edit (multi-file changes, features, tests, refactors) gets passed to XCR. Quick questions and one-line fixes stay in Codex, same as before.
XCR builds it. It hands the heavy steps off to other models, writes the change on a copy of your project, runs your project's own checks (type check, lint, tests) and repairs failures within the task's budget.
Codex reviews. It gets a short report back: requirements done, files changed, check results. Then it checks the change against what you asked for.
So your Codex quota goes to the thinking and the reviewing, and the heavy build doesn't run on your Codex window. That's how the quota lasts longer.
On privacy, here's the short version: checks run on your machine. Code is sent to the model only for the task, and XCR doesn't store it.
Open the install page on xcr.ai and sign in with the link that gets emailed to you. No password, no card needed.
In the console, open Install on a computer and pick the Codex tab.
Read "What XCR will change on your computer", tick the box, click Copy install instruction, paste it into Codex and allow the command.
Restart Codex.
Under the hood, XCR registers itself as an MCP server in ~/.codex/config.toml and adds one short rule to ~/.codex/AGENTS.md so Codex knows when to hand work over. Your original files are backed up first.
Then just work normally. Try something like:
Add CSV export to the orders page, with filters by date and status.
When the checks pass, the change lands in your working tree without a commit, so you review it in your usual diff.
A few things that matter if you're cautious (you should be):
Undo: ask Codex to undo the XCR change.
Spending caps: set a daily cap per computer, and every task has its own spending cap.
Pause: pause with one click in the console.
Uninstall: tell Codex "Uninstall XCR from this computer" and it removes exactly what XCR added and restores your files.
The Codex usage limit stings most when you don't know where the usage went. Most of it goes to the build-and-fix loop, not to the thinking. Tighten your habits, check /status before big sessions, and think about moving the heavy builds somewhere other than your Codex window.
AI coding quota always running short? Hand the heavy work to XCR and make your quota last longer.
Original article: Codex usage limit: make your Codex quota last longer

Setup walkthrough: XCR quick start



Disclosure, again: I work on XCR, so weigh my take accordingly.

articles.title: DSPy: The End of Prompt Engineering - Kevin Madura, AlixPartners | 告别提示词工程：用DSPy构建模块化、可优化的AI程序
articles.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-cKUW6n8hBU
想象一下，你以前指挥一个超级聪明的助手（大语言模型）做事，得事无巨细地写小纸条（提示词），比如“请用JSON格式输出，先思考再回答，语气要专业……”，这就像提示词工程，很繁琐，而且换一个助手（换模型）可能就得重写纸条。
现在，有了一个叫 DSPy 的新工具。它让你换个思路：不用再纠结于怎么写小纸条，而是像搭乐高积木一样，用Python代码来设计一个工作流程。
  关键点：


  从“写提示”到“写程序”：你不再跟模型说“你要怎么做”，而是定义一个函数，告诉它“输入是什么，输出是什么”（这叫签名）。至于中间怎么实现，交给DSPy和模型自己去搞定。
  模块化：你可以把复杂的任务拆解成一个个小的、独立的模块（比如“情感分析模块”、“文档摘要模块”），像搭积木一样组合起来。
  自动优化：这是最酷的一点。当你搭好程序后，DSPy可以像一个智能教练，通过反复测试，自动帮你调整那些藏在背后的提示词，让你的程序表现更好，或者换成更便宜的小模型也能达到同样的效果。
简单说，DSPy就是把“写提示词”这种手艺活，变成了“写代码”这种工程活，让你能更快、更稳定地开发基于大模型的应用程序。
 演讲目的与风格：演讲者Kevin Madura开场表示，本次分享会很随意，欢迎大家随时提问。他计划用一半时间讲概念，另一半时间演示代码。
 听众调查：现场大部分人都听说过DSPy，但只有少数人在生产环境中日常使用。演讲者希望今天能转化更多人去尝试。
 DSPy的定义：DSPy是一个声明式框架，用于构建模块化软件。它不是用来迭代提示词的，而是用来构建真正的Python程序。
 个人使用动机：作为一个技术顾问，Kevin经常面对各种不同的问题（如法律调查、流程改进、合同审查）。DSPy让他和他的团队能够非常快速地迭代，构建出解决这些问题的应用。
 核心价值：DSPy最大的好处是能将你的逻辑分解成一个把大语言模型（LLM）当作一等公民的程序。你最终只是在调用一个函数，而这个函数恰好背后是个LLM。DSPy提供了关于输入和输出类型的保证，让你可以专注于构建程序本身。
 恰到好处的抽象层级：DSPy不像LangChain那样会让你感觉受到限制。它不会让你去处理 choices、messages、content 这些底层细节，也不需要你自己写字符串解析器。你只需要声明你的意图。
 创建的是计算机程序：你是在构建一个程序，只是碰巧用了LLM。这比来回调整字符串式的提示词要高级得多。
 系统思维与可迁移性：DSPy的创始人Omar提到，它是用“系统思维”构建的。关键在于，你设计的系统结构和控制流不会因为底层模型能力的快速变化而过时。你可以轻松地在不同模型之间切换，而无需重写整个程序。
 便利性与精确性并存：DSPy提供了开箱即用的便利（如无需手动解析JSON），同时也保留了足够的精度和控制力。如果你想了解底层发生了什么，可以深入查看；否则，只需专注于你想做的事。
 对模型和范式变化的鲁棒性：你可以保留程序的逻辑，同时灵活地嵌入不同的LLM。
 签名 (Signatures)：这是DSPy最核心的概念。它用来指定你想要函数做什么，即定义输入和输出的类型。你可以用简单的字符串（如 "text -> sentiment"）或更复杂的类（基于Pydantic）来定义。字段名本身就充当了微型提示词，会被传递给模型。这是DSPy强大又有点奇怪的地方。


  应对已有好提示词的情况：如果你已经有一个精心打磨过的提示词，完全可以将其作为系统指令注入到签名或模块中，作为优化的起点。
 模块 (Modules)：模块是逻辑上组织程序的方式，基于签名构建。它们类似于PyTorch中的模块概念。DSPy内置了许多常用模块（如 Predict， ChainOfThought， ReAct），你也可以创建自己的模块。例如，一个模块可以先调用LLM，再进行一些硬编码的业务逻辑。
 工具 (Tools)：在DSPy中，工具本质上就是Python函数。你可以很容易地将任何Python函数暴露给LLM使用（例如，一个天气查询函数、一个网络搜索函数）。
 适配器 (Adapters)：适配器位于签名和实际的LLM调用之间。它们负责将你的输入输出签名翻译成最终的提示词格式（如JSON、XML、BAML）。不同的适配器可能会影响模型的表现（性能差异可达5-10%）。
 优化器 (Optimizers)：这是DSPy最引人注目也最有争议的部分。优化器可以自动、量化地提升程序性能。它通过在后台迭代地调整发送给LLM的提示词来实现。这使得模型和用例之间的迁移成为可能，例如，你可以先用强大的模型优化程序，然后将其迁移到更便宜的小模型上，同时保持不错的性能。
 指标 (Metrics)：指标与优化器配合使用，用来定义什么是“成功”。优化器会利用指标来判断每次调整是否有效。指标可以是严格的（如完全匹配），也可以是主观的（如让另一个LLM来评判）。
 环境设置：演示了如何使用Phoenix（Arize的观测平台）来追踪LLM调用。定义了多个LLM（如Claude、Gemini、GPT-4.1 mini），并展示了如何在程序中混合使用它们。
 简单的情感分类器：用一个极其简短的签名 "text -> sentiment" 就创建了一个情感分类器。通过添加额外指令（如“数字越低越负面”）来微调结果。展示了DSPy内置的缓存和用量统计功能。
 处理PDF文档（简易RAG）：使用 attachments 库轻松加载在线PDF（如英伟达的SEC Form 4表单）。无需关心OCR或图像提取的细节，直接将其作为输入传给模型，询问“总共卖出了多少股？”。
 灵活的文档分析：


  无结构输出：创建一个签名，让模型自己决定从文档中提取哪些重要信息，并以字典形式返回。
  有结构输出：预先定义好一个Pydantic模型（如包含交易日期、类型、数量等字段），然后让模型按照这个严格的结构提取信息，方便后续用 . 符号访问数据。
 适配器对比：分别使用默认的JSON适配器和BAML适配器来处理同一个任务，并通过 inspect_history 查看底层生成的提示词。展示了BAML适配器生成的提示词更简洁、更易读，在某些复杂场景下性能更好。
 多模态示例：上传一张包含街道标志的图片，询问“现在可以在这里停车吗？什么时候必须离开？”。演示了DSPy处理图像输入的能力。
 自定义模块：将上述的图像分析逻辑封装成一个Python类（模块），并在其中添加计数器等业务逻辑，展示了模块的可复用性和可扩展性。
 工具调用（ReAct Agent）：创建了一个“简历分析Agent”，它可以使用两个工具（Perplexity搜索和获取URL内容）来查找人物背景。演示了如何异步执行多个这样的Agent，并获取其工具调用的轨迹（trajectory）用于调试。
 优化器（Jeepo）实战：以一个客服消息分类为例，展示了完整的优化流程。


  创建一个包含多个签名和模块的程序。
  定义基于数据集的指标（如“紧急程度是否匹配”）。
  运行优化器，它会使用一个更强大的“教师模型”来提供反馈，迭代地改进提示词。
  优化结果是一个新的、经过优化的程序模块，可以被序列化保存或直接调用。
 综合案例：通用文件处理器：这是一个端到端的示例，演示了如何构建一个能处理多种文件（合同、SEC文件、城市基础设施图片）的单一DSPy程序。


  路由逻辑：程序首先使用一个分类器判断文件类型。
  差异化处理：如果是SEC文件，则提取特定信息；如果是合同，则进行递归摘要；如果是图片，则进行视觉解读。不同的处理步骤甚至可以调用不同的模型（如图片用Gemini，文本用GPT-4.1）。
  文档边界检测：演示了如何通过将PDF页面转为图片，再用一个ReAct Agent进行自我反思和工具调用，来自动识别合同的章节边界（如主文档、附件一、附件二等）。
 优化器的经验：只要你有质量良好、结构清晰的数据（10-100个输入输出对），优化效果就很显著。优化器不仅能提升整体分数，还能按指标分解，帮助你理解模型的强项和弱项。
 优化器的输出是什么：优化器的输出本质上就是一个优化后的程序模块，你可以像使用其他模块一样保存、加载和调用它。其核心是一个被动态构建的、更优的提示词字符串。
 优化器的工作原理：它本质上是LLM引导的，即用AI来构建AI。它通过分析失败案例，发现你没有明说的潜在要求（如“名字必须大写”），并将其添加到提示词中。
 成本与上下文管理：


  成本：DSPy本身不昂贵，成本取决于你调用了多少次LLM。虽然签名会增加一些提示词长度，但这通常不是主要的成本驱动因素。
  长上下文：如果你担心长上下文带来的成本和性能问题，可以在程序或适配器中加入上下文压缩的逻辑。演讲者认为，随着模型上下文窗口越来越大，这个问题未来可能会被抽象掉。
 持续学习：可以将用户反馈（如点赞/点踩）收集起来，加入到训练数据集中，然后定期重新运行优化器，实现离线版本的持续优化。
 总结：DSPy为你提供了构建任意复杂工作流所需的基本构件（primitives）。它让你能够构建模块化、可组合的系统，并且拥有自动优化的能力。

articles.title: Why copying AI answers into Word still breaks (and how I built a client-side converter for LaTeX & tables)
articles.description:
Live Tool:​ https://aitoword.online/en/
If you only work in Markdown, copying responses from ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek is trivial. You click the copy button, paste it into Obsidian, VS Code, or Notion, and everything renders as expected.
The problem starts when you have to hand off a deliverable to someone who lives in Microsoft Word—a client report, a lab assignment, or internal documentation.
Depending on how you copy an AI response into Word, you usually hit one of three failure modes:
Highlighting and copying from the browser UI: Word inherits the web page's inline CSS. You get dark or gray background shading behind every paragraph, mismatched font sizes, and broken table widths.
Clicking the AI's "Copy" button and pasting into Word: Because the clipboard contains raw Markdown, Word treats # headings, ** bold markers, and | table pipes as literal characters.
The LaTeX math wall: ChatGPT and DeepSeek frequently wrap inline and block equations in \(...\) and \[...\] (or $...$ and $$...$$). Pasting these into Word leaves you with raw TeX strings. Worse, many online converters rasterize equations into static PNG images, meaning you cannot fix a single subscript in Word without re-generating the whole document.
To solve this without installing a local Pandoc + LaTeX toolchain on every machine, I built Aitoword—a free, browser-based converter that turns AI Markdown and supported LaTeX into editable .docx files entirely on the client side.
Here is a breakdown of the formatting problems it solves, how the in-browser pipeline works, and the trade-offs involved.
Standard Markdown math parsers usually look for $...$ and $$...$$. However, most LLMs default to LaTeX-style \(...\) and \[...\] delimiters unless explicitly prompted otherwise.
A naive regex replacement across the whole document will accidentally corrupt escaped brackets inside fenced code blocks or inline code spans (for example, array indexing or regex literals in JavaScript).
Before building the .docx document tree, the parser has to isolate code blocks and inline code tokens first, and only normalize math delimiters in prose nodes:
function normalizeMathOutsideCode(markdown) {
  // Split by fenced code blocks and inline code spans first
  const segments = markdown.split(/(```
{% endraw %}
[\s\S]*?
{% raw %}


|[^\n]+`)/g);
return segments
  return segment
    // Convert \[ ... \] display math to $$ ... $$
    .replace(/\\\[([\s\S]*?)\\\]/g, (_, expr) => `$$${expr}$$`)
    // Convert \( ... \) inline math to $ ... $
    .replace(/\\\(([\s\S]*?)\\\)/g, (_, expr) => `$${expr}$`);
})
.join('');

}

Once normalized, supported expressions (fractions, roots, subscripts/superscripts, sums, integrals, and basic matrices) are parsed via KaTeX into MathML and mapped into OMML (Office Math Markup Language)​.
When you paste a raw Markdown table into Word, you get lines of pipe characters (|). When you copy an HTML table from a chat window, column widths often overflow the page margins.
Headings (H1–H6) map to native Word heading styles, so they immediately show up in Word's Navigation Pane and can be used to generate an automatic Table of Contents.

Many "free online document converters" work by uploading your text or .md file to a backend server, running a Python or LibreOffice worker, and returning a download link. articles.title: 2026 Node.js Summarize Text API Chat Completions Example for Support Answers
articles.description:
Short answer: for a support agent answering from a private knowledge base, the difficult part is not producing a shorter paragraph. It is producing a valid, bounded answer that preserves the facts the agent is allowed to use. Put that contract in the prompt and application validation, call a chat-completions endpoint, use a temperature around 0.3 to 0.5, and reject output that cannot be parsed. For basic summarization, gpt-4o-mini is a reasonable starting point.
A summary that drops a refund restriction is a data-layer defect wearing a language-model costume.
The model should summarize only supplied passages, preserve restrictions and dates, distinguish an explicit answer from missing information, and return fields that a Node.js service can validate before the result reaches an agent. A useful shape is answer, key_facts, missing_information, and source_ids; it is more useful than asking for “a concise summary” and hoping the prose is safe.
The system prompt should say what to do when retrieval does not answer the question. “I do not have enough information in the supplied knowledge base” is a successful result when the alternative is an invented policy. Determinism helps, but it is not correctness. Validation and retrieval boundaries still carry the load.
The request pattern below uses the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions shape, reads the key and endpoint from the environment, checks HTTP status, parses choices[0].message.content, and retries 429 responses with Retry-After. The same body can be sent from a Node.js openai client or with fetch; the contract is the part worth preserving.
import json
import os
import time
from urllib import request, error


def summarize(question, passages):
    payload = {
        "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash",
        "temperature": 0.4,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": (
                "Summarize only the supplied knowledge-base passages. "
                "Preserve restrictions, dates, and exceptions. Return JSON "
                "with answer, key_facts, missing_information, and source_ids. "
                "If the passages do not answer the question, say so."
            )},
            {"role": "user", "content": json.dumps({
                "question": question, "passages": passages
            })},
        ],
    }
    req = request.Request(
        os.environ["CHAT_COMPLETIONS_URL"],
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected HTTP status: {response.status}")
                result = json.loads(response.read())
            summary = json.loads(result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
            required = ("answer", "key_facts", "missing_information", "source_ids")
            for field in required:
                if field not in summary:
                    raise ValueError(f"missing output field: {field}")
            return summary
        except error.HTTPError as exc:
            if exc.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            time.sleep(float(exc.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt)))
    raise RuntimeError("summary request exhausted retries")

In production, keep the parsed object behind a schema validator and attach retrieved document identifiers before displaying the answer. Do not treat a model-generated source_ids field as proof of citation; compare it with identifiers actually passed to the model.
I think about this as a storage problem before I think about it as a prompt problem. The passages are durable inputs, the summary is a derived record, and the contract is the index that makes the record usable. Store the question, retrieval IDs, model name, prompt version, temperature, raw response, parsed response, and validation result together. A text blob called summary will not explain what was supplied when an answer is challenged.
There is a trade-off. Raw responses improve auditability and replay, but increase retention and access exposure; parsed fields reduce exposure, but make prompt regressions harder to investigate. For customer support, retain both under the same access policy and apply retention to the support record. The knowledge base is private, so a public object URL or public-read storage policy is out of bounds.
Streaming improves perceived responsiveness, but partial JSON is not a valid final record. Buffer the stream, parse it once complete, and publish only after validation. A half-emitted answer is a UI event, not a support record.
The vendor is only one part of the decision. The output contract, data boundary, operational controls, and client portability matter just as much. These are real options, but their semantics differ, so an adapter should own the differences.



Option
Useful fit
Constraint




OpenAI chat completions
Familiar message API and a practical starting point for basic summaries
Validate structured output in the application


Anthropic Messages API
Existing Anthropic integration or prompt format
Different message contract requires an adapter and separate tests


Google Gemini API
Teams already using Gemini models and response configuration
Request configuration is not a drop-in chat-completions swap


Infrai OpenAI-compatible surface
One key and one bill for backend services, with a plain REST surface
Transcription is unavailable, voice sessions are pending and Western-region only, and there is no dedicated moderation endpoint



The last row is a fit judgment, not an endorsement. One credential and billing surface can reduce operational sprawl, but it does not remove capability-readiness checks. For summarization, keep the integration narrow and verify the selected model through the model listing.
I would not choose a provider because one manual response sounds polished. Run a fixed corpus containing refusal cases, missing-policy cases, and exception-heavy answers. Compare schema-valid rate, preserved constraints, and reviewer corrections. Those signals map to the job.
Begin in shadow mode: retrieve the same passages, generate a candidate, validate it, and show it only to reviewers. Log invalid JSON, missing fields, unsupported claims, omitted restrictions, and retrieval mismatches. Five categories make a first dashboard useful without pretending one score explains the system.
Version the prompt and output schema. When either changes, compare new results with stored cases before changing the default. If a request is retried after a timeout, use an idempotency key derived from the question, retrieval snapshot, and prompt version; otherwise one question can produce several records that appear independent.
Keep a human path for incomplete results. The model can summarize evidence; it cannot turn absent policy into policy.
References used:
OpenAI, “Batch API guide”: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch

OpenAI, “Structured outputs”: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs

Anthropic, “Messages API”: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages

Google Gemini API, “Structured output”: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output

JSON Schema specification: https://json-schema.org/specification

articles.title: How ATS Parsers Read Work Experience Dates, Career Gaps & Overlapping Roles (Greenhouse, Workday & iCIMS Breakdown)
articles.description:
When a software engineer or product manager with seven years of full-time experience gets auto-rejected within 90 seconds of applying for a role requiring "5+ years of experience," the culprit is rarely their skill set. In our audits at Smart Resume Analyzer, date-span tokenization failure is the single most common reason an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) miscalculates total Years of Experience (YoE).
Modern hiring platforms—including Workday, Greenhouse, iCIMS, Lever, and Oracle Taleo—do not read work history the way a human recruiter does. Before a recruiter sees your file, an extraction engine (Textkernel, Sovren, DaXtra, or HireAbility) converts your layout into a structured HR-XML or JSON payload. Every PositionHistory node requires an ISO-8601 StartDate and EndDate (YYYY-MM). If a date string fails regex tokenization, the parser defaults EndDate = StartDate (0 months) or drops the role's tenure.
Direct Answer: ATS parsers extract date ranges using strict regular expression tokenizers that expect explicit month-and-year pairs (MM/YYYY or MMM YYYY – Present) anchored on the same horizontal line as the job title or company name. Parsers convert each role into an ISO-8601 interval (YYYY-MM), merge overlapping intervals via interval-union math to prevent double-counting, and sum the non-overlapping months to compute total Years of Experience (YoE).
As covered in my guides on how ATS resume parsers work and how to pass them and resume formatting mistakes that break ATS parsing, document ingestion happens in four sequential stages:
1.
Test how enterprise parsers tokenize your timeline with our ATS Resume Checker and Online ATS Parser.

To understand why certain date formats fail, look at how commercial resume parsers tokenize date strings:
import re

MONTH_TOKEN = r"(?:Jan(?:uary)?|Feb(?:ruary)?|Mar(?:ch)?|Apr(?:il)?|May|Jun(?:e)?|Jul(?:y)?|Aug(?:ust)?|Sep(?:t(?:ember)?)?|Oct(?:ober)?|Nov(?:ember)?|Dec(?:ember)?|0?[1-9]|1[0-2])"
YEAR_TOKEN = r"(?:19[89]\d|20[0-3]\d)"
DATE_POINT = rf"(?:{MONTH_TOKEN}[\s/\.\-]+)?{YEAR_TOKEN}"
CURRENT_TOKEN = r"(?:Present|Current|Now)"
RANGE_SEP = r"(?:\s*(?:[\-–—]|to|through)\s*)"

ATS_DATE_RANGE_REGEX = re.compile(
    rf"\b(?P<start>{DATE_POINT}){RANGE_SEP}(?P<end>{DATE_POINT}|{CURRENT_TOKEN})\b",
    re.IGNORECASE
)

Commercial tokenizers inside Sovren, Textkernel, and Workday fail on four common date patterns:
1.
Day-Month-Year Slash Ambiguity (04/05/2022 - 08/11/2024): Including the day creates locale ambiguity between US (MM/DD/YYYY) and UK/EU (DD/MM/YYYY) formats.
Year-Only Spans (2023 – 2024): Conservative setups in Workday and iCIMS default missing months to 01 (2023-01 to 2024-01), silently shaving up to 11 months off your actual tenure.
Broken Date Block (Undercounts in Workday & Taleo):
Senior Backend Engineer | FinTech Core
'21 (Spring) — Current | Remote (US)
• Architected high-throughput payment ledger processing $1.4B annually.

Why it fails: The apostrophe year '21 combined with (Spring) breaks the StartDate regex token, resulting in 0.0 calculated years for your senior role.
Parser-Safe Date Block (100% Extraction Across All Major ATS Platforms):
FinTech Core — Remote, US
Senior Backend Engineer | March 2021 – Present
• Architected high-throughput payment ledger in Go and PostgreSQL, processing $1.4B in annual transaction volume at 99.995% availability.

Listing multiple promoted titles directly underneath one another without repeating the company context causes older parsers to bind only the first role's dates to the company header and merge the remaining titles into the bullet body.
Broken Stacked Promotion Block (Orphans Earlier Dates):
CloudScale Systems (Jan 2020 – Present)
Lead Platform Engineer
Senior DevOps Engineer
Site Reliability Engineer
• Scaled multi-region Kubernetes clusters from 40 to 320 nodes...

Parser-Safe Stacked Promotion Block (Clean Role-Level Chronology):
CloudScale Systems — Austin, TX
Lead Platform Engineer | June 2024 – Present
• Led a 9-engineer platform team managing multi-region Kubernetes clusters across 320 production nodes.

CloudScale Systems — Austin, TX
Senior DevOps Engineer | April 2022 – June 2024
• Reduced CI/CD deployment times by 64% (from 42 minutes to 15 minutes) by migrating 85 microservices to GitHub Actions.

CloudScale Systems — Austin, TX
Site Reliability Engineer | January 2020 – April 2022
• Automated Terraform provisioning and PagerDuty runbooks, cutting P1 incident MTTR from 48 minutes to 14 minutes.

Repeating the employer above each promoted title ensures every parser binds each tenure span cleanly (Jan 2020 – Present = 6 years, 10 months). For bullet writing, see how to write resume bullet points that quantify impact.
If you worked a full-time engineering job from January 2021 – Present while running a consulting practice from June 2022 – Present, enterprise ATS parsers prevent double-counting using Interval Union Normalization:
Full-Time Role:   [2021-01 ======================== 2026-10] (70 months)
Freelance Role:            [2022-06 =============== 2026-10] (53 months)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Merged Timeline:  [2021-01 ======================== 2026-10] (70 months net YoE)

Overlapping roles also risk Current-Title Overwrite: Greenhouse, iCIMS, and Lever populate Current Title from whichever Present role appears first. Always list your primary full-time Present role at the top and place concurrent consulting below it.
As shown in how to tell which ATS a job is using from the application link, each major ATS handles date normalization and career gaps differently:



ATS Platform
Parser Engine
Preferred Date Format
Overlapping Role Calculation
Career Gap Threshold
Multi-Column Risk




Greenhouse
Custom + Textkernel
MMM YYYY – Present
Deduplicates overlapping months; top Present role sets current title
Timeline highlights gaps >= 3 months

Moderate


Workday
Native + Sovren

MM/YYYY – MM/YYYY or MMM YYYY

Strict interval union; populates structured form fields
Flags gaps > 6 months if rule is active
High


iCIMS
HireAbility / Sovren
MMM YYYY – MMM YYYY
Calculates net non-overlapping YoE per skill cluster
Highlights gaps >= 6 months in summary
High


Lever
Lever Native Parser
MMM YYYY - Present
Merges overlapping calendar months for total YoE
Shows chronological list in UI
Low-Moderate


Oracle Taleo
Legacy Taleo
MM/YYYY - MM/YYYY
Truncates if YYYY-only dates or apostrophes ('22) are used
Flags unlabelled gaps > 90 days

Critical



You can test your resume against platform-specific rules using our Workday Resume Checker, Greenhouse Resume Checker, and iCIMS Resume Checker.
Most modern ATS configurations do not auto-reject on a chronological gap alone. Instead, an unlabelled career gap hurts you via Skill Recency Decay (engines like Sovren weight skills by the EndDate of the job where they were used) and visual gap alerts in the recruiter UI.
Never try to hide a gap by switching your resume to Year-Only Dates (2023 – 2025). Instead, if a gap exceeds 6 months, include a clean 1-line entry explaining the period constructively:
Independent Technical Sabbatical & Cloud Architecture Study — Remote
Career Break (AWS Solutions Architect Professional Certification & Open-Source) | May 2024 – November 2024
• Completed AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional (SAP-C02) and contributed 14 merged PRs to open-source Go observability tooling.

[ ] Standardize Every Date to MMM YYYY or MMMM YYYY: Use Mar 2022 – Present consistently across every role and degree.
[ ] Use Only Present or Current for Active Roles: Avoid ambiguous phrases like To Date or Ongoing.
[ ] Keep Dates on the Same Horizontal Line as Title or Company: Never put dates inside a narrow left-hand table column.
[ ] Repeat Company Names for Stacked Promotions: Ensure every promoted title has its own explicit MMM YYYY – MMM YYYY range.
[ ] Order Concurrent Present Roles with Your Full-Time Role First: Prevent side projects from overwriting your Current Title.
[ ] Include Explicit Months on Internships & Short Contracts: Writing May 2024 – August 2024 credits the full 4 months instead of 0.
[ ] Verify Your Parsed YoE Output Before Applying: Run your file through the Smart Resume Analyzer ATS Resume Checker.
MM/YYYY (03/2022) or MMM YYYY (Mar 2022) better for ATS parsing?


Both parse with >99% accuracy across Workday, Greenhouse, iCIMS, Lever, and Taleo, but MMM YYYY (Mar 2022 – Present) is preferred because it eliminates numeric slash ambiguity and reads faster during a human hiring manager scan.
Most parsers sum all roles inside Work Experience unless the section is titled Internships, though enterprise Workday and iCIMS setups often filter for post-graduation experience using your bachelor's degree completion year.
If you graduated within the last 8–10 years, include May 2018 so the ATS anchors your post-graduation timeline.
Two-column table layouts or dates placed on a floating line above the company name cause PDF coordinate streams to bind the date of Job #2 to the bottom of Job #1.
Combine the tenure under the permanent employer and note the conversion on the title line: Senior Frontend Engineer (Contract-to-Hire) | February 2023 – Present.
—), en-dash (–), or hyphen (-) between dates?


All three parse cleanly as long as you put a single space on both sides of the dash (Mar 2022 – Oct 2026) and avoid custom Canva/Figma ligature glyphs.

Moonshot expone K3.1 Pro a través de tres superficies de API. Elige la que tu biblioteca cliente o agente ya utilice; el modelo, la clave y la facturación son los mismos en las tres.



Interfaz
Formato
Endpoint
Cliente típico




Chat Completions
OpenAI
https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/chat/completions
SDK openai, la mayoría de frameworks


Responses API
OpenAI Responses
https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/responses
Codex (wire_api = "responses")


Messages API
Anthropic
https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic/v1/messages
SDK de Anthropic, Claude Code



Se diferencian en cómo se establece el TTL de la caché y dónde se registra el uso (ver el almacenamiento en caché más abajo). ¿Vienes de K3? Nuestra guía de la API de Kimi K3 sigue siendo válida; K3.1 Pro es un K3 post-entrenado con el mismo contexto de 1.048.576 tokens.
Necesitas una cuenta con saldo y una clave del producto correcto. Cuatro pasos:
Recarga al menos 1 $ en la plataforma Kimi API. K3.1 Pro es un modelo insignia y solo se desbloquea tras una recarga correcta.
Crea una clave en la consola de claves de API y expórtala como MOONSHOT_API_KEY.
Confirma que el modelo es visible para esa clave con GET /v1/models.
Llama a kimi-k3.1-pro desde el código.




curl https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MOONSHOT_API_KEY" | grep -o '"kimi-k3.1-pro[^"]*"'

Si el modelo no aparece en la lista, soluciona eso primero. Kimi API, Kimi Code y Kimi Membership son productos distintos: una clave de Kimi Code no funcionará en el endpoint de la API, y una membresía no se convierte en saldo de API.
La mayoría de los parámetros de OpenAI se comportan como esperas. Estos son los que difieren o suelen pillar desprevenido a la gente:



Parámetro
Qué hay que saber




reasoning_effort
Campo de nivel superior: "low", "high" o "max" (por defecto "max"). El razonamiento siempre está activado.


thinking
No lo envíes. K3.1 Pro no lo admite; usa reasoning_effort en su lugar.


max_completion_tokens
Por defecto 131072. La salida máxima es 1.048.576 menos tus tokens de prompt.


response_format

json_schema con strict: true. Analiza solo message.content, nunca reasoning_content.


partial
Pon "partial": true en un mensaje final del asistente para continuar desde un prefijo.


tool_choice

"required" fuerza al menos una llamada a herramienta; "auto" deja que el modelo decida.


prompt_cache_options

{"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "5m" o "1h"} en Chat Completions y Responses.



Los tokens de razonamiento cuentan para tu uso, así que usa "low" para clasificación y extracción. El razonamiento preservado siempre está activado, por lo que cada mensaje del asistente vuelve con su reasoning_content intacto (guía de modelos con razonamiento).
Un bucle de herramientas de producción en K3.1 Pro sigue cuatro reglas de la documentación de Moonshot:
Fuerza una llamada a herramienta en el primer turno con tool_choice="required" y luego cambia a "auto".
Añade el mensaje completo del asistente, incluidos reasoning_content y tool_calls.
Envía un mensaje tool por cada tool_call_id.
Limita el número de turnos para que un modelo confundido no pueda entrar en un bucle infinito.




import json, os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI([REDACTED CREDENTIAL],
                base_url="https://api.moonshot.ai/v1")

TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "get_order_status",
    "description": "Look up an order's shipping status by ID",
    "parameters": {"type": "object",
                   "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                   "required": ["order_id"]}}}]

def get_order_status(order_id):
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order A-1042?"}]
tool_choice = "required"
for _ in range(8):  # hard cap on turns
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k3.1-pro", reasoning_effort="high",
        messages=messages, tools=TOOLS, tool_choice=tool_choice)
    msg = resp.choices[0].message
    messages.append(msg)  # whole message, not msg.content
    if not msg.tool_calls:
        print(msg.content)
        break
    for call in msg.tool_calls:
        result = get_order_status(**json.loads(call.function.arguments))
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                         "content": json.dumps(result)})
    tool_choice = "auto"

El error clásico es añadir msg.content en lugar de msg, lo que descarta tool_calls y reasoning_content.
Cuando tu agente tiene decenas o cientos de herramientas, no envíes todas las definiciones en cada solicitud. La buena práctica de llamada a herramientas de K3 de Moonshot recomienda este flujo:
Declara una función search_tools (tu backend la implementa) más unas pocas herramientas principales.
Establece tool_choice: "required" en el primer turno para que el modelo recupere antes de responder.
Inyecta las definiciones de herramientas coincidentes mediante un mensaje system que lleve un campo tools.
Deja que el modelo llame a las herramientas cargadas en turnos posteriores, con tool_choice de nuevo en "auto".




# after search_tools returns ["create_github_pr"]
messages.append({"role": "system",
                 "tools": [CATALOG["create_github_pr"]]})

Las definiciones inyectadas usan el formato tools de nivel superior y se aplican a partir de ese mensaje. El servidor no las conserva, así que mantén el mensaje en solicitudes posteriores. Ni cambiar tool_choice ni añadir una definición rompe la caché de prefijo.
K3.1 Pro acepta imágenes y vídeo junto con texto y devuelve texto. Convierte content en un array de partes: una parte image_url (el ejemplo del inicio rápido envía una URL de datos en base64 y señala que las URL de imágenes públicas no son compatibles) o una parte video_url que apunta a un archivo subido con un ID ms://.
from pathlib import Path

video = client.files.create(file=Path("demo.mp4"), purpose="video")
content = [{"type": "video_url", "video_url": {"url": f"ms://{video.id}"}},
           {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this video."}]

Pasa content como mensaje del usuario y elimina el archivo con client.files.delete(video.id) cuando termines.
El almacenamiento en caché es automático para prefijos repetidos con un TTL predeterminado de 5 minutos. Los aciertos de caché se facturan a 0,20 $ por millón de tokens frente a 2,00 $ para la entrada no cacheada, y una escritura de 1 hora cuesta 4,00 $ frente a 2,00 $ por 5 minutos. En un prefijo de 1 M de tokens, el TTL de 1 hora se amortiza tras dos aciertos.
Coloca primero el contenido estable (prompt de sistema, definiciones de herramientas, documentación), el contenido cambiante al final, y sin marcas de tiempo en el prefijo. Con el SDK openai, pasa el TTL a través de extra_body:
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k3.1-pro",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": DOCS},
              {"role": "user", "content": question}],
    extra_body={"prompt_cache_options": {"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "1h"}},
)
d = resp.usage.prompt_tokens_details
print(resp.usage.prompt_tokens, d.cached_tokens,
      getattr(d, "cache_write_tokens", 0))

La API de Anthropic establece el TTL con un campo cache_control de nivel superior; los marcadores dentro de los mensajes se ignoran:
curl https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic/v1/messages \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MOONSHOT_API_KEY" \
  --data '{"model": "kimi-k3.1-pro", "max_tokens": 256,
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"},
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'

Dónde aparece el uso de la caché depende de la interfaz:



Interfaz
Lectura de caché
Escritura de caché




Chat Completions
usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens
usage.prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens


Responses
usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens
usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens


Messages
usage.cache_read_input_tokens
usage.cache_creation_input_tokens



Al hacer streaming de Chat Completions, establece stream_options.include_usage=true para obtener el uso en el fragmento final. Cada acierto renueva el TTL, que queda fijado en la primera escritura. Reglas completas: la guía de almacenamiento en caché de contexto.
La mayoría de los fallos se engloban en seis patrones. Comprueba error.type en cada 429, porque la solución depende de ello.



Síntoma
Causa
Solución




401 o 404
Clave de producto incorrecta, discrepancia de región, sin saldo o nombre de modelo incorrecto
Usa una clave de Kimi API, comprueba el saldo, confirma el modelo en GET /v1/models, limpia variables de entorno y proxies obsoletos


429 engine_overloaded_error

Capacidad del servidor
Espera según Retry-After, aplica retroceso, reduce la concurrencia. Recargar saldo no ayudará.


429 rate_limit_reached_error

Tu organización alcanzó los límites de concurrencia, RPM, TPM o TPD
Ve más despacio o sube de nivel


429 exceeded_current_quota_error

Saldo bajo, cuenta vencida o cupón caducado
Consulta la API de saldo y recarga


finish_reason: "length"
La salida alcanzó max_completion_tokens

Aumenta el límite o continúa con el modo partial


La misma herramienta se llama una y otra vez
Estructura de mensajes rota
Añade el mensaje tal cual, haz coincidir cada tool_call_id, ensambla por completo los tool_calls transmitidos y luego añade detección de repeticiones en el cliente



Cuidado con los reintentos. El SDK de OpenAI reintenta 2 veces de forma predeterminada ante errores de conexión, 408, 409, 429 y 5xx, así que una llamada puede convertirse en tres solicitudes contra tu RPM. En un nivel bajo, reduce el max_retries del cliente y aplica tú mismo el retroceso según error.type. Las solicitudes interrumpidas por un 429 no se cobran.
Si un agente de terceros falla, llama a la API directamente con la misma clave, endpoint y modelo. Si eso funciona, el problema es la herramienta. Consulta la página de solución de problemas y los códigos de error.
Tu recarga acumulada determina tu nivel en la página de límites:



Nivel
Recarga acumulada
Concurrencia
RPM
TPM




Tier0
$1
1
3
500.000 (1,5 M al día)


Tier1
$10

100
2.000.000


Tier2
$20

3.000.000


Tier3
$100

3.000.000


Tier4
$1,000

Tier5
$3,000

El nivel Tier0 permite 3 solicitudes por minuto, y cada turno de un bucle de herramientas es una solicitud. Una ejecución de agente de cinco turnos ya supera un minuto en ese nivel, así que presupuesta 10 $ acumulados antes de probar agentes en serio.
Una prueba de contrato detecta el día en que tu bucle de herramientas deja de recibir tool_calls. Deja que tu agente de programación la construya con Apidog CLI. Instala e inicia sesión una vez:
npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
apidog skill install

Luego indica a Claude Code, Codex o el agente que uses:
In Apidog project <projectId>, create an environment for https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
and an endpoint for POST /chat/completions. Add a test case that sends model
kimi-k3.1-pro, reasoning_effort "low", one get_order_status tool and
tool_choice "required". Assert status 200 and that choices[0].message.tool_calls
is non-empty. Run it and report failures.

El agente lee el esquema, valida su payload y ejecuta el caso:
apidog environment create kimi-prod --project <projectId> --base-url https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file ./endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

Los casos de prueba necesitan una categoría válida; apidog test-case category --project <projectId> las lista. Una vez que la ejecución pase, cambia -r cli,json por -r junit con --out-dir y la misma comprobación controlará tu CI, como muestra nuestra guía de CI/CD con Apidog CLI. La configuración del agente está en Apidog CLI en Claude Code. El plan gratuito de Apidog cubre hasta 4 usuarios.
  
  



  
  
  Preguntas frecuentes



  
  
  ¿Cuál es la URL base de la API de Kimi K3.1 Pro?


https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 para Chat Completions y la API de Responses, y https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic para la API de Messages compatible con Anthropic.
thinking?


No. El razonamiento siempre está activado. Contrólalo con el campo reasoning_effort de nivel superior ("low", "high" o "max").
Lee error.type. engine_overloaded_error es capacidad del servidor y una recarga no lo solucionará. rate_limit_reached_error significa los límites de tu nivel, y Tier0 solo permite 3 RPM.
Un campo de lectura de caché distinto de cero en usage significa un acierto: prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens en Chat Completions o cache_read_input_tokens en Messages.
No. La API requiere una recarga mínima de 1 $. El chat gratuito en la app de Kimi es la vía de 0 $, tratada en cómo usar Kimi K3.1 Pro gratis. Para conocer el modelo, consulta qué es Kimi K3.1 Pro.

articles.title: A beginner's guide to the Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized model by Abenzerps on Huggingface
articles.description:
This is a simplified guide to an AI model called Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized maintained by Abenzerps. If you like these kinds of analysis, you should join AImodels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized is a set of quantized local image-generation weights based on the upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 model. Maintained by abenzerps, it provides GGUF, Safetensors, and Apple Silicon–oriented MLX files for use with ComfyUI. Its defining practical feature is the absence of a built-in safety checker or content filter: prompts can produce adult, NSFW, and sensitive imagery without refusals or blacked-out outputs. The README does not specify the model architecture beyond identifying it as an image-generation model, nor does it give a parameter count, training data, training steps, output resolution, or measured generation speed. Plan around the full component set, not just the diffusion file: ComfyUI also needs a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder and a VAE. The repository reports 2,188,658 downloads, but that figure does not establish image quality or performance.
Local generation of adult or sensitive imagery. The release explicitly removes built-in safety filtering, so it suits workflows where a safety checker would block intended prompts. That also means the operator is responsible for prompt handling, access controls, and compliance with applicable laws and platform rules.
ComfyUI workflows with limited GPU memory. The GGUF options include a 4.60 GB Q4_K_M diffusion file, and the README recommends keeping the diffusion model in GPU VRAM while running or offloading the text encoder to system RAM. This separates the component that runs during sampling from text encoding, which runs once per prompt.
Apple Silicon image-generation setups. The repository includes MLX 4-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit variants, described as optimized for Apple Silicon. These provide a platform-specific option rather than requiring a GGUF or GPU-oriented Safetensors file.
Local experimentation across quality and memory tradeoffs. The available formats range from 4.00 GB MLX 4-bit and 4.05 GB base Q4_0 GGUF to 14.23 GB BF16 GGUF. This lets practitioners compare quantization levels in their own workflow, though the README provides no measured quality or speed results for each variant.
Text-to-image and image-editing workflows in ComfyUI. The README points to official Comfy-Org templates for both tasks. It does not provide task-specific benchmark scores, so test the intended prompts and edit cases before relying on it in production.
The README does not report output resolution, parameter count, training data, training compute, inference speed, or benchmark methodology. The benchmark image is provided, but no numerical results or hardware details accompany it. Do not infer a resolution, quality level, or generation time from the file sizes.
The smallest diffusion files reduce storage and memory needs, but quantization can involve quality tradeoffs; the repository recommends Q4_K_M as a size-quality balance for GGUF without publishing comparative measurements. The full setup also has substantial memory and storage demands: the text encoder is 17.53 GB in BF16 or 9.35 GB in INT8, and the VAE is 676 MB. The recommended lower-memory arrangement places the INT8 text encoder in system RAM and the Q4_K_M diffusion model in VRAM. The README’s description of this as saving “9–17 GB” of VRAM is consistent with the listed encoder sizes; it does not give a minimum system RAM or GPU VRAM requirement.
The model has no built-in content filter. That is a deliberate property, not a guarantee that every prompt will produce a particular result. The README does not document other known image-quality failure modes, biases, or safety mitigations.
The stated license is the Qwen Research License, described in the repository as “other.” The provided information does not establish commercial-use rights or the license terms, so review the license before commercial deployment.
Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF is the better fit if you want the same upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 base weights in GGUF without choosing this release’s explicitly uncensored package. This model is the clearer choice when the absence of a built-in safety checker is a requirement and when you want additional formats such as Safetensors and MLX; the supplied information does not provide measured speed or quality differences between them. The alternative’s notice says a fully uncensored version is in development, so check its current status before choosing it for an uncensored workflow.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Abenzerps-GGUF is another GGUF distribution of uncensored Qwen-Image-2.1 weights. Choose this model if you need the documented Safetensors or MLX variants, companion text encoder and VAE files, and ComfyUI setup guidance in one repository; choose the alternative if its distribution better matches your existing GGUF workflow. The provided information does not establish a quality, speed, or cost advantage for either distribution.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-GGUF is another uncensored GGUF option based on the same upstream model. This repository is a stronger fit when you want multiple non-GGUF quantization formats and explicit companion-file instructions. The alternative’s notice reports a Q8_0 tensor shape mismatch in ComfyUI during sampling and recommends Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, or Q6_K instead; the supplied information does not confirm whether that issue applies to this model’s Q8_0 file.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-GGUF is also described as an uncensored GGUF distribution using the upstream base weights. Pick this model for the documented MLX and Safetensors choices, or the alternative if its repository and files suit your existing setup. No comparative benchmark, inference-speed, or cost data is provided, so there is no supported basis to claim that one produces better images or runs faster.
Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF targets low-VRAM ComfyUI use with GGUF quantizations and describes its quantization as reducing memory pressure while preserving detail, composition, and prompt alignment. This model is the better fit when you need an explicitly uncensored release and Apple Silicon MLX or Safetensors options; the alternative may suit a workflow centered on its stated low-VRAM GGUF profile. The supplied information does not provide comparable hardware tests or measured quality results.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized packages quantized versions of the upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 weights. The source revision is b3179ad355be050328e483a9dfdd9e60cd62adfa. The README identifies conversion using stable-diffusion.cpp commit 1330cebae8f2ba99249df846cc0c9444fcbd4308 and comfy-kitchen. The text encoder and VAE source is Comfy-Org/Qwen-Image-2.1. The stated license is the Qwen Research License.
Available uncensored diffusion files:



Format or quantization
File size




BF16 GGUF
14.23 GB


FP8 Safetensors
6.63 GB


INT8 ConvRot Safetensors
6.76 GB


NVFP4 Safetensors
4.20 GB


MLX 4-bit Safetensors
4.00 GB


MLX 6-bit Safetensors
5.78 GB


MLX 8-bit Safetensors
7.56 GB


Q8_0 GGUF
7.59 GB


Q6_K GGUF
5.88 GB


Q5_K_M GGUF
5.22 GB


Q4_K_M GGUF
4.60 GB


Q4_0 GGUF
4.15 GB



The repository also lists non-UC GGUF files: Q8_0 at 7.59 GB, Q6_K at 5.88 GB, Q5_K_M at 5.22 GB, Q4_K_M at 4.60 GB, and Q4_0 at 4.05 GB. It recommends Q4_K_M for the best balance of GGUF size and quality. It describes INT8 ConvRot and NVFP4 as high-performance options on supported GPUs, without naming supported GPU models or providing speed measurements. MLX files target Apple Silicon.
ComfyUI companion files are a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder in BF16 (17.53 GB) or INT8 ConvRot (9.35 GB), plus a BF16 VAE (676 MB). The README recommends the INT8 encoder for lower memory use. It suggests keeping the diffusion model in GPU VRAM and running or offloading the text encoder to system RAM; text encoding runs once per prompt. For VRAM out-of-memory errors, it recommends starting ComfyUI with --lowvram.
Supported workflow components include ComfyUI, the leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF custom node, ComfyUI’s UNETLoader, CLIPLoader, and VAELoader nodes, and official Comfy-Org text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates. For GGUF, use Unet Loader (GGUF); for Safetensors, use UNETLoader. Set the text encoder’s CLIPLoader type to qwen_image. The README warns that the older city96/ComfyUI-GGUF may produce an “Unknown model architecture!” error; it recommends the leejet fork or adding ModelQwenImage to tools/convert.py.
The README does not specify architecture details beyond the image-generation task, parameter count, training dataset, training steps, compute, maximum resolution, inference speed, or batch-size guidance.
Text prompts: The model is presented for text-to-image generation. The README does not specify prompt syntax, token limits, or supported languages.
Image inputs: An official image-edit workflow template is listed, but the README does not document accepted image formats, dimensions, or editing constraints.
Runtime components: A diffusion-model file, a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder, and a VAE are required for the documented ComfyUI setup. Choose a compatible diffusion quantization and encoder precision.
Generated images: The repository describes local image generation and provides text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates. It does not specify output resolution, image format, or post-processing requirements.
Content filtering: The release has no built-in safety checker or content filter; output behavior depends on prompts and the execution environment.
The README documents a ComfyUI workflow rather than a Python inference API, so it does not provide a supported Python model-loading or generation call. To run the documented setup, place the selected diffusion file in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/, the text encoder in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders/, and the VAE in ComfyUI/models/vae/. For example, use qwen-image-2.1-UC-Q4_K_M.gguf, qwen3vl_8b_int8_convrot.safetensors, and qwen_image_2.1_vae_bf16.safetensors.
Install the maintained ComfyUI-GGUF fork in ComfyUI/custom_nodes/:
cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes
git clone https://github.com/leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF

In ComfyUI, load the GGUF diffusion file with Unet Loader (GGUF). Load the text encoder with CLIPLoader and set its type to qwen_image; load the VAE with VAELoader. For a Safetensors diffusion file, use UNETLoader instead. If VRAM runs out, start ComfyUI with --lowvram. The README also points to official text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates.
Q: Can I use Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized commercially?
A: The repository states the Qwen Research License. The provided information does not specify commercial-use permissions, so review the license terms before commercial use.
Q: How much VRAM do I need to run it?
A: No minimum VRAM requirement is stated. The recommended setup uses a Q4_K_M diffusion file of about 4.6 GB in VRAM and an INT8 text encoder of about 9.35 GB in system RAM; the VAE is 676 MB. Use --lowvram if ComfyUI reports a VRAM out-of-memory error.
Q: Which quantization should I choose for ComfyUI?
A: The README recommends Q4_K_M as the best balance of GGUF size and quality. It lists Q4_K_M at 4.60 GB, Q5_K_M at 5.22 GB, Q6_K at 5.88 GB, and Q8_0 at 7.59 GB, but does not publish comparative quality or speed measurements.
Q: How does it compare with Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF for uncensored generation?
A: This release explicitly has no built-in safety checker or content filter. The similar model’s notice says a fully uncensored version is in development, so this release is the documented choice when uncensored behavior is required now; the supplied information does not establish a quality or speed difference.
Q: What are the known image-quality issues?
A: The README provides a benchmark image but no numerical results, documented failure modes, or output-resolution details. It recommends Q4_K_M for a GGUF size-quality balance, but does not quantify quality loss across quantizations.
Q: Can I fine-tune this model?
A: The README documents quantized files for local inference through ComfyUI, not a fine-tuning workflow. It does not specify fine-tuning support or a training framework.
Q: How fast is inference, and what batch size should I use?
A: The README gives no inference-time, throughput, or batch-size measurements. It says to keep the diffusion model in GPU VRAM because speed matters during sampling, and to run or offload the text encoder to system RAM because it encodes once per prompt.
Q: Does the model filter NSFW prompts?
A: No. The release has no built-in safety checker or content filter and can generate adult, NSFW, and sensitive imagery without prompt refusals or blacked-out images.
Click here to read the full guide to Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized

articles.title: Taming SQLAlchemy Implicit Flushes: Mitigating Unexpected Deadlocks and Serialization Failures Under High Concurrency
articles.description:
Taming SQLAlchemy Implicit Flushes: Mitigating Unexpected Deadlocks and Serialization Failures Under High Concurrency


Database deadlocks in high-throughput applications are rarely the result of overt logic errors. In many Python services built on SQLAlchemy, they stem from an ergonomic feature operating silently in the background: implicit autoflush. 
When building high-concurrency microservices, developers often focus on choosing between optimistic locking (version checking) and pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). However, if your ORM flushes state to the database at unpredictable junctures, your locking sequence will invert, holding exclusive row locks far longer than anticipated and triggering deadlocks (OperationalError: DeadlockDetected or database-specific errors like PostgreSQL's 40P01 / MySQL's 1213).
This article analyzes how SQLAlchemy’s implicit autoflush triggers concurrency collisions, details an architectural pattern incorporating explicit flush boundaries, Pydantic v2 data validation, and jittered exponential backoff, and provides a deep dive into environment diagnostics and production infrastructure readiness.
By default, SQLAlchemy initializes its Session with autoflush=True. Under this setting, whenever a read query—such as session.execute(select(...)) or session.scalars(...)—is evaluated, SQLAlchemy inspects the session’s internal Identity Map for dirty or pending objects. If modified state exists in memory, SQLAlchemy silently executes an intermediate session.flush() before dispatching the SELECT query.
flowchart TD
    subgraph ClientSession ["Client Application Session"]
        A["Step 1: Mutate Model A in Memory"]
        B["Step 2: Run SELECT query for Model B"]
        C["Step 3: Mutate Model B"]
        D["Step 4: Explicit Commit"]
    end

    subgraph DatabaseEngine ["RDBMS (PostgreSQL / MySQL)"]
        E["Row A: Locked via Implicit Flush (UPDATE)"]
        F["Read Query Executed"]
        G["Row B: Locked (UPDATE)"]
        H["Transaction Completed (RELEASE ALL LOCKS)"]
    end

    A -- "Object marked dirty" --> B
    B -. "Implicit Autoflush triggered before SELECT" .-> E
    E -- "Proceed with read" --> F
    F --> C
    C --> D
    D -- "Flush remaining & COMMIT" --> G
    G --> H
This implicit behavior introduces three severe concurrency pitfalls:
Premature Row Lock Acquisition: Exclusive row-level locks (UPDATE / INSERT) are claimed earlier in the transaction lifecycle than expected, holding locks during subsequent computation or querying phases.
Lock Order Inversion: When two concurrent threads (Worker 1 and Worker 2) process overlapping entities, an uncoordinated implicit flush will alter the physical SQL execution order, resulting in circular wait conditions (deadlock).
Traceback Obfuscation: The resulting OperationalError does not fail at session.commit(), but rather at an innocuous session.scalars(select(...)) query, baffling engineers during incident triage.
To eliminate non-deterministic locking and build a resilient persistence layer, we adopt three design constraints:
Explicit Flush Control (autoflush=False): Disable automatic flushes at the session maker level. State transitions must cross the persistence boundary strictly when explicitly designated via session.flush() or session.commit().
Strict Domain Validation via Pydantic v2: Enforce model invariants, version checks, and serialization boundaries prior to modifying ORM entities in memory.
Resilient Retry Loop with Truncated Exponential Backoff & Full Jitter: Intercept database-level transient contention (OperationalError) and retry the entire transaction boundary with decorrelated delay patterns.
Below is the complete, self-contained verification script implementing these architectural requirements. It defines domain schemas with Pydantic v2 (featuring automated serialization fallback for high-performance orjson), explicit SQLAlchemy ORM models, transaction boundary managers, and a decorated retry mechanism with jittered backoff.
import time
import random
import logging
from typing import Generator, Dict, Any
from contextlib import contextmanager

try:
    import orjson
    HAS_ORJSON = True
except ImportError:
    import json
    HAS_ORJSON = False

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker, Session
from sqlalchemy.exc import OperationalError

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class AccountPayload(BaseModel):
    account_id: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    balance: int = Field(..., ge=0)
    version: int = Field(..., ge=0)

    def serialize(self) -> bytes:
        data_dict = self.model_dump()
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            return orjson.dumps(data_dict)
        else:
            return json.dumps(data_dict).encode("utf-8")

    @classmethod
    def deserialize(cls, data: bytes) -> "AccountPayload":
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            parsed = orjson.loads(data)
        else:
            parsed = json.loads(data.decode("utf-8"))
        return cls.model_validate(parsed)

    @classmethod
    def decode_to_dict(cls, data: bytes) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            return orjson.loads(data)
        else:
            return json.loads(data.decode("utf-8"))

Base = declarative_base()

class AccountModel(Base):
    __tablename__ = "accounts"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    balance = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)
    version = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)

DATABASE_URL = "sqlite:///:memory:"
engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL, echo=False, future=True)

# Session configured with autoflush=False to prevent mid-transaction implicit locks
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    class_=Session,
    autoflush=False,
    autocommit=False,
    expire_on_commit=False
)

def init_db():
    Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)
    with SessionLocal() as session:
        acc1 = AccountModel(id=1, balance=1000, version=0)
        acc2 = AccountModel(id=2, balance=1000, version=0)
        session.add_all([acc1, acc2])
        session.commit()

@contextmanager
def get_session() -> Generator[Session, None, None]:
    session = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield session
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        session.close()

def update_account_with_retry(account_id: int, amount: int, max_retries: int = 3) -> None:
    attempt = 0
    while attempt < max_retries:
        attempt += 1
        try:
            with get_session() as session:
                stmt = select(AccountModel).filter_by(id=account_id)
                account = session.scalars(stmt).first()

                if not account:
                    raise ValueError(f"Account {account_id} not found")

                payload = AccountPayload(
                    account_id=account.id,
                    balance=account.balance,
                    version=account.version
                )

                new_balance = payload.balance + amount
                if new_balance < 0:
                    raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")

                account.balance = new_balance
                account.version += 1

                # Explicitly flush changes to the DB when the domain state is complete
                session.flush()
                logger.info(f"Successfully updated Account {account_id}: new balance = {new_balance}")
                return

        except OperationalError as e:
            logger.warning(
                f"Lock conflict/deadlock detected on attempt {attempt}/{max_retries} for account {account_id}: {e}"
            )
            if attempt >= max_retries:
                logger.error(f"Max retries reached for account {account_id}. Aborting.")
                raise
            # Exponential Backoff with Jitter
            sleep_time = (2 ** attempt) + (random.randint(0, 1000) / 1000.0)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

def run_verification():
    init_db()
    logger.info("Database initialized with test data.")

    update_account_with_retry(account_id=1, amount=500)
    update_account_with_retry(account_id=2, amount=-200)

    with SessionLocal() as session:
        acc1 = session.get(AccountModel, 1)
        acc2 = session.get(AccountModel, 2)

        p1 = AccountPayload(account_id=acc1.id, balance=acc1.balance, version=acc1.version)
        p2 = AccountPayload(account_id=acc2.id, balance=acc2.balance, version=acc2.version)

        logger.info(f"Final State Account 1: {AccountPayload.decode_to_dict(p1.serialize())}")
        logger.info(f"Final State Account 2: {AccountPayload.decode_to_dict(p2.serialize())}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_verification()

When executing verification scripts in fresh staging containers or CI environments, operations may fail immediately during bootstrap with an unhandled exception:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/phenox/gemini-sandbox/TOAI_Workspace/V2_SandBox/V2_PROD_20261025_051946_test.py", line 16, in <module>
    from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String, select
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sqlalchemy'

This failure is not a flaw in transaction semantics, ORM mapping, or deadlock resolution logic. It represents an environment provision failure: the runtime environment lacks the required distribution package (sqlalchemy). 
Notice how the script gracefully handles performance optimizations:
try:
    import orjson
    HAS_ORJSON = True
except ImportError:
    import json
    HAS_ORJSON = False

While application-level conditional imports (e.g., falling back from orjson to Python standard library json) protect optional accelerators, foundational dependencies such as SQLAlchemy and Pydantic cannot be treated as optional. When the base interpreter environment lacks these dependencies, execution halts during AST evaluation before a single line of business logic can run.
Preventing execution drift between development, CI, and production requires treating environment provisioning with the same rigor applied to SQL isolation levels.
requirements.txt)


Declare core dependencies with explicit minimum version constraints to guarantee SQLAlchemy 2.0+ query syntax (select(), session.scalars()) and Pydantic v2 compatibility:
sqlalchemy>=2.0.0
pydantic>=2.0.0
orjson>=3.0.0

For deterministic production deployments, utilize lockfiles pinned to exact hashes via tools like pip-tools, uv, or poetry:
# Generating locked requirements with hashes
uv pip compile requirements.in --generate-hashes -o requirements.txt

In continuous integration pipelines and test runners, dependency synchronization must precede script evaluation:
# Upgrade build tools and install pinned dependencies
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

In containerized architectures (Docker/Kubernetes), bake dependencies directly into the immutable base image:
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .
CMD ["python", "verification_script.py"]




Concern
Anti-Pattern
Recommended Solution




Session Flush Policy
Default autoflush=True triggering random intermediate flushes
Configure sessionmaker(..., autoflush=False) or isolate read blocks with session.no_autoflush



Lock Duration
In-memory mutations held while subsequent queries run
Defer mutations until required, execute explicitly via session.flush() directly before commit


Transient Contention
Raw failures on OperationalError deadlocks
Truncated exponential backoff with full jitter wrapped around the transaction boundary


Data Boundaries
Passing active ORM entities across external API boundaries
Validate and serialize via Pydantic v2 schemas (BaseModel) before and after persistence


Dependency Integrity
Ad-hoc package installations resulting in ModuleNotFoundError

Declarative dependency manifests (requirements.txt) enforced by automated containerized CI pipelines



Sophisticated transactional designs and concurrency controls cannot function without reproducible runtime environments. Ensuring strict synchronization between infrastructural manifests and transactional logic is essential for resilient, high-concurrency Python architectures.
