articles.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming with HLS, explained for web developers
articles.description:
Disclosure: I work at TPStreams, a video hosting and streaming platform. This post explains the general technique, which applies whichever provider (or none) you use.
If you've ever put an MP4 behind a <video> tag and watched it stall on a phone over 4G, you've hit the problem adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming solves. Here's how it works with HLS, the format you'll meet most often.
A single MP4 has one resolution and one bitrate. Encode it at 1080p and 5 Mbps and viewers on slow connections buffer; encode it at 480p and everyone on fibre gets a blurry picture. The network a viewer has at minute one is also not the network they have at minute ten.
ABR fixes this with two moves:
Encode several renditions of the same video, for example 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p and 1080p, each at a different bitrate.
Cut each rendition into short segments (typically 2 to 6 seconds) aligned at the same timestamps, so the player can switch rendition at any segment boundary.
The player measures how fast segments are downloading and picks the best rendition the connection can sustain, switching up or down as conditions change.
HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) describes all this with plain-text playlists (.m3u8).
The multivariant (master) playlist lists the renditions:
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1400000,RESOLUTION=854x480,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
1080p/index.m3u8

Each media playlist lists that rendition's segments:
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXT-X-MAP:URI="init.mp4"
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_0001.m4s
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_0002.m4s
#EXT-X-ENDLIST

Everything is served over ordinary HTTP, so any CDN can cache it. That is a big reason HLS won: no special streaming server is needed.
A minimal two-rendition ladder:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 \
  -filter_complex "[0:v]split=2[v1][v2];[v1]scale=-2:720[v720];[v2]scale=-2:360[v360]" \
  -map "[v720]" -c:v:0 libx264 -b:v:0 2800k -maxrate:v:0 3000k -bufsize:v:0 5600k \
  -map "[v360]" -c:v:1 libx264 -b:v:1 800k -maxrate:v:1 900k -bufsize:v:1 1600k \
  -map a:0 -map a:0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k \
  -g 48 -keyint_min 48 -sc_threshold 0 \
  -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 \
  -master_pl_name master.m3u8 \
  -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0 v:1,a:1" \
  out/%v/index.m3u8

The flags that matter most for ABR:
-g, -keyint_min and -sc_threshold 0 give a fixed keyframe interval (2 seconds at 24 fps here), so every rendition has keyframes at the same points. Without aligned keyframes, switching causes visible glitches.
-maxrate and -bufsize cap bitrate spikes, so the BANDWIDTH value the player relies on is honest.
-hls_time sets segment length. Shorter segments react faster to network changes but mean more requests.
Safari plays HLS natively. Elsewhere, use a library such as hls.js:
<video id="v" controls></video>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/hls.js@1"></script>
<script>
  const video = document.getElementById('v');
  const src = '/out/master.m3u8';
  if (video.canPlayType('application/vnd.apple.mpegurl')) {
    video.src = src;
  } else if (Hls.isSupported()) {
    const hls = new Hls();
    hls.loadSource(src);
    hls.attachMedia(video);
    hls.on(Hls.Events.LEVEL_SWITCHED, (_, d) =>
      console.log('Now playing level', d.level));
  }
</script>

Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, throttle to "Slow 4G", and you'll see the player drop to the 360p segments, then climb back up when you remove the throttle.
Unaligned keyframes across renditions (see above).
A ladder that's too sparse. Jumping straight from 360p to 1080p makes every switch obvious. Add steps in between.
No low rung. A 240p rendition at a few hundred kbps keeps mobile viewers watching instead of buffering.
Forgetting CORS on the CDN when the player page and the segments live on different domains.
Treating HLS as security. Splitting a video into segments does not stop downloading; tools reassemble HLS easily. Protection needs encryption, DRM (Widevine and FairPlay) and access tokens, which is a separate topic.
Running FFmpeg yourself is fine for a handful of videos. At scale you'll also need a job queue, storage, a CDN, captions, analytics and possibly DRM. Managed services such as Mux, Cloudflare Stream, Bunny Stream, Gumlet, VdoCipher, AWS Elemental MediaConvert and TPStreams generate the rendition ladder for you; compare them on output formats, DRM support, pricing model and where your viewers are.
If you want to see how we handle multi-rendition transcoding (240p to 4K, HLS and DASH), it's described here: https://tpstreams.com/transcoding-video/

articles.title: RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search
articles.description:
RagLeap has two new releases focused on an important part of building reliable AI systems: understanding what agents do and improving how they retrieve information.
ragleap-core v0.13.1 introduces structured audit log lines for agent actions.
ragleap-memory 0.3.0 adds optional vector and hybrid search using an embedder function supplied by the developer.
Both releases are open-source and designed for self-hosted environments.
AI agents can propose and execute actions across different channels. As these systems become more capable, understanding what happened during an action becomes increasingly important.
RagLeap Core v0.13.1 introduces structured JSON audit log lines through the ragleap.audit logger.
Every supported agent action writes an audit line beginning with AUDIT.
The new audit events include:
action_proposed
action_executed
action_error
action_rejected
action_skipped
action_forced_approval
Each event includes structured information such as:
UTC timestamp
Action type
Channel and agent role
Target, limited to 200 characters
Approval or rejection details
An action_id connecting a proposal to its decision
SHA-256 hashes of the content and result
An important privacy detail: The actual content text is not written into these audit lines. This makes it possible for operators to retain structured action records without placing the underlying text in this particular log output.
The lines can also be collected and retained using an external log shipper.
To disable structured audit log lines:
AUDIT_LOG_LINES=false
This is a small application change:
No database schema change
No new API route
No new dependency
Rebuild and restart the application
There are also important limitations. GET reads, chat routes, per-step agent-run events, approved-action send failures, and database-table retention or purge controls are not covered yet.
Audit logs alone do not make an installation compliant with any law or security standard. Log retention depends on the operator's infrastructure and configuration.
Release: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/v0.13.1
The second release focuses on memory retrieval.
Ragleap Memory 0.3.0 adds vector and hybrid search while keeping keyword search as the default.
One design decision is particularly important: the library does not include provider-specific embedding code, API keys, or network access.
Developers supply their own embedder function.
This gives applications control over where embedding requests go and which embedding implementation they use.
The library supports three search modes:
keyword — the default and existing search behaviour.
vector — cosine similarity over stored vectors.
hybrid — combines keyword and vector results using reciprocal rank fusion.
Example:
results = store.search(
    "relevant information",
    mode="hybrid",
    query_vector=query_vector,
)

The exact embedder and vector-generation workflow are controlled by the application.
The new embed_pending() method allows developers to generate vectors for entries that do not have them.
It supports:
Scope selection
Batch limits
Dry-run mode
Replacing stale vectors
A useful safety detail: add() never calls the embedder automatically. Embedding is an explicit operation.
With dry_run=True, developers can inspect what would be sent without actually sending it.
Version 0.3.0 introduces a daily embedder-token cap per tenant.
The quota is checked before each embedder call. If a batch exceeds the remaining allowance, only entries that fit are embedded. If none fit, QuotaExceededError is raised before the embedder function is called.
The library also introduces EmbedderError for failed or unusable embedder responses. Its error message does not contain the original text or vectors, and the failed batch is not stored.
This release introduces schema version 3.
Databases created with versions 0.1.0 or 0.2.0 are migrated in place on first open, within one transaction.
Back up your database before upgrading.
After migration, the database cannot be opened by version 0.2.0 or earlier.
Other changes include vector cleanup when entries are forgotten, erased, or expired, along with new usage counters for embedded tokens and embedding calls.
There are important limitations developers should understand:
Stored vectors are currently unencrypted and may reveal information about the original text.
Text sent to an embedder leaves the process wherever that embedder sends it.
Vector search scans at most max_vector_candidates eligible entries.
Retrieval quality depends on the selected embedder and has not yet been measured.
No independent security review has been completed.
These limitations are documented in the library's threat model.
Release: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-memory-v0.3.0
Testing and release verification were important parts of ragleap-memory 0.3.0.
The reported verification results include:



Verification
Result




CI checks for PR #1284
52 passed


Memory tests on VPS
472 passed


Sandbox tests on Python 3.12.3
472 passed


Sandbox tests on Python 3.10.20
472 passed


Mutation testing
177/177 mutations killed on both sandbox versions



The published wheel was also installed fresh from PyPI. A database created with version 0.2.0 was opened and migrated to schema 3. Usage counters were retained, and embedding and search were exercised with tenant isolation checks.
The released wheel's four Python files were verified against the files merged through PR #1284.
These results do not mean every environment has been verified. Windows, macOS, big-endian systems, real embedding providers, retrieval quality, and multi-process or network-filesystem behaviour remain unverified.
The wheel also has a PyPI provenance record from GitHub Actions trusted publishing.
RagLeap Core v0.13.1 also includes documentation and CI improvements:
Updated SECURITY.md with supported versions, scope, and limitations.
Added a security incident runbook for operators.
Added a host time synchronisation guide.
Fixed GitHub Pages build, README rendering, and broken links.
Added retries to terraform init when GitHub returns HTTP 504 responses.
These improvements help make the project easier to operate, understand, and maintain.
These releases address two different engineering concerns.
Auditability: Structured action logs provide operators with more visibility into supported agent actions and their approval decisions.
Memory retrieval: Optional vector and hybrid search give developers more flexibility in how their applications retrieve stored information, without forcing a particular embedding provider into the library.
Neither feature removes the need for careful deployment, security review, or application-level testing. The goal is to provide useful building blocks while being transparent about their current limitations.
RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform. We welcome developers, testers, technical writers, and contributors interested in building practical AI infrastructure.
Explore the project:
GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core


Website: https://ragleap.com


Documentation: https://docs.ragleap.com


Packages: https://packages.ragleap.com


Core v0.13.1: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/v0.13.1


Memory 0.3.0: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-memory-v0.3.0



If you're interested in AI agents, memory systems, security, Python engineering, or open-source infrastructure, take a look and consider contributing.
Build openly. Test carefully. Be transparent about limitations.

articles.title: One Afternoon of Our AI Coding Sessions, and Why They Don't Collide
articles.description:
This is one afternoon of our AI coding sessions, replayed.
Video: one afternoon of our sessions, replayed at 12-15x
We run AI coding sessions as a team with IST (Integrated Session Tools). A manager session takes a goal, splits it up and hands the parts to worker sessions. Several managers run at once, each with its own workers.
The video is three ten-minute windows from the afternoon of October 25 (KST), sped up 12 to 15 times.
Each box is a session. A shaded area is one team: a manager and its workers.
Dots moving along a line are messages between sessions: a manager handing out a task, a worker reporting back, one manager asking another.
A small loop on a session is a routine permission prompt that was approved automatically.
It was drawn by switchboard, a viewer we built for ourselves. It reads the logs our session tools already write and replays them.
One of the teams in the video is switchboard-mgr, the team building switchboard itself. That day its manager had one worker on the collector, which reads the session logs and turns them into events, and another on the viewer, which draws them, running in parallel.
The two workers committed side by side through the evening, each in its own repository. The viewer didn't read the collector's source; it depended on released versions. As the collector released new versions, the viewer moved to them, from ^0.1.0 that afternoon to ^0.6.0 by evening, about six hours later. When the viewer needed types the collector now published, it dropped its local copy and imported them from the release.
switchboard has since grown to twelve packages, each in its own repository.
We build with MWD (Microwise Development):
Microwise Development (MWD) builds software as small packages, each in its own repository, that depend on each other only through published, versioned releases. It was designed for working with AI coding agents, including several agents working in parallel.
What that means when many sessions run at once:
1 repository = 1 package. Packages sit next to each other on disk, grouped by project, so any session can still read across them.
The only thing we don't allow is two sessions editing the same codebase at the same time. Everything else is open.
One worker can own several packages. A manager can also hand a whole project to other managers, each with workers of its own.
Because each package already has its own repository, we don't need git worktrees to keep parallel workers apart.
switchboard is an internal tool, and it isn't part of what you can try. The session tools are: you can run a manager and its workers in your browser with GitHub Codespaces, starting with one manager and a 30-minute workshop.
→ Open ist-codespace

articles.title: Byg et før-og-efter billedværktøj med HTML, CSS og JavaScript
How a 3D multiplayer stealth game runs in a browser tab: shared sim, Durable Objects, a 5-byte input protocol
articles.description:
Night Nabbers is a free 3D stealth game that runs in a browser tab: you play a raccoon on a night street, sneak past guard dogs and searchlights, steal eggs and hatch odd little buddies. You can play solo against bots or with up to 16 players in the same street. There is no download and no sign-up. This post is a tour of how it is built and a few decisions that paid off. You can try it at nightnabbers.com while you read.
TypeScript (strict) and Vite for the client
three.js on WebGL2 for rendering, with a post-processing chain
Preact and signals for the UI layer (menus, HUD, shop), kept out of the render loop
glTF models, compressed with meshoptimizer, so the first load stays small on phones
Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects for online rooms, D1 for persistence
12 languages, with the strings loaded per locale
The most useful decision was to write the game rules once. A deterministic simulation that runs at a fixed 30 Hz step lives in a shared/ folder. The browser runs it for single player and for client-side prediction. The server runs the very same code inside a Durable Object for online rooms.
That gives you three things at once:
Single player works with no server at all.
Prediction is exact, because the client and the server step the same function with the same fixed timestep. When the server's answer arrives, there is rarely anything to correct.
The server can re-validate every input. Clients are a view, not an authority.
Each street is a room. A Durable Object holds several streets and ticks them from a single loop at 10 Hz, with the simulation stepping three 30 Hz substeps per tick. Packing many streets into one object matters because an object that is ticking can never hibernate, and you are billed for its wall-clock time. When no street has a human for 30 seconds it is dropped, no timer is left pending, and the object is evicted and stops costing anything. A matchmaker object places players into streets, and a server-side check marks an object "hot" when its tick lag grows, so no new players are sent to it.
CPU turned out not to be the limit. One full street costs on the order of tens of microseconds per tick in Node, so the real levers are how many streets share an object and how often you wake it up.
Traffic is WebSocket frames with hand-packed bytes rather than JSON:
A client input is 5 bytes: a message type, a 16-bit sequence number, a packed stick (16 direction sectors, 4 magnitude levels, the gait) and a flags byte. It is sent only when the quantised value changes, at most 10 times a second. Prediction uses exactly the bytes that were sent, which is what keeps it exact.
Server updates are deltas, one per tick per client and only if something changed. Positions are quantised over the world size.
Each client only receives entities within an area of interest (32 m, with a wider exit radius of 38 m so something walking along the edge does not flicker in and out).
The street-wide part of a delta is encoded once per tick. Each client's message splices in the pre-encoded records it can see, so the per-client cost is a distance check and a memcpy. A fuzz test checks that the spliced output is byte-identical to the reference encoder.
The protocol has a version number, and a client that meets a different version simply stays offline instead of misreading frames.
Rooms snapshot their state to storage, so a crashed or redeployed object rebuilds the street on the first reconnect. We killed the local worker process on purpose to measure it: players were back in a few seconds with their coins intact. Inputs are strictly decoded and rate limited, there is a per-address socket cap, and the tests throw 50 thousand random frames, every truncated server frame, and 16 simulated players mashing random input for two simulated minutes at the protocol. The rule is that a bad frame produces an error or a decode, never a hang.
Keep the simulation free of any platform types, so it runs in the browser, in Node tests and in a Worker unchanged.
Spend effort on bytes early, because bandwidth and object time are what the bill is made of.
Test the failure paths on purpose: restore from a snapshot, protocol fuzzing, long soak runs in real browsers.
The game is made by a small team with the help of AI tools. Some 3D models and early promotional art were generated with AI tools and then edited, rigged and tuned by hand. Code and text were written with AI assistants under human direction and review. All sound and music is synthesised by the game's own code, and every screenshot and video of the game is a real capture.
Free in the browser, desktop or phone, no account: nightnabbers.com. Trailer: youtu.be/SnSh6b3PVSs. Press kit: nightnabbers.com/press. Questions about the netcode or the tooling are welcome in the comments.

articles.title: Developer Changelog Retrieval: Freshness, Tenant Isolation, Citation Control
Your Agent Said It Right. Did the Caller Hear It? Live Call Testing in Voicetest
articles.description:
A voice agent can pass every text simulation and still fail on a real call. The LLM produces the right sentence, and then the speech pipeline mangles it: a phone number read as a quantity, a drug name the TTS voice can't pronounce, an appointment time that STT on the other end turns into a different time. Text simulations never see any of this, because they stop at what the model meant to say.
Voicetest now runs test cases as live audio calls. The same simulated caller that drives text runs joins a real WebRTC call, speaks through TTS, and listens through STT. Nobody has to be on the line. Every turn ends up with two texts: what was intended, and what was heard.
This post covers how live calls work, what they catch, and how to run one.
In a cascade voice pipeline (STT → LLM → TTS), the LLM's output is not what reaches the caller. It is an input to TTS, and the caller hears whatever TTS produced. A defect at that boundary looks like this:




Text





Intended (content)
If you need to reschedule, call us at 415-555-0123.



Heard (heard)
If you need to reschedule, call us at four hundred fifteen, five hundred fifty-five, one hundred twenty-three.



Both lines say the same thing to an LLM judge reading text. Only one of them is usable by a person writing a number down.
Voicetest records this by adding an observer to each call. The observer subscribes to the audio each side publishes and transcribes it, so every turn in the transcript carries:
content: the intended text, which is the agent's LLM output or the simulated caller's line.
heard: what the observer transcribed from the audio the other side actually received.

The runs view marks up each turn with a word-level diff of the two, so a mangled number or a dropped "not" stands out without re-reading the whole call.
A finished live call is saved as a normal result, marked source_kind="live", next to simulated and imported results in the same run history. It is judged three ways:
The test case's metrics, against the intended transcript.
The same metrics again, against the heard text. These are stored as audio metrics.
The agent's global metrics.
The second pass is the point. A metric like "Agent gave the caller the callback number" passes on the intended text above, and may well pass on the heard text too, since a number was technically given. Write the metric the way the caller experiences it, "Agent read the callback number digit by digit," and the two passes disagree:

The text metric passes, because the LLM wrote the digits. The audio metric fails, because the caller never heard them. That's the TTS regression a text-only suite lets through.
Voicetest already had audio evaluation. It takes a finished text simulation and round-trips the agent's lines through TTS and STT afterwards. That's cheap, and it catches the same class of pronunciation defect.
Live calls run the whole conversation over audio instead. The agent responds to what it heard the caller say, not to clean text, so STT errors on the caller's side change the course of the call the way they would in production. If the agent mishears "Tuesday" as "Thursday" in turn 3, the rest of the conversation follows from that mistake, and the transcript shows where it happened.
Use audio evaluation as a fast check across a whole suite. Use live calls for the test cases where hearing matters: numbers, names, dates, confirmations, and anything a caller has to act on.
Live calls need the voice services: a LiveKit server, a faster-whisper STT server, and a Kokoro TTS server. voicetest up starts all of them in Docker along with the backend:
uv tool install voicetest
voicetest up

Then run a test case as a call. In the Web UI, each test in the Tests tab has a Call button. It starts the call and switches to the Runs tab, where the transcript streams in turn by turn and the result is saved when the call ends.
From the CLI, point at an agent in the database and a test by name:
voicetest call \
  --agent-id <agent-id> \
  --tests tests.json \
  --test "Refill with callback number"

Over REST, it's POST /api/agents/{id}/calls/start with a test_id. Leave out test_id, or use the Talk button on the agent page, and the call waits for a human caller to join from the browser instead. Those calls are saved as runs too, judged against the agent's global metrics, which is useful for checking a prompt change by ear before writing a test for it.
voicetest down stops the services.
The whole stack can run on your machine. The voice services are already local, and the agent, the simulated caller, and the judge can use a local model through llama.cpp's llama-server:
brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
judge = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"

This is also how voicetest tests itself. Its CI starts the stack in Docker and runs real calls end to end against a local model, with no external keys. Nothing in the call path needs a cloud account.
Observation works on the published audio, regardless of how each side produced it. Today that's the cascade pipeline. A native speech-to-speech agent, with no separate text step, would be observed the same way.
Timing isn't measured yet. Latency to first audio, dead air, and barge-in handling are the next metrics, and they need the same observer that's already on the call. If you run voice agents in production and have a timing failure you want caught, open an issue: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest/issues.
Voicetest is open source under Apache 2.0. GitHub: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest

articles.title: I Pointed My Dev Sandbox At 22 Public APIs. Only Three Answered Cleanly.
articles.description:
I sat down this morning to write a data post the way I usually do: pick a handful of public APIs, pull something comparable from each, build the piece around what the numbers actually show. Twenty minutes in, I still had nothing, because almost nothing I pointed my sandbox at would talk to me.
So I stopped trying to route around it and just measured it instead.
I'm writing this from a locked-down dev sandbox — the kind more and more of us are working in now, whether that's a corporate CI runner, a devcontainer with default-deny networking, or one of the AI-agent execution environments that turned "outbound egress needs an explicit allowlist" from a niche security opinion into standard practice this year. I'd read the arguments for it. I hadn't actually sat down and counted what it costs you on an ordinary Tuesday.
I picked 22 public API/data domains — a mix of what I'd normally reach for: government data (SEC, FDA, USGS, Congress.gov, EU tenders), reference APIs (Wikipedia, arXiv, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, CourtListener, Stack Exchange, Open Library), a couple of dev-adjacent services (Hacker News, dev.to, the platform I publish actors on), and a few package registries. Same session, same tooling, one request per domain, no retries beyond what the tools do automatically.
17 of the 22 never answered at all. Not a 403, not a 429 — the connection itself was refused before any application on the other end got a chance to say anything. From the sandbox's point of view, data.sec.gov and api.fda.gov and en.wikipedia.org and arXiv's export API and CourtListener and Stack Exchange and Hacker News's own Firebase-backed API might as well not exist. Even google.com — not an API, just the homepage — got nothing back.
Three came back clean: the npm registry, PyPI, and the crates.io sparse index. All three answered in well under a second with normal, well-formed JSON, no different from how they'd behave on an unrestricted connection. If your research diet is "check whether a package name is taken," you're fine. Anything else, you're not.
The interesting failures weren't the silent ones. Two domains actually reached a real backend and then told me, in their own words, why I still wasn't getting anything.
api.github.com/rate_limit answered normally. But api.github.com/repos/facebook/react — a plain, public, unauthenticated-friendly endpoint — came back with a 403 and this body:
"This GitHub API path is not available: sessions are bound to their configured repositories. Use repository-scoped endpoints (repos/{owner}/{repo}/...)."
That's not GitHub's rate limiter talking. That's the sandbox's own proxy, sitting in front of a real GitHub App connection, deciding that "GitHub" for this session means one specific repository and nothing else GitHub hosts — including GitHub's own public search index. The /search/repositories endpoint got the identical message. From inside the box, GitHub's API is technically reachable and functionally unusable for anything but the one repo I'm already attached to.
Google's Books API did something different: it let the request through to the real backend, which then told me the shared daily query quota for that API key was already gone — a 429 with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and a straight explanation, not a proxy stonewall. Same failure mode from where I'm sitting (no data), completely different cause (a quota, not a policy), and I'd have had no way to tell them apart without reading the response body.
I'd planned to measure something with GitHub's search API today — specifically, how many of the most-starred repos on GitHub haven't been pushed to in two years, the "famous but abandoned" problem that makes picking a dependency more nerve-wracking than it should be. I can't answer that from here, not today. That's the actual, slightly embarrassing outcome of this post: the tool I wanted to use for research is scoped out of doing research, in this specific environment, right now.
It's also exactly the gap something like a hosted GitHub search actor exists to sidestep — you're not running the query from inside your own network policy, you're asking a platform that already has a working, rate-limit-managed connection to GitHub's search API to run it for you and hand back normalized rows. I'm not claiming that's a universal argument for outsourcing every API call — for npm, PyPI and crates.io, my own sandbox is fine, no help needed. But "is GitHub search reachable from where I'm running this" turned out to be a real, non-obvious question today, not a hypothetical one, and it was the domain that failed in the most specific, most informative way of the 22.
This is one sandbox, one session, one point in time — not a claim about "AI agents can't reach the internet" in general, and not a claim about any particular product's policy being right or wrong. A different environment, a different day, or a different allowlist would very plausibly give you a different 16-and-3 split; I have no idea how representative this specific configuration is of what other people are running. I also can't fully separate "blocked by policy" from "blocked for some other reason" for every one of the 16 silent domains — a couple could in principle be down for unrelated reasons, though 16 out of 22 all failing identically, instantly, and only on domains outside three package registries makes coincidence a stretch.
What I can say with more confidence: two completely different failure modes (a proxy that answers with a scoped, GitHub-specific message, and a quota that answers with a normal HTTP error) look identical from the outside — "I got nothing useful back" — until you actually read what came back. If you're debugging something similar, that distinction is probably worth 30 seconds before you assume it's your code. And a 17-of-22 failure rate on a completely ordinary research task is a bigger number than I expected going in — I'd have guessed maybe half, not more than three-quarters.
If you're running dev tools, agents, or CI inside something similarly locked down — what's actually on your allowlist, and how did you decide? I'm curious whether anyone's settled on a shortlist that covers 90% of real research/data work, or whether everyone's just adding domains reactively the way I apparently am.

articles.title: 【アジャイルFAQ 今日は実験室】「AIいいなり開発」への不安を、BMADは解消してくれるのか？（前編）
articles.description:
この記事を読んでいただきありがとうございます。アジャイルグループに所属する、藤井智弘です。
 そこで、この実験室では、ここしばらく（マジで）ハマっている BMAD Method（以下、BMAD）を実際に試してみます。手っ取り早く知りたい人と、自分でも試したい人の両方がいると思うので、前編は実際のやり取りの例と評価、後編は試してみたい人向けの手順書（深みもなにもない）としました。
いいなりになると、どうなるか
AIとの対話は、成立するか
その対話は、単なる質疑応答ではなく、人の側のアイディアを洗練させる助けになっているか
結論
#
観点1：人が何も答えずに進めても、道具は推測に印を付け、確かめるべき問いを残しました。ただ、その推測をもとに586行の要求仕様までできあがっており、人が答えてみると、前提の多くが実際とは違っていました
観点2：対話は成立しました。AIは聞いたことを言い直して確かめ、答えに応じて次の問いを変え、「分からない」という答えも受け止めました
観点3：洗練の助けになりました。お題は「サイトを新しく作る」から「今あるサイトが使われない理由を探る」に書き換わり、私の見立ては「確かめるべき仮説」に置き直されました。ただし洗練は一方通行ではなく、AIの提案を人が直す場面も同じくらい大事でした
 道具が問いを立ててくれても、答えるのは人です。答えないまま進めば、結局は「AIいいなり」に近づいてしまいます。
BMADとは
#
 BMADは Breakthrough Method for Agile AI-Driven Development の略で、オープンソースのAI駆動開発の手法です。Claude Code のようなコーディング用のAIツールに組み込んで使います。
段階
主な役割
主な成果物




分析
アナリスト
製品概要（brief）、PRFAQ


計画
PM、UXデザイナー
要求仕様（PRD：Product Requirements Document）、UXの設計


設計
アーキテクト、PM
アーキテクチャ、エピックとストーリー


実装
開発者ほか
スプリント計画、コード、レビュー、振り返り



 規模に応じて計画を省くこともでき、どの段階でも、誰が何をどう決めたかが記録ファイル（.memlog.md）に一行ずつ残ります。
仕様が決まる「前」をBMADがどこまで支えてくれるかだけです。設計や実装、コードの品質、他の手法との比較は扱いません。
実験の条件
#
 お題は、架空のソフトウェアベンダーのこんな要望です。
当社製品の利用者向けのサポートサイトを作り、顧客の利便性を最大化したい。
 起点は、たったこれだけ。
項目
内容




BMADの版・環境
v6.12.4（安定版）、Claude Code（開発コンテナの中）


カスタマイズ
なし（会話と文書の言語を日本語にしただけ）


実験1：AIだけで通す
要望の一文だけを渡し、人に一切聞かない進め方（ヘッドレス）で、製品概要と要求仕様（PRD）を作らせる


実験2：人が答えて通す
アナリストの問いに私が答えながら、製品概要を作る（進め方は「速い道（Fast path）」）







実験1：製品概要
実験1：PRD
実験2：製品概要




かかった時間・手間
約6分
約13分
対話7往復


推測の印（[ASSUMPTION]）
5か所
31か所
5か所


決定の記録（.memlog.md）
20件
29件
39件


文書の大きさ
約2,800字
約2万字（586行、機能要求27件）
約3,600字



 表の「決定の記録」は、前述の記録ファイルに残った行の数です。「推測の印」は、観点1で詳しく説明します。
観点1：いいなりになると、どうなるか
#
 BMADはかなりの量の文書を出力するので、この記事で紹介する出力は、いずれも要所の抜粋です。全体は、ぜひ後編の手順で実際に試して確かめてみてください。
当社製品の利用者が、困ったときに自分で答えを見つけられ、見つからなければ迷わず人にたどり着けるサポートサイトを作る。依頼にある「利便性を最大化」は、このままでは測れない。そこでこの概要では、困りごとが早く、確実に解決することと言い換える。
 正直に言って、よくできています。AIは誰にも聞かずにWeb調査まで行い、測れない「利便性の最大化」を測れる言葉に言い換えていました。推測の箇所には、きちんと印も付いています。
[ASSUMPTION]（英語で「仮定」）という印を付けます。「ここはAIの推測で、まだ誰も確かめていない」という目印です。人に質問しない実験1では、分からないことをすべて推測で埋めるしかないため、この印が多く付きます。また、推測では埋められず、人にしか答えられない問いは、文書の末尾に「未確認の問い」としてまとめられます。
[ASSUMPTION] が、その印です。
当社側 [ASSUMPTION]
同じ質問が繰り返し届き、サポート担当者の時間がそこに取られる。
回答がどこにも残らないため、次の担当者に引き継がれない。
 末尾の「未確認の問い」には、まさに確かめるべき問いも残っていました。
既存のFAQ・マニュアル・問い合わせ窓口は何があり、誰が管理しているか。
目的は顧客満足か、サポートコストの削減か。両方なら、ぶつかったときにどちらを優先するか。
 続けて作らせたPRDは586行。機能要求は27件に番号が振られています。PRDには、利用者が製品をどう使うかを、名前の付いた人物の物語として書く「利用場面（ユーザージャーニー、UJ）」という節があり、その1つ目はこう始まります。
UJ-1. 経理担当の佐藤さんが、月末の締め作業の途中で出たエラーを自分で片づける。
 「佐藤さん」は、製品概要には出てきません。PRDのこの節の冒頭に、AI自身がこう注記していました。
製品概要には利用者が実際に使う場面の記述がない。以下は製品概要の「誰のためか」「つくるもの」から組み立てた想定である。
 つまり佐藤さんは、PRDの段階でAIが新たに思い描いた人物で、推測の上にさらに推測が重なっています（この場面にも、もちろん推測の印が付いています）。では、実際はどうだったのか。実験2で私が答えた内容と並べます。
実験1の文書の前提（推測）
人が答えた実際




製品はB2Bの業務ソフトウェア
営業支援システム。ここは当たり


利用者は製品に詳しくない業務担当者。PRDの主人公は「経理担当の佐藤さん」
現場の営業社員


サポート担当者がいて、同じ質問に時間を取られている
サポート担当はいない、または少ない。担当営業が開発者に回している


マニュアルやFAQがばらばらに置かれている
簡単なサポートサイトは既にある。それでも操作の質問が問い合わせに流れている


目的は顧客満足かコスト削減か（問いとして残した）
優先は利用者の満足度。問いとして残したのが正解



 公平のために書くと、道具はやるべきことをやっています。ただ、推測の印は、人が読んで確かめてこそ意味があります。 印を確かめずに次へ渡すと、27件の機能要求が、実際にはいない「サポート担当者」や「経理担当の佐藤さん」を前提に組み上がってしまうおそれがあります。
いいなりで気をつけたいのは、間違った文書ができることより、もっともらしい文書が、確かめられないまま次の工程の前提になりやすいことです。

観点2：AIとの対話は、成立するか
#
 実験2で同じ要望を渡すと、アナリストはいきなり文書を作らず、まず頭の中を全部出すように求めてきました。私が製品のこと、いまの問い合わせの流れ、きっかけ、優先したいことを思いつくままに書くと、聞いたことを表にまとめ直して返してきました。
聞いたこと
進め方への影響（アナリストの返答を要約）




製品：現場の営業社員が毎日使う営業支援システム
利用者は「業務の途中で手が止まった人」。すぐ答えにたどり着けるかを中心に見る


優先：開発者の負担より利用者の満足度
成功の物差しは利用者側の指標を主にする


いまの窓口：簡単なサポートサイトはある
新しいサイトを作る話ではなく、今あるのに使われていない理由を探る話になる



 聞いたことを言い直して確かめ、どこに引っかかっているかを示す。上手な聞き手がやることと同じです。「速い道」を選ぶと残りの不明点を6問にまとめて聞かれ、私が「不明」と返したところは、推測の印付きで埋めるか「分かっていないこと」として残しました。後から送った追加の答えも、きちんと反映されました。
対話は成立します。 ただし「速い道」では問いがまとめて来るので、やり取りは質疑応答に近づきます。ちなみに、一問ずつ押し返されながら進む「じっくりの道（Coaching path）」という進め方もあります。ぜひ皆さんで試してみてください。
観点3：対話は、人のアイディアを洗練させたか
#
 いちばん知りたかったのは、ここです。
お題が書き換わり、手段の選択肢が広がった
 「簡単なサイトは既にある」と答えた時点で、アナリストはお題を「今あるのに使われていない理由を探る」に書き換え、こう付け加えました。
操作の質問が多く、利用者が作業の途中だとすると、「サイト」という形自体が正しいかどうかも後で問い直すかもしれません。
 実際、のちに「範囲はサイトだけか、製品の画面から呼び出すヘルプまで含めるか」と、同業他社の調査結果を添えて聞いてきました。私は「早く公開することを優先しているので、まずはサイトだけ」と答えています。選択肢を広げたのはAIで、選んだのは私です。
見立てが、仮説に置き直された
 「いまのサイトが役に立たないのはなぜか」に、私は「記事が足りない、探しにくいのだと思う」と答えました。製品概要には、こう書かれました。
「操作の質問が多い」「記事が足りない、探しにくい」は、どちらも見立てであり、確かめた結果ではない。
 否定もせず、事実扱いもせず、「まず確かめるもの」に置き直す。第3回から第5回で「現行機能」をまず確かめる話をしましたが、同じ動きが要望の段階で起きています。
物差しが、使えるものになった
 満足度は「アンケート、解約、更新時の声を総合的に勘案して判断している」と答えると、アナリストは「結果が出るまで時間がかかる指標なので、手前で早く動く指標を置きました」と、解決までの時間などを足してきました。作り直したサイトが効いているかを途中で確かめる手立てがないことに、言われて初めて気づきました。
答えられない問いが、残った
 下書きのあと、アナリストはいちばん弱い点を押し返してきました。
記事を書き、更新し続けるのは誰ですか？
 私は答えられず、「いまは決められない」とだけ返しました。それは製品概要の「分かっていないこと」の先頭に残りました。答えの出ていない問いを、いちばん目立つ場所に置くことも、洗練のうちだと思います。
洗練は、一方通行ではなかった
 逆向きの場面もありました。アナリストは下書きの冒頭で、お題を「操作の質問を、人に聞かずに短い時間で解決できるようにする。残る質問は開発者ではない窓口が受ける」と言い換えていました。そして仕上げの段階で、それがまだ私の了承を得ていない提案であることを申告してきました。読み返すと、開発者が流れから抜け落ちていました。実際には、一次窓口で受けきれない問い合わせは開発者にエスカレーションしますし、AIも活用したい。そう伝えると、言い換えは次のように修正されました。
操作の質問の多くを、利用者がサイトで（AI の助けも借りて）短い時間で自己解決できるようにする。自己解決できない質問は一次窓口が受け、一次窓口で解決できないものだけを開発者にエスカレーションする。
 アナリスト自身が置いていた「最初の版にAI自動応答は含めない」という推測も、このとき取り下げられ、記録ファイルに残りました。
洗練の助けになります。 ただし、AIが一方的に磨いたのではありません。AIの問いが人の見立てを揺さぶり、人の答えがAIの提案を直す。振り返れば、実験1が「サイトを作る」をそのまま受け取ったように、私も「サイト」という手段や自分の見立てを疑わないまま答えかけていました。違いは、問いを立てる相手がいたかどうか、だけです。

強み：「AIいいなり」を防ぐ仕掛けが、道具の側にある
#
代わりに考えない：製品概要のスキルの指示書には「考えを代わりにしない」「答えが薄ければ押し返す」と書かれています（原文は英語。引用は筆者訳。以下同じ）。実際の振る舞いも、観点2・3のとおりでした
推測に印を付け、決めていないことを残す：PRDの指示書は、人に聞かずに進めるときも「成功指標やスコープの判断を作り出してはならない、記録せよ」と定めています。実際、目標値は空欄のまま残り、PRDは自分の状態を「完了」ではなく「一部完了（人の確認が要る）」と報告しました
AIの提案と人の決定を、区別する：了承前の言い換えを「提案」と申告したのは、観点3で見たとおりです。「AIいいなり」を防ぐうえで、いちばん大事な性質かもしれません
歯止めの指標を置く：PRDには「問い合わせ件数——減らすこと自体を目標にしない。入口を隠せば簡単に減るからである」という指標が置かれました。第9回・第10回で書いた、指標を成績表にしない話そのものです
決めていないWhatは、次の段階へ流れない：エピックとストーリーへの分割のスキルには、人に聞かずに進める道がありません。指示書には「人の入力なしに内容を生成するな」とあり、実装前の判定でも「記録されていない判断を作り出さずに実装できるか」が問われます。いわゆる「Readyの定義」と同じ問いです
決定の記録が残る：推測の取り下げまで一行ずつ残ります。第5回の「謎の挙動の判断一覧」や、意思決定の記録（ADR）と同じ考え方です
注意点：仕掛けが働くかどうかは、使い方しだい
#
推測も、整った文書の中に収まる：586行の中の31か所の印を、すべて確かめきるのは大変です。文書が整っているほど、確かめずに先へ進みたくなるので、意識しておきたいところです
調査は一般論：調査そのものは確かでした。製品概要が引いたGartnerの調査（2024年8月）は実在し、数字も出典どおりです。ただ、Web調査で分かるのは世の中の一般論で、「サポート担当がいない」というこの会社の事情は出てきません。調査が確かなぶん、推測の部分まで確かに見えやすい点には、注意が必要かもしれません
手段を問い直すのは、人が答えたときだけ：実験1は「サイトを作る」を最後まで前提にしていました
段取りが、ウォータースクラムフォールに見える：これをシステム全体について一度にやり、文書を契約で凍結すれば、撲滅の回で書いた「AIで速く打鍵するウォーターフォール」になりかねません。途中で方針を直す仕組み（Correct Course）も用意されているので、上手に使いたいところです
文書が増える：一文の依頼から13分で586行。誰が、いつ読む文書なのかを見極める規律は、AIで書くほど必要になるでしょう
答える時間は、人が出すしかない：BMADは「案を作る」側を大きく肩代わりしますが、「決める」時間は肩代わりしません

使うなら、この4つ
#
推測の印と未確認の問いを、人がすべて潰してから次へ進む。印の数は、そのまま「人が確かめるべきことの数」だと考える
最初の作業は「見立てを確かめる」にする。要望や見立てを事実として扱わない
全体ではなく、エピック単位で回す。文書は契約の付属書ではなく、学んだら直すファイルとして扱う
AIの提案と人の決定を、混ぜない。言い換え、成功の物差し、何を作らないかは、人が了承したものだけを決定として扱う
道具が速くなるほど、基本の値段が上がる
#
 第1回で、CASE、RAD、ローコードと、新しい道具が来るたびに「基礎は不要では」と問われてきた、と書きました。結論は毎回同じで、道具は「どのように作るか」を変え、「何を作るか」「何を学ぶか」は外に残ります。BMADはその「何を作るか」の手前まで入ってきましたが、使ってみると、残る側の仕事は消えたのではなく、はっきり見えるようになったのでした。
言葉にする作業そのものは、AIがかなり手伝ってくれます。
中身のほうです。現場の事実を知っていること。見立てと確かめた事実を分けられること。「いまは決められない」と言えること。AIの提案のどこが違うかを指摘できること。要求を「書く」技能より、「引き出し、確かめ、決める」技能のほうが、AIの時代には重くなります。上流工程を長く仕事にしてきた身として、少しうれしい発見でした。
道具がどれだけ賢くなっても、Whatの中身を持っているのは人です。だから、人が大事なのです。
 書き終えてみて、「作業」と「仕事」の違いにも気づかされました。決められた手順を機械的にこなすのが作業で、意味のある結果をもたらすのが仕事です。「AIいいなり」と「AIとの対話」の違いは、ここにあるのだと思います。AIと対話しているあいだ、私は考えてもいなかった条件に思いをはせ、これが何の役に立つのかを考えていました。
AIは、POの成熟を助ける相手になれるのではないか。何を作るかを決めるPOの隣で、問いを立て、見立てを揺さぶり、答えの出ていないことを目の前に並べてくれる。AIの位置づけとしては、こちらのほうがずっと大切です。
 さて、ここまで読んでくださった皆さんに伺います。
 …と尋ねつつ、筆者自身がまだまだBMAD初心者なので、もっと精進しなければ。
後編（手順編）：「BMADを動かしてみる——環境づくりから『AIだけ』と『人が答える』の比べ方まで」／次回: 「POが多忙でチームに来ません」（12/1）／本編の連載一覧は第1回をご覧ください。

articles.title: 【アジャイルFAQ 今日は実験室】BMADを動かしてみる——環境づくりから「AIだけ」と「人が答える」の比べ方まで（後編・手順編）
articles.description:
この記事を読んでいただきありがとうございます。アジャイルグループに所属する、藤井智弘です。
手元で再現するための手順書です。
この記事でやること
#
開発コンテナを用意し、その中に Claude Code と BMAD を入れる
会話と文書を日本語にし、呼び名を決める
実験1：要望の一文だけを渡し、AIだけで製品概要と要求仕様（PRD）を作らせる
実験2：AIの問いに人が答えながら、製品概要を作る
2つの結果を並べて、「人が確かめるべきこと」を読み取る
 手順は、2026年11月時点の BMAD v6.12.4（安定版） と Claude Code で確かめました。BMADは版の変化が速く、プレビュー版のV7ではコマンドの体系そのものが違います。版は固定して試してください。
1. 準備するもの
#
項目
今回使ったもの




OS
macOS


コンテナの実行環境
OrbStack（Docker Desktop でも可）


開発コンテナを動かす道具
VS Code の Dev Containers 拡張機能、または devcontainer CLI


Claude のアカウント
Claude のサブスクリプション（Claude Code が使えるもの）



 Node.js、Python、uv、Claude Code は、すべてコンテナの中に入れます。
 ただし、手元の Mac にも ~/.claude フォルダと ~/.claude.json ファイルが必要です（次の手順で、この2つをコンテナと共有するためです）。どちらもない場合は、先に Mac で Claude Code を一度起動しておいてください。devcontainer CLI を使う場合は、npm i -g @devcontainers/cli で入れておきます。
2. 開発コンテナを用意する
#
 BMADは npx でインストールし、Python のスクリプトも使います。試すたびに手元の環境が汚れないよう、開発コンテナの中で動かします。作業用のフォルダに .devcontainer/ を作り、次の2つのファイルを置きます。
.devcontainer/Dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/typescript-node:22
# Node.js 22（BMAD v6.12 は 20.12 以上が必要）、git、zsh が入っている

# Claude Code をコンテナ内に入れる
RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

USER node


  

.devcontainer/devcontainer.json
{
  "name": "bmad-lab",
  "build": { "dockerfile": "Dockerfile" },
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/python:1": { "version": "3.12" },
    "ghcr.io/va-h/devcontainers-features/uv:1": {}
  },
  "remoteUser": "node",
  "mounts": [
    "source=${localEnv:HOME}/.claude,target=/home/node/.claude,type=bind",
    "source=${localEnv:HOME}/.claude.json,target=/home/node/.claude.json,type=bind"
  ],
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "extensions": ["anthropic.claude-code"],
      "settings": { "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.linux": "zsh" }
    }
  }
}


  

 ポイントは mounts です。手元の ~/.claude をコンテナと共有しておくと、Claude Code のログイン情報がコンテナの外に残ります。コンテナを作り直しても、ログインし直さずに済みます。
devcontainer up --workspace-folder .
devcontainer exec --workspace-folder . zsh   # コンテナの中のシェルに入る


  

 最初の起動では Python を組み立てるため、数分かかります。以降の手順は、すべてコンテナの中のターミナルで行います。
3. Claude Code にログインする
#
 コンテナの中で claude を起動し、/login と入力して「Claude account with subscription」を選びます。つまずきやすい点が2つあります。
URLのコピーが途中で切れる：コンテナからはブラウザを開けないので、ログイン用のURLが画面に表示されます。とても長く、画面の幅で折り返されるため、選択してコピーすると途中で切れがちです。切れたURLを開くと「無効な OAuth リクエストです」と表示されます。ターミナルを十分に広げてURLを1行に収めてからコピーしてください
コードを別の画面に貼ってしまう：承認後にブラウザに表示されるコードは、URLを発行した Claude Code の画面でしか使えません。別のターミナルの Claude Code に貼ると「That code wasn't accepted」と表示されます
 「Login successful」と出たら完了です。続けて聞かれるフォルダの信頼では「Yes, I trust this folder」を選びます。既定の「No, exit」のまま Enter を押すと、Claude Code が終了してしまいます。
4. BMADをインストールする
#
 作業用のフォルダ（ここでは trials/support-site）を作り、BMADを入れます。対話式なら次のコマンドで、AIツールに Claude Code、モジュールに bmm（BMad Method）を選びます。
mkdir -p trials/support-site && cd trials/support-site
npx bmad-method@6.12 install


  

 毎回同じ設定で入れたい場合は、選択肢をオプションで渡せます。
npx -y bmad-method@6.12 install --yes --tools claude-code --modules bmm \
  --communication-language Japanese --document-output-language Japanese \
  --directory "$PWD"


  

 インストールが終わると、フォルダの中に次のものができます。
場所
中身




.claude/skills/bmad-*
Claude Code から呼び出すスキル（BMADの各役割と手順の指示書）


_bmad/
設定とスクリプト。_bmad/custom/ は利用者が上書きするための場所


_bmad-output/
成果物の置き場所。計画の文書は planning-artifacts/ に入る




5. 会話と文書を日本語にし、呼び名を決める
#
 インストール時に --communication-language Japanese を指定していれば、BMADが実際に読む設定は日本語になります。ただし、紛らわしい点が2つあります。
インストーラーが書き出す基本の設定ファイル（_bmad/config.toml）を開くと、会話の言語が English と書かれています。実際に使われる値は別のファイルから決まるので、これだけを見て慌てる必要はありません
エージェントがあなたを呼ぶ名前は、既定ではOSのユーザー名になります。開発コンテナの中では「Node」と呼ばれます
 基本の設定ファイルは、再インストールのたびに上書きされるので、直接は書き換えません。代わりに、上書き用の _bmad/custom/config.toml の末尾に、次を足して固定しておくと安心です。
[core]
user_name = "Tom"
communication_language = "Japanese"
document_output_language = "Japanese"
project_name = "support-site"


  

 project_name は、成果物のフォルダ名に使われます。実際に使われる設定は、次のコマンドで確かめられます。
uv run _bmad/scripts/resolve_config.py --project-root .


  

 出力の先頭が、次のようになっていれば成功です。
{
  "core": {
    "user_name": "Tom",
    "communication_language": "Japanese",
    "project_name": "support-site",
    "document_output_language": "Japanese",
    "output_folder": "_bmad-output"
  },


  

 最後に Claude Code を起動して /bmad-help を呼び、BMADのスキルの案内が返ってくれば、準備は完了です。
手順4と5を、1本のスクリプトで
#
 前提の確認、インストール、設定の固定、確認までを1本にまとめると、次のようになります。開発コンテナの中で bash setup_bmad.sh trials/support-site Tom のように実行します（2つ目の引数が呼び名です）。新しいフォルダで最後まで通ることを確かめてあります。
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# BMAD v6.12 の実験環境をつくる（開発コンテナの中で実行）
#   bash setup_bmad.sh [作業フォルダ] [呼び名]
#   例：bash setup_bmad.sh trials/support-site Tom
set -euo pipefail
DIR="${1:-trials/support-site}"
NAME="${2:-User}"
BMAD_VERSION="${BMAD_VERSION:-6.12}"

echo "== 前提の確認"
ok=1
check() {
  if command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "  ✓ $1 $("$1" --version 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
  else
    echo "  ✗ $1 が見つかりません"; ok=0
  fi
}
check node; check python3; check uv; check git; check claude
[ "$ok" = 1 ] || { echo "足りないものを入れてから、もう一度実行してください"; exit 1; }

echo "== BMAD v${BMAD_VERSION} をインストール：$DIR"
mkdir -p "$DIR"
npx -y "bmad-method@${BMAD_VERSION}" install --yes --tools claude-code --modules bmm \
  --communication-language Japanese --document-output-language Japanese \
  --directory "$(cd "$DIR" && pwd)"

echo "== 会話と文書を日本語に固定（_bmad/custom/config.toml）"
cd "$DIR"
if ! grep -q '^\[core\]' _bmad/custom/config.toml 2>/dev/null; then
  cat >> _bmad/custom/config.toml <<EOF

[core]
user_name = "${NAME}"
communication_language = "Japanese"
document_output_language = "Japanese"
project_name = "$(basename "$PWD")"
EOF
fi

echo "== 設定の確認"
uv run _bmad/scripts/resolve_config.py --project-root . \
  | grep -E '"(user_name|communication_language|document_output_language|project_name)"'
echo "完了。次は：cd $DIR && claude を起動し、/bmad-help を呼んでください"


  


6. 今回使うスキル
#
 v6.12.4 には30ほどのスキルがあります。分析と計画の段階で、今回使うのは次のものです。
スキル
役割
何をするか
成果物




bmad-help
案内
いまの状態を見て、次に使うスキルを勧める
なし


bmad-product-brief
アナリスト
対話で要望を引き出し、製品概要を作る
briefs/…/brief.md


bmad-prd
PM
製品概要などから要求仕様を作る
prds/…/prd.md


bmad-prfaq
アナリスト
完成時のプレスリリースから逆算して構想を試す（製品概要の代わり）
PRFAQ


bmad-advanced-elicitation
随時
プレモーテムなどの手法で、下書きをさらに叩く
改訂した下書き



 どのスキルも、成果物と一緒に記録ファイル（.memlog.md）を作り、決めたこと・推測したこと・取り下げたことを一行ずつ残します。
7. 実験1：AIだけで通す（ヘッドレス）
#
 製品概要とPRDのスキルには、人に質問せず、手元の情報と推測で文書を仕上げる進め方（ヘッドレス）があります。これを使って、「人が何も答えなかったら、どんな文書ができるか」を見ます。
-p（一回だけ実行して終わる形）で起動し、スキルを呼び出します。
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions \
'/bmad-product-brief ヘッドレスで実行してください（headless: true、intent: create）。
入力はこの一文だけです。ほかの情報はありません。
「当社製品の利用者向けのサポートサイトを作り、顧客の利便性を最大化したい。」
人に質問せず、スキルの Headless Mode の指示に従って製品概要を完成させ、最後に JSON の状態を返してください。' \
  < /dev/null > headless_brief.log 2>&1


  

 --dangerously-skip-permissions は、ファイルの書き込みやコマンドの実行を、確認なしに許す指定です。人に聞かずに最後まで走らせるために付けていますが、使ってよいのは、今回のように使い捨てのコンテナの中だけにしてください。
_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/briefs/brief-support-site-2026-11-09/
├── brief.md      製品概要
├── addendum.md   製品概要に入りきらない材料（調査の要点など）
└── .memlog.md    決定・推測・調査結果の記録


  

 フォルダ名の日付は、コンテナの時刻（協定世界時）で付きます。日本時間の朝に実行すると、前日の日付になります。
次の実験と混ざらないよう、ここでフォルダの名前を変えておきます。 実験2の製品概要も同じ日付のフォルダ名を使おうとするからです。
mv _bmad-output/planning-artifacts/briefs/brief-support-site-2026-11-09 \
   _bmad-output/planning-artifacts/briefs/brief-support-site-headless


  

 続けて、この製品概要からPRDを作らせます。
B=_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/briefs/brief-support-site-headless
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions \
"/bmad-prd ヘッドレスで実行してください（headless: true、intent: create）。
入力は製品概要 $B/brief.md と $B/addendum.md だけです。人に質問せず、スキルの references/headless.md の指示に従って PRD を完成させ、最後に JSON の状態を返してください。" \
  < /dev/null > headless_prd.log 2>&1


  

 今回は約13分かかり、586行のPRDができました。prds/prd-support-site-…/ には、PRDと記録ファイルのほかに、スキル自身が書いたレビュー（review-rubric.md、review-polish-*.md）と、入力の製品概要との突き合わせの結果（reconcile-brief.md など）も残ります。
{
  "status": "partial",
  "intent": "create",
  "open_questions": [
    "★Q1 製品は何か（業務ソフトウェア／消費者向け／機器）。利用者の人数と職種",
    "Q2 現状の問い合わせ件数・内訳・解決までの時間（目標値と最初の記事の選び方が決まる）",
    "★Q3 既存の FAQ・マニュアル・問い合わせ窓口は何で、誰が管理しているか。問い合わせ窓口から何を取り込めるか",
    "…（全10件）"
  ],
  "assumptions": [
    "製品は業務ソフトウェアで、利用者は製品の専門家ではない業務担当者",
    "…（全12件）"
  ]
}


  

 status が complete（完了）ではなく partial（人の確認が要る）になっていること、そして open_questions（人が答えるべき問い）と assumptions（推測で置いた前提）が並んでいることを確かめてください。AIだけで作った文書の価値は、本文よりも、この2つの一覧にあります。
実験1を、1本のスクリプトで
#
 製品概要、フォルダ名の変更、PRDまでを1本にまとめたものです。お題を変えたいときは、REQUEST="（あなたの要望）" bash run_experiment1.sh のように、要望の一文を差し替えて実行します。ログは trials/support-site/logs/ に残ります。実行するのは、trials/ がある作業フォルダの最上位からです。
 やり直すときは、先に古い brief-support-site-headless フォルダを消すか名前を変えてください。残したままだと、新しい製品概要がその中に入れ子で移されてしまいます。
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 実験1：要望の一文だけを渡し、AIだけ（ヘッドレス）で製品概要とPRDを作らせる
# 開発コンテナの中で実行：bash run_experiment1.sh [作業フォルダ]
# お題を変えるとき：REQUEST="（あなたの要望）" bash run_experiment1.sh
set -euo pipefail
cd "${1:-trials/support-site}"
REQUEST="${REQUEST:-当社製品の利用者向けのサポートサイトを作り、顧客の利便性を最大化したい。}"
BRIEFS=_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/briefs
HEADLESS="$BRIEFS/brief-$(basename "$PWD")-headless"
mkdir -p logs

echo "== 1/3 製品概要をAIだけで作る（数分かかります）"
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions \
"/bmad-product-brief ヘッドレスで実行してください（headless: true、intent: create）。
入力はこの一文だけです。ほかの情報はありません。
「${REQUEST}」
人に質問せず、スキルの Headless Mode の指示に従って製品概要を完成させ、最後に JSON の状態を返してください。" \
  < /dev/null > logs/headless_brief.log 2>&1

echo "== 2/3 実験2と混ざらないよう、フォルダ名を変える"
SRC=$(ls -dt "$BRIEFS"/brief-* | grep -v -- '-headless$' | head -1)
mv "$SRC" "$HEADLESS"
echo "   $SRC → $HEADLESS"

echo "== 3/3 その製品概要から、PRDをAIだけで作る（十数分かかります）"
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions \
"/bmad-prd ヘッドレスで実行してください（headless: true、intent: create）。
入力は製品概要 $HEADLESS/brief.md と $HEADLESS/addendum.md だけです。人に質問せず、スキルの references/headless.md の指示に従って PRD を完成させ、最後に JSON の状態を返してください。" \
  < /dev/null > logs/headless_prd.log 2>&1

echo "完了。最後の JSON（status、open_questions、assumptions）を確認してください："
echo "  tail -60 $PWD/logs/headless_prd.log"


  


8. 実験2：人が答えて通す
#
 同じ要望で、今度はAIの問いに人が答えながら製品概要を作ります。Claude Code を普通に起動して、対話で進めます。
claude


  

 スキルを呼び出して要望を書きます。実験1のフォルダを再開しないよう、一言添えます。
/bmad-product-brief 製品概要を新しく作成したいです（既存の briefs/brief-support-site-headless は別の実験なので再開しないでください）。

当社製品の利用者向けのサポートサイトを作り、顧客の利便性を最大化したい。


  

 アナリストは、次の順で進めてきます。
頭の中を全部出す：製品、利用者、困りごと、きっかけを、順番を気にせず書くよう求められます。手元の資料の有無も聞かれます
ほかにないか：関わる人、過去の失敗、避けたいこと
進め方を選ぶ：「速い道（Fast path）」（残りを数問にまとめて聞き、推測の印付きで一気に下書き）か、「じっくりの道（Coaching path）」（一節ずつ、押し返されながら書く）か。日本語で動かすと、エージェントはこの2つを「速い道」「じっくりの道」のように訳して示してきます
下書きと押し返し：いちばん弱い点を問い返され、推測した箇所の正誤も聞かれます
仕上げ：記録ファイルの各項目の反映先を確かめ、文書の見直しをかけて完成です
 答えられない問いには「不明」「いまは決められない」と答えて構いません。アナリストは、推測の印付きで埋めるか、「分かっていないこと」として残します。分からないことを分からないと言えるのが、この進め方のいちばんの使いどころです。途中で調査の結果が届くこともあります。アナリストが裏で Web 調査を走らせているからです。
claude -p --resume で1往復ずつ進めましたが、普段は対話で十分です）。この製品概要からPRDに進むときは、勧められるとおり新しい会話で bmad-prd を始め、実験1のPRDのフォルダと名前がぶつからないよう注意してください。
9. 結果の読み方
#
 前編では、次の3つの観点で評価しました。
観点
主に見る実験
見るもの




1. いいなりになると、どうなるか
実験1
推測の印、未確認の問い、それらの上に積み上がった文書の量


2. AIとの対話は、成立するか
実験2
聞いたことの言い直し、答えに応じて次の問いが変わるか、「不明」をどう扱うか


3. 対話は、人のアイディアを洗練させたか
実験1と2の比較
お題の書き換え、見立ての扱い、AIの提案を人が直した記録



 2つの実験ができたら、次の順で読み比べます。①が観点1、②と④が観点2と3、③が3つすべてに効きます。
① 推測の印を数えて、一覧にする
cd trials/support-site/_bmad-output/planning-artifacts   # 作業フォルダの最上位から
grep -n "\[ASSUMPTION" briefs/brief-support-site-headless/brief.md
grep -c "\[ASSUMPTION" prds/*/prd.md


  

 今回、実験1の製品概要には5か所、PRDには31か所ありました。この数が、人が確かめるべきことの数です。なお、製品概要の grep には「推定で補った箇所には [ASSUMPTION] を付け…」という説明の文も1行ヒットするので、その分は差し引いて数えます。
 数や行数、所要時間は、実行するたびに変わります。検証のためにもう一度通したときは、PRDが482行、推測の印が27か所でした。記事の数字は目安と考えてください。
② 記録ファイルで、取り下げられた推測を見る
 .memlog.md の各行には、decision（決定）、assumption（推測）、override（取り下げ・上書き）、insight（調査の発見）、gap（分かっていないこと）などの種類が付いています。
grep "^- (assumption)" briefs/*/.memlog.md
grep "^- (override)"   briefs/*/.memlog.md


  

 記録ファイルの中身は、たとえば次のようになっています（今回の実物から抜粋）。実験1では推測と調査の発見が、実験2では人の答えによる決定と取り下げが並びます。
# 実験1（AIだけ）の記録から
- (assumption) 製品は B2B の業務ソフトウェア（パッケージ/SaaS）と仮定。根拠なし：『当社製品の利用者』『顧客』の語のみ。B2C や物理製品なら構成が変わる
- (assumption) 現状の問い合わせ窓口は電話・メール中心で、FAQ/マニュアルは分散または PDF と仮定
- (insight) 調査：自己サービスで完全解決は14%、最大の失敗理由は『関連情報が見つからない』43%（Gartner 2024）。サイトの核は記事の量より『見つかること』

# 実験2（人が答える）の記録から
- (decision) 現状の窓口：簡単なサポートサイトが既にある。問い合わせはメール・電話・担当営業経由
- (decision) 今のサイトが役立たない理由：記事が足りない（c）・探しにくい（b）とユーザーは見ている（確かめた結果ではなく見立て）
- (decision) 言い換え（AIの提案、ユーザー未確認）：『サイトを作る』ではなく『操作の質問を、利用者が人に聞かずに短時間で解決でき、それでも残る質問は開発者でない窓口で受ける』状態をつくる
- (override) 『AI自動応答を最初の版に含めない』の仮定を取り下げ、AIの活用を最初の版の範囲に入れた（ユーザー回答：AIも活用したい）。使い方は PRD で決める（候補：記事をもとにした回答／記事の下書き作成／一次窓口の補助）


  

 実験1の1行目と2行目が、実験2の1行目で覆されていることが分かります。こうして記録を突き合わせると、前編の表がそのまま作れます。
 実験2で override になっている行は、AIの推測を人の答えが覆した記録です。今回は、「最初の版にAIによる自動応答は含めない」という推測が、私の「AIも活用したい」の一言で取り下げられていました。
③ 実験1の推測と、実験2の答えを突き合わせる
 実験1の assumptions と open_questions を左に、実験2で人が答えた内容を右に並べます。前編の表は、この突き合わせから作りました。当たった推測、外れた推測、問いとして残したのが正解だったもの、の3つに分けると、道具の振る舞いが見えてきます。
④ AIの提案と、人の決定を分ける
 実験2の製品概要を読み、「人が答えたこと」と「AIが提案して、人がまだ了承していないこと」を分けます。今回は、アナリスト自身が、冒頭の言い換えを「私の提案で、まだ了承をもらっていない」と申告してきました。了承していない提案は、決定として次の工程に渡さないでください。
10. つまずいたところ
#
症状
原因と対処




ブラウザで「無効な OAuth リクエストです」
ログインURLのコピーが途中で切れている。ターミナルを広げて1行に収めてからコピーする


「That code wasn't accepted」
URLを発行したのと別の Claude Code にコードを貼った。発行した画面に貼る


初回起動で Claude Code が終わってしまう
フォルダの信頼の確認で、既定の「No, exit」を選んだ。起動し直して「Yes」を選ぶ


エージェントに「Node」と呼ばれる
呼び名の既定はOSのユーザー名。_bmad/custom/config.toml で user_name を設定する


_bmad/config.toml に English と書かれている
実際に使われる値は別に決まる。resolve_config.py の出力で確かめる


成果物のフォルダの日付が前日になる
コンテナの時刻が協定世界時。実害はないが、記録するときは注意


実験2が実験1の続きを始めようとする
同じ日付のフォルダ名を使うため。実験1のフォルダ名を変えておき、呼び出し時にも一言添える




おわりに
#
 手順そのものは思ったより簡単で、インストールに数分、AIだけの実験に20分ほどです。いちばん時間がかかったのは、実験2でAIの問いに私が答える時間でした。それこそが、この道具の正しい使い方なのだと思います。
open_questions と assumptions の一覧を手に、人が答える実験に臨むことです。自分が何を分かっていないのかが、驚くほどはっきりします。ぜひ、手元のお題で試してみてください。
前編：「『AIいいなり開発』への不安を、BMADは解消してくれるのか？」／次回: 「POが多忙でチームに来ません」（12/1）／本編の連載一覧は第1回をご覧ください。

articles.title: ElevenLabs launched 13 products this week. Only 3 matter if you build voice agents.
articles.description:
Disclosure: this piece contains an affiliate link. If you sign up through it, I earn a commission at no extra cost to you.
ElevenLabs held its New York Summit on 11 November and announced 13 new products and upgrades. The headline is that it stopped being a voice tool. It is now a platform for voice agents, and the announcements split into two groups: things you can use today, and things that are for large enterprises with a sales call in between.
I tested the tools that claim to do the same work I do, so here is the split that matters if you build agentic workflows.
1. ElevenAgents Campaign Manager — live now. Announced 9 November, and it is the one I would try first. It runs outbound campaigns: you give it contacts and a goal — a qualified lead, a confirmed appointment — and it works each contact toward that goal, retrying when nobody picks up, calling back when someone asks for Thursday at 4pm, and stopping when a person opts out. It runs on the agents and phone numbers you already have in ElevenAgents, and contacts go in by CSV or API. Phone calls and WhatsApp voice and messaging work today; email and SMS are coming soon. It ran live beta campaigns across insurance, banking and ecommerce before launch.
This is the loop I build by hand in n8n today: call, check the outcome, retry on a schedule, keep the context between touches. Campaign Manager puts that loop inside the voice platform. The honest read is that the voice agent is the front door and something still has to do the work behind it — the CRM lookup, the booking, the follow-up. That is where n8n sits in my stack, and it is still where it sits after this launch.
2. Scribe v3 and Scribe v3 Live — live now. Announced 10 November. Scribe v3 is the recorded-audio transcription model, covering 102 languages. Scribe v3 Live is the low-latency real-time variant, with speaker labelling as it goes, and it is live in ElevenAgents today. Both are in ElevenAPI. If you run voice agents, transcription quality is the part that decides whether the agent understands the caller at all, and this is the piece of the Summit that is already in the product rather than on a roadmap.
3. ElevenAI — free early access, open now. A workplace app that listens to spoken conversations, including in-person meetings, and turns them into notes, summaries and action items. It can also give live assistance during a call. ElevenLabs built notice and consent mechanisms into it, which matters — a meeting recorder that does not ask first is a liability, not a feature. Early access is free and open with the announcement. This is the one to try with no budget and no sales call.
The rest of the Summit is real, but it is not for a solo builder today, and I will not pretend otherwise.
The Marketplace is a curated catalog of partner-built industry apps — healthcare, financial services, insurance, education, retail, government — from more than 20 partners at launch, including Salient for borrower servicing calls, Gail by Lula for insurance inquiries, and Zendesk for customer service. You can browse the apps and contact the developers today. You cannot buy through it yet: purchasing through existing ElevenLabs commitments is planned to start in 2027.
Model customization lets selected enterprises work with ElevenLabs researchers to fine-tune open-source language models and ElevenLabs voice models on data from their own live deployments, tuned to metrics like customer satisfaction. It begins in the coming months, for selected enterprises first. Scribe v3 Medical — a transcription model built for healthcare terminology — already exists, and a financial-services model is in development. If you are not a large enterprise, this is a roadmap item, not a product you can sign up for.
The Interaction Engine is a preview: a system that manages turn-taking, interruptions and model selection inside a conversation. Memory (an agent keeps context across interactions, so callers stop repeating themselves) and Routines (multi-step work before, during and after a conversation) are coming to ElevenAgents. None of the three is shipped yet.
The Partner Program itself is now 550+ partners across 44 countries, including Google Cloud, IBM, Deloitte, DXC and Genesys. ElevenLabs also expanded its NVIDIA work — Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is in ElevenAgents, with 15 MW of Vera Rubin compute planned on top of existing Blackwell Ultra systems. A Unity SDK for ElevenAgents landed 5 November, so game players can talk to NPCs out loud — desktop and WebGL supported, iOS, Android and XR in beta. None of that changes what I build this week.
Campaign Manager is a real product, not a demo. It shipped after live beta campaigns, it runs on the agents and numbers you already have, and the retry and callback logic is the part that usually takes a builder a week to get right.
Scribe v3 Live is in the product today. Real-time transcription with speaker labelling, inside ElevenAgents, no waitlist mentioned.
ElevenAI early access is free and open. No sales call to try the one consumer-shaped product in the whole announcement.
The API is still the product. ElevenAPI carries the new models, and the whole stack is built to be called from outside — which is why it fits an n8n workflow instead of fighting it.
Nothing about ElevenLabs broke this week. The hard part is the gap between the announcement and the product.
Three honest limits:
Most of the Summit is not shippable yet. Marketplace purchasing waits until 2027. Customization starts in the coming months for selected enterprises. Memory, Routines and the Interaction Engine are coming, not live. If you buy on the keynote alone, you are buying a roadmap.
Campaign Manager is phone and WhatsApp only for now. Email and SMS are coming soon, and new customers have to go through sales rather than signing up in the app. Existing ElevenAgents users find it under Campaigns in the Agents sidebar.
The enterprise pricing is undisclosed. No prices were given for the customization work or the Marketplace. The self-serve plans are public — Free at $0, Starter at $6, Creator at $22, Pro at $99, Scale at $299, Business at $990 a month — but the Summit's biggest items have no number attached.
None of that is a reason not to use it. It is a reason to use the three things that are live, and to wait on the rest until it ships.
ElevenLabs fits if you run voice agents in real workflows — outbound calls with a goal, meeting notes that need to be right, transcription in more than one language — and you want the voice layer to be an API you call from n8n rather than a dashboard you babysit.
It fits agencies that run outbound for clients: Campaign Manager is the first piece of this launch that does a job an agency bills for, today.
It does not fit if you only need text-to-speech for a video or a voiceover. The free tier covers that, and the Summit news is about agents, not voices. And if you are a solo builder waiting on the Marketplace or model customization, the honest answer is to try ElevenAI and Scribe v3 now and check back when the enterprise pieces ship.
ElevenLabs' programme pays 22% of payments on Starter, Creator, Pro and Scale plans for the first 12 months of a referred subscription, and 11% on the Business tier, through PartnerStack. Enterprise purchases earn nothing. Commissions clear about 90 days after the payment they come from. If you try it through my link, that is the arrangement: https://whoisalfaz.me/go/elevenlabs
And if the voice agent you build sits behind n8n schedules, check the 3.0 guide before December. The Cron node your workflows use today is gone in 3.0: https://whoisalfaz.me/blog/how-to-upgrade-to-n8n-3-without-breaking-workflows/
ElevenLabs is now a platform for voice agents, not a voice tool. Three of the 13 announcements are live and worth your time this week. The rest is a roadmap — a good one, but a roadmap.
Alfaz Mahmud Rizve — GTM & RevOps Architect. I build autonomous revenue systems for scaling agencies and SaaS: SEO & organic growth, high-speed Next.js apps, and self-healing n8n workflows. whoisalfaz.me

articles.title: How to Build an MVP Without Wasting 6 Months
articles.description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.
To build an MVP without wasting six months, start from one painful problem and one type of customer, write down the single job your product must do, cut every feature that doesn't serve that job, and put a working version in front of real users within weeks rather than quarters. Anything you can do by hand behind the scenes, do by hand at first. The goal of a minimum viable product is learning what customers will actually use and pay for, not shipping a smaller copy of your dream app.
This guide walks through how to create an MVP step by step, how to decide what to cut, and the mistakes that turn a six-week project into a six-month one.
Eric Ries, who popularised the term in The Lean Startup, describes the MVP as the version of a product that lets a team learn the most about its customers for the least effort. The term itself is older: it is generally credited to Frank Robinson in 2001, with Steve Blank and Ries spreading it later.
Two parts of that definition matter more than people expect:
"Learn" is the output. An MVP is a tool for answering a question, such as "Will restaurant owners pay monthly for this?" or "Will people upload their files to us instead of emailing them?" If you can't name the question, you aren't building an MVP yet.
"Least effort" is relative. Ries himself stresses that there is no formula for how small an MVP should be. For some ideas it's a landing page and a payment link. For others, like anything that handles money or health data, the minimum still has to be secure and reliable.
A useful test: if your first version answers your riskiest question, it is viable. If it also answers ten questions nobody asked, it isn't minimal.
Slow MVPs rarely come from slow coding. They come from decisions made before the first line of code. The usual causes:
Building for every future customer. Multiple user roles, team accounts, an admin dashboard with analytics, and five integrations, all before one person has signed up.
Perfecting things users haven't asked for. Custom design systems, animations, and settings pages for preferences nobody has.
Automating work that happens ten times a month. Writing an invoicing engine when you could send ten invoices by hand.
Scope that changes every week. Without a written, frozen scope, every conversation adds a feature.
Waiting for a big launch. Holding the product back until it feels "ready", then launching to silence.
Ries gives a good example of the cost of guessing: his team at IMVU once spent weeks on a feature nobody wanted, when a simple ad test could have shown the lack of demand far sooner. The fix for all five causes above is the same. Decide what you need to learn, and build only that.
"Independent wedding card sellers lose orders because customers can't see designs and prices online" is a usable problem. "A platform for events" is not. Pick one customer type you can actually reach this month.
Usually it is one of three: people don't have this problem, they won't switch from what they do now, or they won't pay. Your MVP exists to test that one assumption first.
Map the shortest path from "user arrives" to "user gets value". For a booking product, that's: see availability, pick a slot, confirm. Everything outside that path goes on a "later" list.
Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" is full of examples: Airbnb's founders recruited hosts door to door in New York, and Stripe's founders quietly set up merchant accounts for early users by hand. You can do the same. Approve signups manually, send reports by email, handle payments with a payment link, and take orders over chat.
Pick a fixed window, for example four to eight weeks, and cut scope to fit the window rather than stretching the window to fit the scope. Write the scope down and treat changes as trade-offs: something comes in, something goes out.
Graham's point about launches is blunt: big launches rarely matter, and what counts is a small core of users who genuinely like the product. Ship to 10 to 50 people you found yourself, watch how they use it, and talk to them weekly.

Photo: Patrick Perkins on Unsplash
This is the part founders find hardest, so here's a practical way to sort features. Ask of each one: "If this were missing, would a user in our core flow fail to get value?" If the answer is no, it waits.



Feature
In the MVP?
What to do instead




Sign up and log in
Usually yes
Use a managed auth provider instead of building your own


The core flow (book, order, upload, track)
Yes
This is the product


Payments
Only if testing willingness to pay
A hosted checkout or payment link


Admin dashboard
Minimal
A simple internal page, or the database console


Team accounts and roles
Rarely
Add when a paying customer asks


Native iOS and Android apps
Rarely
A responsive web app or PWA first


Analytics and reporting
No
Basic event tracking plus talking to users


Notifications
Maybe one
One email or push for the moment that matters


Integrations
Rarely
Manual export or a single webhook



A real example: when I co-founded and built Shahi Bulawa, a wedding card and e-invitation store, we went from zero to launch in about a month. Instead of building a full cart and checkout, each product leads customers to WhatsApp to request a quote or a free mockup. The Next.js catalogue, an admin panel and SEO-friendly pages were in scope; a complex ordering system was not. The store got around 15 orders a month from the first month. You can read the full Shahi Bulawa case study.
The best MVP stack is the one your developer can ship fastest and that won't need a full rewrite if the idea works. For most web MVPs, that means:
A mainstream framework such as Next.js or React, so hiring help later is easy.
A managed backend such as Firebase or Supabase for auth, database and storage, so nobody spends weeks on infrastructure.
Hosted payments rather than custom billing logic.
Simple hosting with automatic deploys.
AI app builders like Lovable, Bolt and Replit can get a prototype on screen in days, and for testing demand they are often a great value starting point. The catch is what happens when real users and real data arrive. We've covered the common security holes in AI-built apps separately; if you go this route, plan for a review before you take payments or store personal data.
Minimal is not the same as insecure: Cutting features is fine. Cutting security is not. Even a two-week MVP needs proper access rules on the database, secrets kept off the client, and validated input on every form. A data leak in month one can end a product before it starts.
Every project differs, but a focused web MVP often follows a shape like this:
Week 1: Scope. Problem statement, riskiest assumption, core flow, written feature list, and a "later" list.
Weeks 2 to 5: Build. Core flow first, then auth, then the minimum admin tools. A working preview every week.
Week 6: Private launch. Ten to fifty hand-picked users, manual onboarding, direct feedback.
Weeks 7 onward: Iterate. Fix what blocks users, add only what several users ask for, and decide whether the core assumption held.
If you want a sense of budget for each stage, see our breakdown of web app development cost in 2026 and the fixed options on the pricing page.
Building an MVP is a business decision before it is a technical one. Before you hire anyone or open an AI builder, you should be able to answer:
What single question will this MVP answer?
Who are the first 20 users, by name or by channel?
What is the one flow they must complete?
What will we do by hand for now?
What result would make us stop, change direction, or keep going?
If you can answer those, a capable developer can usually get a first version live in weeks. If you can't, no amount of code will save the six months.
If you'd like help scoping and shipping your first version, take a look at how I approach product development from idea to launch.
What is an MVP? (Lean Startup Co., quoting Eric Ries)
Do Things That Don't Scale, Paul Graham (July 2013)
Minimum viable product (Wikipedia)
Shahi Bulawa case study
Cover photo: Kvalifik on Unsplash
I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

articles.title: How to import a Flowise export into Cuttlely
articles.description:
Already have flows? Bring them over.
Cuttlely opens a chatflow or agentflow that you exported from Flowise as a JSON file. A browser wizard checks the file, lists the fixes it made, and opens the flow on the right canvas. You pick your credentials again, check the graph, and save. It's one flow at a time. Import from the Chatflows page for a new flow. Import from the gear menu on an open canvas of the same type and it replaces what's on that canvas, so Save overwrites that flow. Nothing is saved until you select Save.
Here's what you need:
Cuttlely 1.7.3 or later, installed and signed in. Haven't set it up yet? The quickstart gets you there.
The exported JSON file for each flow you want to move.
Your model keys. Keys don't travel in the file, so you'll add them in Cuttlely under Credentials.
The import runs in the browser wizard. There's no import API or CLI for it.
In Flowise, open the flow on its canvas.
Select the Settings gear in the canvas header.
Select Export Chatflow. On an agent canvas, the item is Export Agents.
Flowise downloads a JSON file named after the flow, such as Bakery helper Chatflow.json. The file holds the flow's nodes and edges. Flowise leaves password, file, and folder fields out of the export, and it strips saved credential ids too.
Cuttlely also accepts a saved flow whose flowData holds the nodes and edges, and template files that have nodes and edges. A whole-workspace export won't import. That's the file with several flows, tools, and variables in it. Export each flow on its own instead.
In Cuttlely, open Chatflows. Select Import at the top right, then select Import Flowise JSON. On a chatflow canvas, the gear menu has Import Flowise JSON too.
The Flowise migration wizard opens on its Upload step. Select Choose Flowise JSON and pick your file.

Start the wizard by choosing a Flowise chatflow JSON file. API keys are not copied.
On Scan, read what the wizard found. It counts the nodes and edges and lists what it fixed, such as a credential it cleared. Select Next.
On Credentials, note each card that needs a credential. Select Next.
On Nodes, look over the list. It shows older nodes that still work but are on their way out, and nodes Cuttlely can't place. Select Next.
On Result, select Open migrated canvas. Green means the wizard found nothing left for you to do. Amber means the canvas can open but something still needs you. Expect amber on most imports, because the wizard clears every saved credential.
The flow opens on the canvas that fits it. A chatflow goes to the chatflow canvas, and an agentflow goes to the agentflow canvas. Select a credential on each card the wizard named. With the default compact cards, select the card and set its credential in the side panel.

The imported flow opens on the canvas with its connections in place. Connect your OpenAI credential before you run it.
Select Save. The first save creates the published flow. Your next canvas save is a draft.
Want the rule-by-rule detail on what Scan checks? It's in Flowise migration wizard.
Don't put an imported flow to work straight off the wizard. Go over the canvas first and make sure each card connects to the cards you expect. Scan lists the edges the wizard removed so you can connect them again by hand, but check every connection yourself rather than relying on that list.
Then try the flow in the canvas chat. The chat runs your draft, so you can test it before anything goes live.
Here's what comes across:
Nodes. A node whose name is in Cuttlely's node catalog opens with its settings. The catalog has about 300 nodes. On a chatflow, a node saved with no version or an older one is refreshed to the current node.
Retiring nodes. Older nodes that are on their way out still open, and the wizard lists them.
Chatflows and agentflows. Each opens on its own canvas. Older multi-agent and sequential-agent flows open on the legacy agentflow canvas. They run and save there, but that canvas isn't offered for new work.
Custom tools. On Tools, Load reads an exported tool JSON file and opens it in the Add New Tool dialog, ready to save.
Some things won't come across. The partial list:
Keys, passwords, and saved credential ids. Cuttlely removes them before the canvas opens.
A whole-workspace export. Import one flow at a time.
LlamaIndex nodes. The wizard names each one and doesn't open the file.
A node Cuttlely doesn't have, or a node saved without its input and output lists. The wizard names it and doesn't open the file.
The Arize, LangFuse, LangSmith, LangWatch, Lunary, Opik, Phoenix, and AssemblyAI configuration cards. The wizard drops each one with a note on Scan and still opens the file. Set up tracing in Chatflow Configuration > Analytics, and transcription in Speech to Text.
Matching or creating credentials inside the wizard. You pick them on the canvas after it opens.
The saved zoom and position of the canvas.
The full list, including moving a whole install with its database, is in Bring your existing flows.
Select Publish when the flow is ready. On a chatflow or agentflow, the Publish dialog can run a few questions against your draft first. Every save is kept in version history. Both are covered in Drafts and Publish.
New to Cuttlely? Run the quickstart and you'll have it running on Docker before you open the wizard. If this got your flows across, star Cuttlely on GitHub so other devs can find it.

articles.title: Deleting your losers buys 4.1 points of hit rate: an audit protocol for model retirement
articles.description:
Every prediction system eventually grows a lifecycle manager: models get born, promoted, demoted and killed. Ours has 8,789 model rows and a retirement pipeline that runs every two hours. For a long time the number we published was computed over whatever models happened to still exist at query time — a mistake whose size is measurable.
46,160 graded predictions carry a boolean hit. The all-cohort rate is 57.05% (26,334 correct). The rate over models still in a live lifecycle state is 61.17% (19,281 of 31,520). Nothing about the models changed between those queries — only the WHERE clause did. A 4.12-point swing produced entirely by bookkeeping. In a system that retires models automatically, survivorship bias is not an edge case; it is the default output. What follows is the audit protocol we now run before any retirement decision.
There is no single "deleted" state. A model leaves the visible cohort through six different doors, and the aggregate rate treats each differently.

Three things stand out. First, the worst cohorts are also the smallest. demoted holds 2,937 model rows but only 1,014 graded predictions — 0.35 per model. pending_retrain holds 56 models and 318 predictions at 28.30%. These are not measured failures; they are barely-measured ones. A rule that fires on 0.35 observations per model is not selecting on quality, it is selecting on noise.
Second, eliminated is a real signal. 801 models, 7,950 graded predictions, 45.11% — 11.98 points below the evolving cohort on a sample worth reading.
Third: 4,854 graded predictions reference 525 model_id values that no longer exist in ai_models at all. Their score, 56.61%, is close to the pool average, and any metric written as JOIN ai_models silently drops every one of them. We also keep an ai_models_archive table with 4,054 rows, while archived_at is NULL on all 8,789 live rows — the primary table cannot tell you when anything was retired.
The protocol: publish two numbers from one query so they cannot drift apart — the headline, and its complement over the full historical cohort including rows whose model row is missing.
-- Cohort audit: the same graded rows, seen through two different filters.
WITH graded AS (
    SELECT p.id,
           p.model_id,
           p.hit,
           p.created_at,
           COALESCE(m.lifecycle_status, 'hard_deleted') AS lc
    FROM ai_predictions p
    LEFT JOIN ai_models m ON m.id = p.model_id
    WHERE p.settled = TRUE
      AND p.hit IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT 'all_cohort'      AS view,
       COUNT(*)          AS n,
       SUM(hit::int)     AS hits,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2) AS hit_rate
FROM graded
UNION ALL
SELECT 'live_only', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('evolving', 'active', 'incubating', 'validating')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'retired_cohort', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('eliminated', 'demoted', 'archived');

     view      |   n   | hits  | hit_rate
---------------+-------+-------+----------
 all_cohort    | 46160 | 26334 |    57.05
 live_only     | 31520 | 19281 |    61.17
 retired_cohort|  8964 |  3931 |    43.85
