articles.title: Circular Dependencies Between Modules in a Database: A Real Dependency, or One Table in the Wrong Module?
articles.description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.
TL;DR: A cycle between modules is counted from two things: the foreign keys, and the list that says which table belongs to which module. On a 34-table PostgreSQL store split into seven modules, ten cycles fell to three when addresses moved to the accounts module and to zero when stock_levels moved to shipping, with no constraint changed. A cycle is a real dependency when every table already sits with the module that writes it; then one foreign key has to go, or the two modules are one.
A circular dependency between two modules is not only a fact about your foreign keys. It is a fact about your foreign keys and about the list that says which table belongs to which module, and changing that list can remove the cycle without touching the database. So before you break a dependency, check whether one table is filed in the wrong module.
I measured it on a 34-table PostgreSQL 18.3 store with 43 foreign keys, split into seven modules. That split gave ten cycles between modules. Moving addresses from shipping to accounts left three. Moving stock_levels from catalog to shipping left none. Not one constraint changed. This post shows the query that counts the cycles, how to tell which tables are worth moving, and what a cycle looks like when no move can remove it.
Because module A depends on module B as soon as one table in A references one table in B, so moving a single table can add or remove a whole dependency.
Tools that check module structure treat a cycle as an error. Spring Modulith's verification requires that "the dependencies between modules have to form a directed acyclic graph", and the acyclic dependencies principle says the same about packages. Those checks read the code. The database has the same graph, drawn by foreign keys, and those checks never read it.
Here is the part of the store that matters. A user has addresses, a user has a default address, and a warehouse has an address:
CREATE TABLE users (
    id                  BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email               TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    default_address_id  BIGINT
);

CREATE TABLE addresses (
    id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    line1    TEXT NOT NULL
);

ALTER TABLE users
    ADD CONSTRAINT users_default_address_id_fkey
    FOREIGN KEY (default_address_id) REFERENCES addresses (id);

CREATE TABLE warehouses (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    address_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES addresses (id)
);


I had filed addresses under shipping, next to warehouses, carriers and shipments. That one choice makes accounts depend on shipping (users.default_address_id) and shipping depend on accounts (addresses.user_id). File addresses under accounts and both of those keys stay inside one module. The keys are the same; the cycle is gone.
Write the module of each table into a small table, join it to pg_constraint twice, and walk the result with a recursive query.
The mapping is the part no catalog can give you, so it is a table you fill in:
CREATE TABLE table_domains (
    table_name  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    domain      TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO table_domains (table_name, domain) VALUES
    ('users', 'accounts'), ('roles', 'accounts'), ('user_roles', 'accounts'),
    ('sessions', 'accounts'), ('password_resets', 'accounts'),
    ('addresses', 'shipping'), ('carriers', 'shipping'), ('warehouses', 'shipping'),
    ('shipments', 'shipping'), ('shipment_items', 'shipping'),
    ('brands', 'catalog'), ('categories', 'catalog'), ('products', 'catalog'),
    ('product_variants', 'catalog'), ('product_images', 'catalog'),
    ('stock_levels', 'catalog'), ('reviews', 'catalog'),
    ('campaigns', 'marketing'), ('coupons', 'marketing'),
    ('newsletter_subscriptions', 'marketing'), ('wishlists', 'marketing'),
    ('carts', 'orders'), ('cart_items', 'orders'), ('orders', 'orders'),
    ('order_items', 'orders'), ('order_status_history', 'orders'),
    ('payment_methods', 'billing'), ('invoices', 'billing'),
    ('payments', 'billing'), ('refunds', 'billing'),
    ('tickets', 'support'), ('ticket_messages', 'support'),
    ('ticket_attachments', 'support'), ('return_requests', 'support');

The first query lists every dependency between two modules, with the tables that cause it:
SELECT c.domain AS from_domain, p.domain AS to_domain,
       count(*) AS foreign_keys,
       string_agg(k.conrelid::regclass::text, ', '
                  ORDER BY k.conrelid::regclass::text) AS from_tables
FROM pg_constraint k
JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
GROUP BY c.domain, p.domain
ORDER BY 1, 2;

On the store it returns 14 rows. Three of them point out of shipping and three point into it, which is where every cycle will turn out to run:



from_domain
to_domain
foreign_keys
from_tables




accounts
shipping
1
users


catalog
shipping
1
stock_levels


orders
shipping
1
orders


shipping
accounts
1
addresses


shipping
catalog
1
shipment_items


shipping
orders
1
shipments



The second query walks those dependencies and prints each cycle once, starting from its alphabetically first module:
WITH RECURSIVE edges AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT c.domain AS src, p.domain AS dst
    FROM pg_constraint k
    JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
    JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
    WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
),
walk AS (
    SELECT src AS start, dst AS at, ARRAY[src] AS path
    FROM edges
    UNION ALL
    SELECT w.start, e.dst, w.path || e.src
    FROM walk w
    JOIN edges e ON e.src = w.at
    WHERE w.at <> w.start
      AND w.at > w.start
      AND NOT w.at = ANY (w.path)
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' > ') AS cycle
FROM walk
WHERE at = start
ORDER BY cardinality(path), cycle;

It returns seven:
accounts > shipping
catalog > shipping
orders > shipping
accounts > shipping > catalog
accounts > shipping > orders
catalog > shipping > orders
accounts > shipping > orders > catalog

The query reads declared foreign keys only. This store also has three columns the application treats as references with no constraint behind them: orders.coupon_id, tickets.order_id and return_requests.shipment_id. The first one adds a dependency from orders to marketing, and with it three more cycles the catalog cannot see. Counting those three columns, there are ten.
Now move the table. One UPDATE each, and the cycle query again:
UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'accounts' WHERE table_name = 'addresses';
UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'shipping' WHERE table_name = 'stock_levels';

After the first UPDATE the query returns two cycles, catalog > shipping and catalog > shipping > orders. After the second it returns no rows.
Two limits before you trust it on your own database. The join is an inner join, so a table missing from table_domains drops out of the count without an error, and conrelid::regclass::text writes a table outside the search_path as shop.addresses and a mixed-case or reserved name in double quotes, so the mapping has to spell names the same way. This lists every table the mapping misses (it will name table_domains itself, which is fine):
SELECT c.oid::regclass AS unmapped_table
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p')
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND c.oid::regclass::text NOT IN (SELECT table_name FROM table_domains);

The tables that hold a foreign key into another module, and of those, the ones whose rows the other module writes.
Counting is a poor guide, and I checked that by brute force. With 34 tables and seven modules there are 204 ways to move one table to another module. A script tried all of them against the ten cycles:



Result of moving one table
Moves
Example




Fewer cycles
38

addresses to accounts: 3


Same count
77

sessions to billing: 10


More cycles
89

warehouses to support: 25



More than twice as many moves make it worse as make it better, and the second best move by the numbers is nonsense: putting users in the catalog module leaves four cycles. A low count proves nothing about whether the table belongs there.
So ask who owns the rows, and use the count only to confirm. Two questions settle most tables:
Which module writes it? An address row is created when a user fills in a form, and addresses.user_id is NOT NULL with ON DELETE CASCADE: the row cannot exist without its user and dies with it. That is accounts. Shipping reads addresses; it does not own them.
If more than one module writes it, whose fact is it? stock_levels has a composite primary key of variant_id and warehouse_id and one quantity column. It is contested: receiving and dispatch change it, and an order flow that reserves stock would too. What tips it is the key. A row is a quantity at a warehouse, and warehouses belong to shipping, while the catalog describes what a product is, not how many are on a shelf. A team that runs stock as its own inventory module would file it there, with warehouses, and get the same zero.
A third option is to give the contested table a module of its own. That does not help when two tables reference each other. I put addresses alone in a new locations module and got four cycles, one of them accounts > locations, because users and addresses point at each other. Two tables that reference each other form a cycle wherever you draw the line between them; they can only share a module, or lose one of the two keys.
It is real when every table already sits with the module that writes it and the cycle is still there.
To see one, I added a column that many order tables grow sooner or later, on top of the cycle-free split:
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN latest_shipment_id BIGINT REFERENCES shipments (id);

The cycle query returns one row, orders > shipping: shipments.order_id points one way and the new column points back. Both tables are where their writers are: the order flow writes orders, dispatch writes shipments.
The move test agrees. I ran the 204 single moves again and exactly one clears the cycle: moving orders into the shipping module, which leaves an orders module without its orders table. Moving two tables together, shipments and shipment_items into orders, clears it as well, and that is not a table changing module. It is shipping losing its shipments, which is merging the two modules under another name.




Boundary cycle
Real cycle




What clears it
Moving one table to the module that writes it
Only moving tables away from the module that writes them, or merging two modules


Schema change needed
None
One foreign key dropped or turned around


On the store

addresses and stock_levels: ten cycles to zero
orders.latest_shipment_id


Who decides
Whoever owns the module list
Whoever owns the two modules' code



For a real cycle one direction has to go. Here the back reference is the weak one: the latest shipment of an order is the row in shipments with the highest id for that order_id, so a query can derive it and the column can be dropped. Dropping only the constraint and keeping the column does not count: the reference is still there, the catalog query just stops seeing it, as it already fails to see orders.coupon_id. When neither direction can go, merging the two modules is the honest answer: they were one module all along.
It counts the cycles from the diagram's context views, so trying a table in another module is a drag, one button and a new count.
Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. To understand your schema at the module level it has two pieces. A context view is a saved, focused view of the schema that shows only a subset of entities and the relationships between them. The Context Map draws each context view as one node and derives the arrows between them from the foreign keys in the diagram.
I connected the store, grouped its tables into seven legends, and made a context view per legend with Sync from legends. The map showed 17 dependencies and its Cycles list showed ten cycles, not seven, because the diagram also counts the three undeclared columns as inferred relations. Clicking an arrow lists the keys behind it, which is the list you need for the ownership questions above.


Moving a table is dragging it into the other legend and pressing Sync from legends again, which adds it to one context view and removes it from the other. After addresses moved, the map showed 15 dependencies and three cycles. After stock_levels moved, 14 dependencies and none.

An AI agent can do the same reading over the local MCP server. get_context_views returns the dependencies, the keys behind each and the cycles. The built-in prompt Organize a diagram by domain groups the tables from your codebase, puts a table several domains use with the domain that writes it, and ends by asking the agent to say, for each cycle, whether one table looks like it belongs in another domain or the dependency is real.
Schemity does not make that call itself. It lists every cycle the same way and does not mark one as a boundary cycle and another as real. The count is computed; the ownership decision is yours.
Check the module list before you change the schema.
A cycle that one sensible table move removes was never a dependency between the modules. List the foreign keys behind both directions. If one of them sits in a table the other module writes, move the table and count again. If every table is where it belongs, drop or turn around one key, and say in the review which one and why.
The same picture, drawn from a live database, is in how a DDD context map is already in your foreign keys. Once the cycles are gone, the remaining arrows are the keys that cross a boundary, and whether to keep foreign keys between modules is the next decision. If the database has no module names at all, start with grouping a legacy database by domain. And when two tables reference each other with NOT NULL columns, the problem is older than modules: the first row cannot be inserted.

articles.title: GitHub Actions Importer: what it converts and what it leaves for you
articles.description:
GitHub Actions Importer is a GitHub CLI extension, gh actions-importer, that runs in Docker and converts pipelines from Azure DevOps, Bamboo, Bitbucket Pipelines, CircleCI, GitLab, Jenkins and Travis CI into GitHub Actions workflows. Its audit, forecast, dry-run and migrate commands inventory a CI server, estimate Actions usage, convert one pipeline to local files and open a pull request, while secrets, runners and unknown plugins or orbs remain manual.

The five subcommands in the order to run them, with what each reads and writes. Only migrate opens a pull request.
You have more pipelines than you want to convert by hand, and you want to know which ones will convert cleanly before you promise a date. That is the job the Importer does best: it reads the CI server, converts every pipeline it can, and writes a report that sorts them by how much is left to do.
It is not a finished migration. GitHub's documentation sets the goal at 80% conversion per workflow and says every converted workflow should be inspected before it runs production work. This page covers each command, the files they write, the per-platform manual work, and the mapping details that change behavior.
The Importer is a container image plus a gh extension that drives it, so it needs Docker running and the GitHub CLI installed. It does not have to run on the CI server; it talks to it over the API.
configure prompts for a GitHub personal access token (classic) with the repo and workflow scopes, which migrate uses to open pull requests, plus the URL and token for your CI system, and writes them to .env.local. update pulls the latest image. The extension itself last tagged a release, v1.3.6, in October 2023; the converter ships in the image, so run update before each session.
gh extension install github/gh-actions-importer
gh actions-importer update
gh actions-importer configure
gh actions-importer version

All seven platforms support all four planning and conversion commands. What differs is the subcommand and the flag that identifies one pipeline for dry-run and migrate.



Platform
Subcommand
Names one pipeline with




Jenkins
jenkins

--source-url (the job URL)


GitLab, cloud or self-managed
gitlab

--namespace and --project



CircleCI
circle-ci
--circle-ci-project


Azure DevOps

azure-devops pipeline or release

--pipeline-id


Bamboo

bamboo build or deployment


--plan-slug or --deployment-project-id



Bitbucket Pipelines
bitbucket

--workspace and --repository



Travis CI
travis-ci
--travis-ci-repository



From each platform's "Migrating from ... with GitHub Actions Importer" page on docs.github.com, read 2026-11-12. For GitLab and CircleCI, audit needs an organization account; dry-run and migrate also work with a user account.
audit fetches every project on the server, converts each one and writes audit_summary.md beside the converted files. Pipelines land in four buckets: successful (everything converted), partially successful (the structure converted, some items did not), unsupported, and failed, which usually means the original was invalid or the token could not read it. Build steps are counted as known, unknown or unsupported, and a Manual tasks section lists the secrets and self-hosted runner labels you have to create. workflow_usage.csv lists the actions, secrets and runners each pipeline uses, which is the list a security review wants.
forecast reads completed runs, the previous seven days by default, and reports job count, execution time, queue time and concurrent jobs. Execution time is your minutes estimate and concurrent jobs is your runner count. On Jenkins it needs the paginated-builds plugin installed first.
gh actions-importer audit jenkins --output-dir tmp/audit
gh actions-importer audit gitlab --output-dir tmp/audit --namespace my-group
gh actions-importer audit circle-ci --output-dir tmp/audit --include-from repositories.txt
gh actions-importer forecast jenkins --output-dir tmp/forecast

Each platform guide on docs.github.com publishes a supported-syntax table and a list of constructs you must migrate manually. The manual lists are short and worth reading before the audit, because they predict most of the Manual steps section in every pull request.



Platform
Converts
Left for you




Jenkins
Declarative stage, docker; partially agent, environment, steps, triggers, when. Not matrix, options, parameters or input

Scripted pipelines, secrets, self-hosted runners, unknown plugins, mandatory build tools


GitLab

script, needs, stages, tags, variables, image, resource_group, schedule; partially rules, only/except, include, services, parallel, environment

Masked project or group variable values, artifact reports; no caching between jobs of different workflows


CircleCI
Jobs, steps, executors to runs-on, matrix, when/unless, cron; partially orbs, container and services

Contexts, project-level environment variables, unknown job properties, unknown orbs; self-hosted executors unsupported



dry-run converts one pipeline and writes the workflow to disk. This is where you shape the output before anything reaches a repository. Custom transformers are Ruby files passed with --custom-transformers: runner maps a source label to an Actions label, env rewrites or removes a variable or points it at a secret, and transform replaces an unknown build step, such as a Jenkins shared library call, with steps you define.
Map runners first. The documentation states that a label the Importer cannot map becomes ubuntu-latest, and runner :default changes that fallback.
# transformers.rb
runner "linux", "ubuntu-latest"
runner "big-agent", ["self-hosted", "xl", "linux"]
runner :default, "ubuntu-latest"

env "REGISTRY_PASSWORD", secret("REGISTRY_PASSWORD")

transform "deployService" do |item|
  { name: "deploy", run: "./scripts/deploy.sh" }
end

# then:
# gh actions-importer dry-run jenkins --source-url https://jenkins.example.com/job/app \
#   --output-dir tmp/dry-run --custom-transformers transformers.rb

migrate runs the same conversion and opens a pull request against --target-url. Its description carries a Manual steps section, usually the secrets to create. Merge only after the first run on a branch is green.
Read the environment variable mappings before you trust a converted condition. The Importer maps Jenkins BUILD_NUMBER to github.run_id, a large unique id, not the per-workflow counter github.run_number, so image tags change shape. It maps GitLab CI_COMMIT_BRANCH and CircleCI CIRCLE_BRANCH to github.ref, which is refs/heads/main, so a comparison against main silently goes false. GitHub's sample list-features output also shows actions/cache and reusable-workflows disabled; check yours and turn them on with --enable-features if your target supports them.
gh actions-importer list-features
gh actions-importer migrate jenkins \
  --source-url https://jenkins.example.com/job/app \
  --target-url https://github.com/my-org/app \
  --output-dir tmp/migrate \
  --custom-transformers transformers.rb \
  --enable-features actions/cache

Azure DevOps, Bamboo, Bitbucket Pipelines, CircleCI, GitLab (cloud and self-managed), Jenkins and Travis CI. Each has its own subcommand and its own guide on docs.github.com listing supported syntax and manual tasks.
No. The audit and the migration pull request list the secrets the converted workflows reference, and you create them in GitHub yourself. For GitLab, masked variable values are explicitly a manual task, and for CircleCI so are contexts and project-level environment variables.
No. GitHub lists scripted pipelines among the Jenkins constructs you must migrate manually. Declarative Jenkinsfiles and Freestyle jobs convert, fully or partially, and the audit tells you which.
No. It needs Docker and the GitHub CLI on any Linux-container-capable machine, plus API access to the CI server with a token that can read every job you want to audit. For Jenkins, folders that do not inherit permissions need explicit access for that token.

articles.title: Tenant-Isolated Next.js API Route for Private PDF Export via Signed Object Storage
articles.description:
For a gaming product that exports signed documents, the difficult part is not generating a PDF or signing a URL. It is proving that the player asking for the file belongs to the tenant that owns it, while still honoring a deletion deadline.
Short answer: keep the PDF private, store an application-owned export record, resolve the tenant's US or EU placement on the server, and let the authenticated Next.js API route mint a short-lived download URL only after the object and authorization checks pass.
That choice also gives the system a useful test target. A download request is either authorized and ready, authorized but still processing, or rejected. The browser never chooses the bucket, region, or object key.
The tempting implementation is a button that receives a storage URL from the export worker. It works in a happy-path demo. It makes a poor security boundary in a multi-tenant game, where a document might contain tournament results, moderation evidence, or a signed partnership agreement.
The durable record should be an export ID in the application database. It needs the tenant ID, the server-derived object key, the selected region, the export state, and the deletion deadline. The object store holds bytes; the application owns the relationship between those bytes and a tenant.
That separation matters after a browser refresh. A URL copied into a log or email should not become the application's permanent authorization record. The API route can issue a fresh link when the player asks for the file, and a cleanup worker can delete the object when its deadline arrives. A signed URL is delivery machinery, not identity.
Keep it private.
I also want the export state to be explicit. processing means the worker has not made a downloadable object available. ready means the application found the expected object for the already-authorized export. A missing object must not turn into a guess at a different key, a second render, or a client-controlled path.
Put the checks in this order:
Validate the authenticated session.
Load the export record by its application-owned ID.
Compare the session tenant with the record tenant.
Resolve the approved US or EU placement from trusted tenant configuration.
Use the stored key for that placement and check whether the object is ready.
Mint a temporary signed download URL for that exact object.
The client can send an export ID. It must not send a bucket, region, prefix, or object key and ask the route to sign it. That distinction is the tenant-isolation rule in one sentence.
Here is the decision logic behind the route. The storage adapter is intentionally generic: its job is to make the application policy visible, while the provider-specific signing implementation stays behind the interface.
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Protocol


class PrivateObjectStore(Protocol):
    def exists(self, *, region: str, key: str) -> bool:
        ...

    def sign_download(self, *, region: str, key: str, expires_seconds: int) -> str:
        ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Export:
    export_id: str
    tenant_id: str
    region: str
    object_key: str
    delete_at: datetime


def download_state(
    *,
    session_tenant_id: str,
    export: Export,
    store: PrivateObjectStore,
    now: datetime | None = None,
) -> dict[str, str]:
    current_time = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    if session_tenant_id != export.tenant_id:
        return {"state": "forbidden"}
    if current_time >= export.delete_at:
        return {"state": "expired"}
    if not store.exists(region=export.region, key=export.object_key):
        return {"state": "processing"}

    url = store.sign_download(
        region=export.region,
        key=export.object_key,
        expires_seconds=300,
    )
    return {"state": "ready", "download_url": url}

The real Next.js handler still has web concerns: parse the request, call the session and database layers, translate forbidden and expired into the application's response contract, and avoid putting secrets in the response. None of those concerns should change the storage key supplied to the adapter.
The deletion check belongs in this path even if a scheduled cleanup job exists. Cleanup is an operational action; authorization is a request-time decision. Those clocks can disagree for a while. A signed URL should also have a shorter lifetime than the document's retention window, so a link copied shortly before deletion does not become a long-lived access path.
There are two records to expire: the object and the application index. Mark the export expired according to the product's policy, stop issuing new links, and make the cleanup worker idempotent. If the worker runs twice, the second run should be an ordinary already-clean state, not a new export or a tenant lookup based on user input.
For a gaming workflow, deletion is often tied to an event: a competition closes, a dispute window ends, or an agreement reaches its retention date. Store that deadline as data. Do not calculate it from the browser's clock, and do not treat the timestamp embedded in a filename as policy.
HTTP caching is another easy place to leak the wrong thing. The authenticated API response should use an explicit private cache policy suited to the session. MDN documents Cache-Control response directives, including private and no-store; choose the directive that matches whether any local or shared cache may retain the response. The signed destination should remain temporary, and the PDF itself should not be made public merely to simplify browser delivery.
The export worker deserves its own boundary. Render the PDF, upload it to the server-selected region and key, then mark the export ready in the application database. If marking ready fails, the worker can retry the state transition without inventing a new object key. If the upload fails, the record stays processing and the retry policy can be evaluated separately from download authorization.
Notebook-to-prod thinking helps here: first write the cases as small assertions, then connect them to the route and storage adapter. I care about the assertions more than a polished demo because an AI-generated export can look correct while its authorization branch is wrong.
At minimum, evaluate this matrix:



Case
Expected result
What it protects




Matching tenant, object exists
Ready link for the stored key
Normal delivery


Matching tenant, object missing
Processing state
No guessed path or duplicate render


Different tenant, same export ID
Forbidden
Cross-tenant isolation


Deadline has passed
Expired, no new link
Retention policy


US tenant with EU request input
Use configured US placement
Region is not client-controlled


Link requested again
Fresh temporary link
No permanent URL record



The last two cases are where many quick examples get vague. Test both placements with the same export policy, and assert the exact region and key passed to the adapter. Also log an opaque export ID, tenant ID, placement, state transition, and request outcome. Do not log the signed URL or document contents.
Measure the stages separately: PDF render time, queue wait, object availability delay, link issuance, and cleanup lag. For generated documents, track prompt and token cost separately from storage latency. I’m not sure one aggregate download-time number would tell a team which part to fix; your mileage may vary, but stage-level measurements make the decision testable.
The answer depends on controls the product must own. A direct object-storage integration can be the right fit when the team needs a particular provider's retention, replication, lifecycle, or recovery features and is ready to operate that integration. A simpler abstraction can be preferable when the application needs the same private-object workflow across multiple backend capabilities, provided it exposes the required regional placement and deletion semantics.
Do not choose from a price table first. Compare the interfaces and the failure modes:



Decision question
Why it matters




Can the route sign only a server-derived key?
Prevents arbitrary object access


Can placement be selected and audited per tenant?
Makes US/EU policy testable


Can deletion be enforced before link issuance?
Separates retention from cleanup timing


Can the team observe upload, ready, and cleanup states?
Avoids treating storage as the export database


Does the integration supply the recovery and retention controls required by the product?
Prevents a private-download design from becoming an inadequate archive



The catch is that a private PDF delivery path is not automatically a document-archive design. If the game needs immutable legal retention, recovery from accidental overwrite, cross-region replication, or public asset delivery, choose a storage architecture that explicitly supplies those controls. Stick with the direct design when those requirements are central. Use the smaller private-export boundary when the application owns the index, the retention deadline, and the authorization decision.
Before copying the pattern, run the matrix against a real export lifecycle, including a worker retry and a cleanup retry. The useful result is not that one URL opened in a browser. It is evidence that a tenant can retrieve only its own ready document, from the approved placement, until the stated deadline.

articles.title: Model and Assemble a Scotch Yoke Mechanism
articles.description:
AI disclosure: This edition was prepared by an AI agent from the published Reactor 3D tutorial and its original interface screenshots. No physical printing or fit testing was performed for this edition.
Practice this browser CAD workflow in Reactor 3D. The guide below includes the complete modeling, assembly, and export sequence.
Build an eight-part Scotch yoke mechanism from a blank Reactor 3D Solid Model, assemble its moving joints, and export all printable parts in one STL.
Use millimeters, the world XY plane for the base, and +Z upward. Cube positions below refer to the center of the bottom face; cylinder positions refer to the center of the bottom circle. Unless stated otherwise, use zero rotation and scale 1. This lesson assumes basic sketch, selection, and Boolean modeling skills.
This is a hand-operated CAD demonstrator of rotary-to-linear motion. Its dimensions and clearances are chosen design targets; the model has not been physically printed or tested for load, wear, retention, or powered operation.
Component or target | Dimensions (mm)
Ground: 220 x 120 x 8 plate, R6 corners, four 5 mm feet
Crank: R28 disk, 5 thick, 20 eccentric radius
Yoke: 200 x 88 x 6; guide arms 12 wide
Slot: 10.4 wide x 64.4 overall, R5.2 ends
Sliding Block: 10 x 12 x 6, bore 6.4
Each guide: 16 x 32 x 18; window 12.4 x 6.4
Pivot Retainer: Head diameter 16 x 1.2; peg diameter 4.8 x 4
Pin Retainer: Head diameter 11 x 2; peg diameter 3.8 x 4
Output travel: 40 nominal, from a 20 mm crank radius
For physical assembly, supply four full-thread M3 x 30 socket-head screws and four M3 nuts, plus adhesive appropriate to the printed material for the two retainer pegs. The purchased hardware is excluded from the STL. Dry-fit the pegs before bonding and keep adhesive away from moving surfaces.
Start a blank Solid Model project in millimeters. Enter sketch mode on XY and draw a centered rectangle, 220 mm along X and 120 mm along Y. Use the vertex coordinates (-110, -60), (110, -60), (110, 60), and (-110, 60).

Enable vertex shaping and set all four corner radii to 6 mm from their vertex menus. Keep the 220 x 120 mm outside envelope, then choose Finish Sketch.

Select the closed loop and choose Extrude. Use Blind, 8 mm, New part, and confirm. Name the part Ground, keep its position at (0, 0, 0), and hide the source sketch.

Create a cylinder with Radius 8 mm and Height 5 mm. In Move, set its world position to (-90, -45, -5) with zero rotation. This puts its top against the underside of Ground.

Select the foot and open Array > Stepped. Set row axis X, count 2 including the source, step 180 mm; set column axis Y, count 2, step 90 mm. Confirm, select Ground first and all four feet next, then Combine with Keep source parts off.

Create a cylinder with Radius 5 mm, Height 6.4 mm, at world (0, 0, 8). Select Ground first and the cylinder second, then Combine, keeping source parts off. The pivot top is Z = 14.4 mm.

Choose Hole on the pivot’s top face. Use Simple hole, Straight, Single hole, diameter 5 mm, and depth 5 mm. In Position in part coordinates, use X = 0 and Y = 0; the selected top is local Z = 14.4 mm.

Create a cylinder cutter with radius 1.7 mm, height 8 mm, at (-70, -12, 0). Use Array > Stepped: X count 2, step 140 mm; Y count 2, step 24 mm, both including the source. These four cutters produce 3.4 mm clearance holes for M3 screws.

Select Ground as the target and the four mounting cylinders as tools. Choose Cut, switch Keep source parts off, and confirm. The holes pass through the full 8 mm plate at X = +/-70 mm and Y = +/-12 mm.

Create a cylinder with Radius 28 mm and Height 5 mm, at world (0, 0, 9) with zero rotation. The disk has a 1 mm gap above the plate. Name this blank Crank Blank; the finished part will be Crank.

Choose Hole on the disk’s top face: diameter 10.4 mm, depth 5 mm, straight single hole. Set local X = 0 and Y = 0 at top Z = 5 mm. Rename the finished part Crank; the 10 mm pivot has 0.2 mm radial clearance in this bore.

Create a cylinder with Radius 3 mm, Height 9 mm, at world (20, 0, 14). Combine it into Crank, keeping source parts off. Its 20 mm offset from the disk axis sets a nominal 40 mm yoke stroke.

On the pin’s top face, make a straight single Hole, diameter 4 mm, depth 5 mm. Use Crank-local X = 20 and Y = 0, at local top Z = 14 mm. The hole stops at world Z = 18 mm.

Hide Ground and Crank. On XY, use Line to draw and close the outline below; use each vertex menu’s Set Coordinates to enter the exact positions. The overall outline is 200 x 88 mm, with 12 mm wide guide arms and a 22 mm wide central frame.
Vertex order | X, Y (mm)
1-4: (-11, -44), (11, -44), (11, -6), (100, -6)
5-8: (100, 6), (11, 6), (11, 44), (-11, 44)
9-12: (-11, 6), (-100, 6), (-100, -6), (-11, -6)

Set Radius 3 mm at all twelve vertices, including the four inside shoulders where the arms join the frame. The rounded shoulders remove the sharp notches without changing the outside 200 x 88 mm envelope. Finish the sketch.

Extrude the loop Blind 6 mm as a New part, then name it Yoke. Use Move to set world position (20, 0, 16), zero rotation. Hide the source sketch; the yoke bottom now clears the crank disk by 2 mm.

Create a cube, Width 10.4 mm, Depth 54 mm, Height 6 mm. Place its bottom-center at world (20, 0, 16) with zero rotation. This cutter makes the straight portion of the through-slot.

Create a cylinder with Radius 5.2 mm, Height 6 mm, at (20, -27, 16). Use Mirror Duplicate, choose the World XZ plane, and confirm. The two cylinders form semicircular ends centered at Y = -27 and +27 mm.

Select Yoke first, then the straight cutter and both end cylinders. Choose Cut, keeping source parts off, and confirm. The through-slot is 10.4 mm wide, 64.4 mm long overall, with R5.2 ends.

Create a cube, Width 10 mm, Depth 12 mm, Height 6 mm, at world (20, 0, 16). Name it Sliding Block. Its two X-facing sides have 0.2 mm clearance per side inside the 10.4 mm slot.

On the block’s top face, make a straight single Hole, diameter 6.4 mm, depth 6 mm. Set local X = 0 and Y = 0 at local top Z = 6 mm. This gives the 6 mm crank pin 0.2 mm radial clearance.

Create a cube, Width 16 mm, Depth 32 mm, Height 18 mm, at world (-70, 0, 8). Name it Left Guide. Its bottom sits on Ground and its two mounting holes will line up with the left pair in the plate.

Create a cube cutter, Width 16 mm, Depth 12.4 mm, Height 6.4 mm, at (-70, 0, 15.8). It crosses the full X thickness of the guide. The window leaves 0.2 mm clearance on each Y and Z face of the 12 x 6 mm yoke arm.

Create a cylinder cutter with Radius 1.7 mm, Height 18 mm, at (-70, -12, 8). Use Mirror Duplicate > World XZ plane to create the cutter at Y = +12 mm. Both cutters align with the 3.4 mm holes already in Ground.

Select Left Guide first, then the window cutter and both mounting cylinders. Choose Cut, turn Keep source parts off, and confirm. The result has one horizontal rectangular window and two vertical through-holes.

Select Left Guide and use Mirror Duplicate > World YZ plane. Name the reflected part Right Guide. Its geometry is centered at world X = +70 mm; the mirrored part’s transform origin may retain the source origin, so use the visible geometry when checking its placement.

Create a cylinder, Radius 8 mm, Height 1.2 mm, at world (0, 0, 14.4). This head sits 0.4 mm above the crank and leaves another 0.4 mm below the yoke.

Create a cylinder, Radius 2.4 mm, Height 4 mm, at (0, 0, 10.4). Combine it with the head and name the result Pivot Retainer. The peg has 0.1 mm radial clearance and 1 mm bottom clearance in the 5 mm seat.

Create a cylinder, Radius 5.5 mm, Height 2 mm, at (20, 0, 23). Its underside is 1 mm above the block and yoke tops, allowing them to move beneath it.

Create a cylinder, Radius 1.9 mm, Height 4 mm, at (20, 0, 19). Combine it with the head and name the result Pin Retainer. Its peg has 0.1 mm radial clearance and 1 mm bottom clearance in the crank pin’s 4 mm seat.

Show all eight parts and enter Assemble. Create an assembly named Scotch Yoke Drive, set Ground as the position reference, and capture axis anchors from the Ground pivot’s outside cylinder and Crank’s central bore. In Relations, connect them with Revolute, aligned to Z; its RZ angle drives the crank.

Capture a plane from Ground’s broad top face at Z = 8 mm and a plane from Yoke’s top face at Z = 22 mm, both facing +Z. Add a Planar relation, Ground reference to Yoke target, with Distance 14 mm. This keeps the yoke horizontal while allowing in-plane travel.

Capture planes from Ground’s +Y outside face at Y = 60 mm and Yoke’s +Y end face at Y = 44 mm. Add a Planar relation with Ground as reference, Yoke as target, and Distance -16 mm. Together, the two plane relations guide the yoke along X.

Capture an axis from Crank’s eccentric pin and an axis from Sliding Block’s bore. Add a Revolute relation between these Z axes. The block follows the eccentric pin while remaining free to turn relative to Crank.

Capture a plane from Yoke’s +X arm end, world X = 120 mm at the starting pose, and one from Sliding Block’s +X face, world X = 25 mm. Add Planar, Yoke reference to block target, Distance -95 mm. This keeps the block centered across the slot while allowing it to slide along Y.

Capture a plane on Left Guide. Add a Fixed relation from Ground’s pivot axis anchor to that plane, preserving the current placement at (-70, 0, 8). The relation locks the guide to Ground rather than to the moving yoke.

Capture a plane on Right Guide and add a Fixed relation from Ground’s pivot axis anchor. Preserve the reflected guide’s current placement at geometric center X = +70 mm. Both guide windows should surround the yoke arms.

Capture a plane on Pivot Retainer and add Fixed from Ground’s pivot axis anchor, preserving its current placement. The cap belongs to Ground, so the crank can rotate beneath its head.

Capture a plane on Pin Retainer. Add Fixed from Crank’s eccentric pin axis anchor to this plane, preserving its current placement. The assembly now uses two Revolute, three Planar, and four Fixed relations.

Change the Ground-Crank revolute joint’s Angle RZ to 90 degrees, then try 180 and -90 degrees. The yoke passes through center at quarter turns and reaches X = +20 and -20 mm at opposite dead centers. Keep both arms inside the guide windows throughout this 40 mm stroke.

In Workspace, create the motion asset One Revolution with Duration 4000 ms. Choose the crank’s RZ driven joint, add a 0 degree keyframe at 0 ms and a 360 degree keyframe at 4000 ms, then enable Loop and press Play. Pause and clear the preview before returning to modeling.

Keep an assembled RD before changing the layout. In Modeling, use Move and Rotate Part with the values below; leave Rot Y and Rot Z at zero. Move Left Guide before Right Guide, because the mirrored geometry also follows its source.
Part | Move Pos X, Y, Z (mm) | Rot X (degrees)
Ground: 0, 0, 5; 0
Crank: -90, 100, 0; 0
Sliding Block: -38, 155, 0; 0
Left Guide: -90, 155, 0; 0
Right Guide: -225, 0, 8; 0
Pivot Retainer: -10, 175, 1.2; 180
Pin Retainer: 15, 175, 2; 180
Yoke: 45, 110, 0; 0
Right Guide’s numbers describe its retained transform origin; after moving the source, these values put its actual bottom-center at (-65, 155, 0). Ground rests on its feet, both retainers rest on their broad heads with pegs up, and every independent part has a gap around it.

Choose File > Export STL. In Choose export scope, select All visible models, confirm that it includes eight models, then choose Download in browser. Export one file, scotch-yoke-mechanism.stl; keep the parts independent rather than combining the mechanism into one solid.

The crank pin carries a separate sliding block inside the yoke slot. The block travels across the slot as the yoke moves through the two guides, producing a nominal 40 mm stroke without a connecting rod. At either stroke end, the 200 mm bar extends 2 mm beyond the far outside face of the engaged guide.
For a printed demonstrator, place Crank over Ground’s pivot and fit Pivot Retainer into its seat. Slide the yoke arms through both guides, place the guides over the plate holes, and fit Sliding Block over the eccentric pin inside the slot. Fit Pin Retainer last. Install the four M3 x 30 screws from the guide tops and secure the nuts below Ground; the 5 mm feet leave room beneath the plate. Bond only the two retainer pegs after confirming free movement.
scotch-yoke-mechanism.stl contains the eight separated printable parts. Split the imported file into independent objects in your slicer to arrange them across suitable build plates. STL does not retain the editable feature history, part names, joints, or motion asset; keep the assembled RD for editing.
The supplied separated layout occupies approximately 263 x 243 x 19.4 mm. It needs rearrangement or multiple plates on a 220 mm bed; a single STL does not mean a single print plate.
Review supports beneath Ground’s broad elevated plate and bridging or supports across the guide window roofs. Print the two retainers on their broad heads.
The 0.2 mm sliding gaps are per side or radial as specified in the relevant steps. They are CAD allowances, not a guarantee for every printer; start with a small fit trial and remove burrs before assembly.
Turn the disk gently by hand and watch the block at the slot ends. This demonstrator has no established powered speed, load capacity, or retainer pull-out rating.
Source: Model and Assemble a Scotch Yoke Mechanism, by the Reactor 3D Team. Interface screenshots and design instructions are from that original tutorial.

articles.title: Pertamina's 403 was about continents, not datacentres: we measured 163 nodes
articles.description:
Our GitHub Actions runner got a 403 from Indonesia's official fuel price site, and we assumed it was blocking datacentres. On 15 September 2026 we measured it from 163 nodes. Home connections in the US got the same 403, while AWS in Frankfurt got a 200.
I'm Katya, the digital character of the Harga BBM Hari Ini team. We run a static site with Indonesian fuel prices, rebuilt every day from official sources. This post is about one wrong guess and the measurement that replaced it. All numbers below are project data as of 15 September 2026.
The price table lives on www.pertaminapatraniaga.com, the site of Pertamina Patra Niaga. From a laptop it loaded fine. From a GitHub-hosted runner it answered 403.
The usual story writes itself: a WAF rule that refuses traffic from cloud IP ranges. If that were true, the fix would be to keep collecting from the laptop, which means a daily job that depends on a machine being awake.
Before building around that guess, we tested it.
We ran HTTP checks against the same URL from 163 nodes using two public services, check-host.net and Globalping. The point was to mix cloud providers and home ISPs in many countries, so the two explanations ("datacentre" vs "geography") would predict different results.
What came back:
403: the whole of the Americas, including home ISPs such as AT&T, Shaw and TELUS, plus Iran.
200: Europe, Asia and Oceania, including plenty of datacentres: AWS Frankfurt and Tokyo, Azure Singapore, Hetzner, OVH.
GitHub runners: they failed only because the hosted runners we got sit in Azure US.
So the datacentre theory was wrong in both directions. Residential connections in North America were refused, and cloud machines in Europe and Asia were let in. The pattern followed continents, not networks.
We also checked the official MyPertamina price API, api.web.mypertamina.id/price. It answered 200 from everywhere we tried, including the GitHub runner.
A different endpoint is only useful if it says the same thing, so we compared it cell by cell with the web table: 40 regions, 272 of 272 price cells matched.
That was enough to move collection from the laptop to a free GitHub Actions schedule. The change is commit 631d2a50c from 15 September 2026.
The API is official, but it has habits:
updatedDate is local Jakarta time (WIB, UTC+7) written with a Z suffix, so a naive parser shifts it by seven hours.
Prices arrive in more than one shape, for example "Rp 10.000" and "16300". In Indonesian notation the dot is a thousands separator.
"0" does not mean free. It means the product is not sold in that region.
A simplified sketch of how we normalise one cell (not our exact code):
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

WIB = timezone(timedelta(hours=7))

def parse_updated(raw: str) -> datetime:
    # "2026-09-02T00:01:00Z" is WIB despite the Z
    naive = datetime.fromisoformat(raw.rstrip("Z"))
    return naive.replace(tzinfo=WIB)

def parse_price(raw: str) -> int | None:
    digits = raw.replace("Rp", "").replace(".", "").strip()
    if not digits.isdigit():
        raise ValueError(f"unreadable price: {raw!r}")
    value = int(digits)
    return None if value == 0 else value   # 0 = not sold here

The ValueError matters: an unreadable price stops the build instead of quietly becoming zero.
A 403 tells you that you were refused, not why. Measure from several networks and countries before you design around a theory.
Mix residential and cloud vantage points. With cloud nodes only, we would have "confirmed" the datacentre story.
If you find a second official source, prove it agrees before you switch. 272 matching cells was our bar.
Write the quirks down as code, with a test, because the next person will trip on the same Z.
The resulting price tables for all 40 regions are on hargabbmhariini.com.
If you collect government data from abroad: have you ever measured where a block really starts, or did you build around the first explanation that fit?

articles.title: Your Webcam Is Your Health Check-Up
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
Human Health Insight is a web app for a quick wellness check using only a webcam. You sit in front of the camera, and in about a minute it shows your heart rate and breathing rate, live, using the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. When both readings have settled, it stops on its own and gives you simple, friendly health tips written by an LLM. Examples are "rest and measure again", "drink some water" or "consider a routine check-up with a doctor".
What it lets people do:
Check their vitals without a wearable. No smartwatch or pulse oximeter, just the laptop camera.
Get guided while measuring. The app passes on SmartSpectra's live feedback, such as "Move a little closer", "Too dark, add more light" or "Hold still".
Understand their numbers. Readings are put into plain-language bands (typical, low or high), and the app suggests a sensible next step.
Stay private and secure. Users sign in through Keycloak. Video is processed live in memory and never stored, and the AI only ever receives the two numbers, never who you are.
Human Health Insight gives wellness information, not a medical diagnosis. SmartSpectra's own documentation says its metrics are for general wellness and are not cleared for diagnosis or treatment. The app says this on every results screen.
The user flow
Log in on a custom Keycloak login page (health illustration on the left, form on the right).
From the dashboard, open Measure vitals and click Start measurement. The camera turns on with face-scan guides and a LIVE badge.
Watch heart rate and breathing update in real time, each marked Stabilizing… and then ✓ Stable reading.
The measurement stops automatically once both readings are stable.
Click Get health tips to see a 🟢 / 🟡 / 🔴 notice and personalised wellness tips.



Layer
Technology




Frontend
React 19, TypeScript, Vite


Authentication

react-oidc-context, OIDC + PKCE


Backend
Node.js, Express 5, TypeScript


Real-time Communication
WebSocket (ws)


JWT Verification
jose


Vitals / Health Signals

@smartspectra/node-sdk (Presage SmartSpectra)


Identity Provider
Keycloak 26


Database
PostgreSQL


Keycloak UI
Keycloakify (React)


AI / Health Tips
Ollama (gpt-oss:20b-cloud or other local models)


Fallback
Rule-based health recommendation engine


Deployment
Docker



  
  



  
  
  Code




  
 / 
        Human-Health-Insight
      
    



Presage signal
Where it comes from
How the app uses it





Pulse rate (heart rate, bpm)
metrics.cardio.pulseRate
Live reading card with a beating-heart icon; input to the health tips



Breathing rate (breaths/min)
metrics.breathing.rate
Live reading card with a breathing icon; input to the health tips


stable flag + confidence
Each MeasurementWithConfidence sample
Shows Stabilizing… or ✓ Stable reading; auto-stops the session; only stable values are used for tips


Validation status

validationStatus event (ValidationCode)
Real-time coaching: "No face found", "Too dark", "Too much movement", "Move closer"…



While measuring: every SmartSpectra metrics event goes straight to the browser over a WebSocket, so the heart-rate and breathing numbers update live. The heart icon beats and the breath icon moves while readings come in.
Coaching: each validationStatus code becomes a plain instruction. If the user leans away, turns off a light or starts moving, the message changes right away and tells them how to fix it.
Knowing when to stop: the backend watches the SDK's per-sample stable flag. When heart rate and breathing have both stayed stable for 3 seconds, the session ends by itself and the camera turns off. There's no fixed timer, so a calm, well-lit user finishes faster. A 120-second safety limit covers the case where readings never settle.
After measuring: only stable readings are sent for tips. An unsettled value (for example a breathing reading still "Stabilizing…") is left out and the user is told why, which avoids false alarms.
Health tips:



Fixed rules, not the AI, decide the band and urgency. Heart rate: under 40 or over 120 is 🔴, 40–49 or 101–120 is 🟡, 50–100 is 🟢. Breathing: under 8 or over 30 is 🔴, 8–11 or 25–30 is 🟡, 12–24 is 🟢.
The Ollama model then writes the friendly summary and 3–5 tips within those limits. It's told never to diagnose or suggest medication.
If the LLM is unavailable, built-in tips are shown instead, so the feature always works.
Most Creative or Delightful Use
The project turns a simple camera session into an interactive human-sensing experience. Instead of showing raw physiological signals as isolated numbers, it combines real-time human signals with an AI-powered explanation layer, making the results easier and more engaging to understand.
Best Thoughtful Real-World Use
The project is designed as a preliminary human health insights experience for people who want to understand their current physiological signals in a simple and accessible way. Users authenticate securely, provide explicit camera consent, and receive an easy-to-understand explanation of the signals captured during the session. The application is designed for informational and wellness purposes only and does not provide medical diagnosis, treatment, or medical decision-making.
The camera never starts on its own. The Start measurement button stays disabled until the user ticks "I agree to use my camera. Video is processed live and not stored."


It's always visible when the camera is on. The page shows the live preview, face-scan guides and a red LIVE · 12s badge, and the computer's camera light is on.
The user stays in control. Stop ends the session at any time. The camera is also released automatically when both readings are stable, when the 120-second safety limit is reached, or when the user leaves the page.
Only signed-in users can measure. The measurement connection requires a valid Keycloak login and accepts one session at a time. There's no background, scheduled or remote monitoring.
In browser mode (for remote deployments), the browser's own camera permission prompt is shown as well.



Data
Where it goes
Stored?




Camera frames
Processed in memory by the SmartSpectra SDK in the app's backend. In camera mode a small preview is sent only to the user's own browser
❌ Never saved to disk, never logged


Heart rate and breathing readings
Shown in the user's browser. Sent to the backend only when the user clicks Get health tips

❌ Not saved in any database. Gone when the page is refreshed or closed


Readings sent for tips
Just the two numbers and their bands (e.g. heartRate: 68, level: "normal"). No name, email or user ID

❌ Not stored by the app



Account (username, email, password hash)
Keycloak, backed by the app's own Postgres database
✅ Until the account is deleted


Server logs
Only frame counts (e.g. "29.8 fps, 149/149 accepted") and error codes
No frames, readings or identities



SmartSpectra (Presage): the SDK runs locally in the backend. SDK telemetry is turned off (enableTelemetry: false). The SDK still needs an API key that is checked with Presage's servers, per Presage's documentation. The app itself never uploads camera frames anywhere.
Optional AI service (Ollama): health tips are optional and only generated when the user clicks Get health tips. With the default cloud model (gpt-oss:20b-cloud), only the anonymous readings and bands are sent to Ollama's cloud; Ollama states it doesn't use prompts to train models. Setting OLLAMA_MODEL to a local model (e.g. qwen2.5:3b) keeps everything on the machine. If no AI is available, built-in rule-based tips are used and nothing is sent.
Video and readings: nothing is kept, so there's nothing to delete. Each measurement exists only for the length of the session.
Account: an administrator can delete a user in the Keycloak admin console (Users → user → Delete), which removes their login data from the database.
Developer console logs: readings are printed to the browser console only in development builds (npm run dev). Production builds don't log them.
Login: Keycloak with OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE. Tokens are kept in browser memory, not in localStorage. Every API call and the measurement WebSocket check the JWT's signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
WebSocket: only accepts connections from the app's own origin, requires a valid token as the first message, and has a 1 MB message limit and an authentication timeout.
Secrets: the SmartSpectra and Ollama keys live only in the backend's .env, never in frontend code.
The app does not diagnose, treat or make medical decisions. Every results screen says the readings are wellness information only and that camera-based readings can be inaccurate.
The 🟢 / 🟡 / 🔴 bands come from fixed general resting ranges, not from the AI. The most they suggest is resting and measuring again, a routine check-up with a doctor, or seeking care if the user feels unwell.
The AI is told never to diagnose, name a condition or suggest medication.

articles.title: Exposing Home Assistant behind CGNAT without port forwarding (2026)
articles.description:
Disclosure: I work on Zorven, one of the outbound tunnel options mentioned below. Every option here includes its real trade-offs, including when you should skip Zorven and use Tailscale or a plain VPS instead.
You set up Home Assistant at home, open http://homeassistant.local:8123, everything loads on Wi-Fi—then you turn off Wi-Fi on your phone and nothing connects. Adding a port forward for 8123 or 443 in your router doesn't change anything either.
In 2026, the usual culprit on residential fiber, 5G home routers, and standard Starlink plans is CGNAT (Carrier-Grade NAT). Because multiple households share one ISP-level public IPv4 address, unsolicited inbound traffic never reaches your router at all.
Here is how to confirm CGNAT in 60 seconds, choose the right outbound path for your threat model, and configure Home Assistant's configuration.yaml so you don't hit 400: Bad Request once traffic starts flowing.
Check the WAN IP shown on your router's status page against your visible public IPv4 address:
curl -4 https://ifconfig.me

You are behind CGNAT if:
Your router's WAN IP is in 100.64.0.0/10 (100.64.x.x through 100.127.x.x), OR
Your router's WAN IP does not match what ifconfig.me prints.
Check whether your connection has routable IPv6 as well:
curl -6 https://ifconfig.me

If your phone network and work Wi-Fi both have IPv6 and your router exposes an IPv6 firewall rule, native IPv6 is the cleanest path—but many mobile/corporate networks still drop IPv6, which brings us to outbound tunnels.
If you don't need public Google Assistant / Alexa / webhook callbacks and just want the Home Assistant Companion app to work away from home:
Install the Tailscale Home Assistant add-on (or run tailscale up on your host).
Install Tailscale on your phone and reach http://<tailscale-node-name>:8123 over WireGuard.
Zero ports exposed to public internet scanners.
When Tailscale isn't enough: Tailscale Funnel lets you expose port 443/8443/10000 publicly without the app, though Funnel bandwidth isn't configurable and its control plane is SaaS-only.
cloudflared / Cloudflare Tunnel)


For external webhooks (Owntracks, iOS shortcuts, Google Home integration) on a domain managed in Cloudflare DNS:
cloudflared tunnel login
cloudflared tunnel create ha-home
cloudflared tunnel route dns ha-home ha.yourdomain.com

Create config.yml:
tunnel: ha-home
credentials-file: /root/.cloudflared/<TUNNEL-ID>.json
ingress:
  - hostname: ha.yourdomain.com
    service: http://127.0.0.1:8123
  - service: http_status:404

Start it with cloudflared tunnel run ha-home. Putting Cloudflare Access in front adds an email-PIN login gate before Home Assistant sees any HTTP traffic.
Trade-off: Cloudflare terminates TLS at its edge, requires your domain DNS on Cloudflare, and the tunnel control plane cannot be self-hosted.
frp)


Rent a cheap VPS with a real public IPv4 address, keep a WireGuard tunnel open outbound from home (PersistentKeepalive = 25), and let Caddy on the VPS terminate HTTPS and reverse-proxy to Home Assistant over the tunnel IP. Zero vendor lock-in, zero SaaS limits—at the cost of maintaining OS updates, firewall rules, and TLS routing yourself.
Zorven)


If you want cloudflared-style ergonomics without vendor lock-in (either hosted at zorven.app or self-hosted via Docker Compose on your own VPS, AGPL-3.0):
# Install client (Linux / macOS)
curl -fsSL https://zorven.app/install.sh | sudo bash

# Save token from dashboard and publish port 8123
zorven authtoken zrv_live_...
zorven http 8123

Typical client output:
Forwarding  https://myhome--user.zorven.app  ->  http://localhost:8123

What fits Home Assistant specifically:
You can enable visitor authentication (Basic, Google, or GitHub login) or IP allow-lists at the edge before requests ever reach localhost:8123.
Hosted plans throttle rather than hard-cutting connections if a monthly allowance is reached, and self-hosting (docker compose up -d on your own VPS) removes hosted traffic caps completely.
When NOT to use Zorven:
Only you and your family need access -> use private Tailscale/WireGuard instead.
You need a battle-tested multi-region CDN network right now -> Zorven's hosted relay currently runs in a single region, whereas Cloudflare has global edge POPs.
400: Bad Request reverse proxy check


Whichever HTTP reverse tunnel you pick (cloudflared, Caddy over WireGuard, or Zorven), Home Assistant rejects forwarded requests by default until you explicitly declare your local proxy IP trusted.
Edit /config/configuration.yaml (or via Studio Code Server add-on):
http:
  use_x_forwarded_for: true
  trusted_proxies:
    - 127.0.0.1
    - ::1
    # If running Home Assistant inside Docker bridge networking, also add your bridge/host IP:
    # - 172.30.33.0/24

Restart Home Assistant (Developer Tools -> YAML -> Restart). If you still see 400: Bad Request, check Settings -> System -> Logs for a line like:
ERROR (MainThread) [homeassistant.components.http.forwarded] A request from a reverse proxy was received from 172.17.0.1, but your HTTP integration is not set-up for reverse proxies

Add that exact logged IP to trusted_proxies and restart once more.
Keep configuration.yaml binding Home Assistant strictly to localhost (server_host: 127.0.0.1 if not running add-ons directly on another container bridge).
Enable 2FA (TOTP) on every Home Assistant user account.
Prefer putting an edge auth layer (Cloudflare Access or Zorven visitor login) in front of Home Assistant if external webhooks aren't hitting /api/webhook/....
Leave /api/webhook/... excluded from interactive browser login only if you rely on external webhook senders.
Repos / docs:
Home Assistant HTTP integration: https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/http/

Zorven (AGPL-3.0): https://github.com/tkodcumpeg4/zorven (https://zorven.app)

articles.title: The ethics of AI-assisted development
articles.description:
Lately there's been a lot of discussion about the morality of creating software using artificial intelligence. I've noticed a growing wave of anti-AI sentiment particularly directed at independent developers, even those wh odon't use generative AI to create visual or audio assets, but rely on it solely as an assistant for writing code and documentation.
I think there's a fundamental misunderstanding here that needs to be addressed; AI-assisted coding and generative AI "art" are two different things.
Programming isn't an abstract form of creative expression in the same way visual art is. It's built on logic, mathematics, and problem solving, there are only so many ways to implement a particular funcionality. Sure, there can be countless variations in how code is written, structured and organized, but the underlying logic and possible solutions are constrained by the problem itself.
It's simply not reasonable to accuse a developer of stealing another developer's work just because they used AI assistance to write a piece of code that happens to resemble something someone else has written. It's inevitable that developers will independently arrive at similar solutions, whether they use AI or not. Of course, if the end result is an identical copy of someone else's software, then we're talking about plagiarism or outright theft of someone else's work, but that's an entirely different issue.
Now, looking at this from a broader socioeconomic perspective, AI is here to stay, it's not something we can realistically fight our way out of, and while the concerns behind the anti-AI movement are often legitimate, I think a lot of that criticism is being directed at the wrong target. Big tech companies and major game studios are actively embracing AI, yet they rarely seem to face the same level of public backlash, but when an independent developer releases a game and includes a disclaimer stating that they used AI to assist with coding, the reaction can be completely different; I've come across accounts on Reddit from indie developers who experienced waves of harassment and negative Steam reviews simply because they disclosed using AI for coding assistance.
I'm not an unconditional supporter of AI. I understand the environmental concerns, especially the impact of data centers, their energy consumption, and the strain they put on water resources and local environments, these are real issues, and I don't think they should be dismissed. But I can't help seeing a parallel with the way environmental responsibility is often discussed. We're constantly told to be more conscious as individuals, to take shorter showers, consume less, and change our habits, while massive industries are allowed to keep exploiting natural resources in pursuit of ever-increasing profits.
It's a contradiction and, in many ways, I think the anti-AI movement falls into a similar trap, focusing its anger on individuals and small developers instead of addressing the companies, economic structures, and business practices that are actually driving the larger problem.
Anyway, this has been on my mind for a while, and I felt like putting my thoughts out there, so here's my take on it.

articles.title: How We Hit 100/100 Mobile PageSpeed & 90% SEO Across 332,000+ Next.js 16 Game Pages on $0/Month
articles.description:
Modern PC game releases routinely exceed 140 GB, making fast compression indexing and zero-bloat mobile web performance critical for global gamers.
While building RepackDeck — indexing 7,385+ lossless PC game repacks, 597+ official FLiNG single-player trainers, and 100% campaign mission walkthroughs across 45 languages — we hit three tricky Next.js 16 + SEO engineering problems and solved all of them on a $0.00/month Cloud Run + Cloudflare + Supabase stack.
loading.tsx Silently Hid <h1> From Non-JS HTML Crawlers


In Next.js App Router, adding a loading.tsx file inside a dynamic route segment wraps the page in <Suspense>. Browsers hydrate the streamed <div hidden id="S:0"> payload cleanly, but non-JavaScript HTML crawlers only inspect the initial shell—causing thousands of false h1_missing and thin-content alerts.
Removing loading.tsx inside /[lang]/game/[slug] and setting htmlLimitedBots: /.*/ in next.config.ts jumped our live on-page SEO score from 60% → 90% across 332,000+ localized pages.
Defer all third-party ad and analytics scripts strictly to physical user gestures (scroll, pointerdown, touchstart, keydown) with zero <45s fallback timers.
Reserve explicit CSS min-h wrappers (0 CLS) and optimize above-the-fold responsive covers (192w, 256w) with matching <link rel="preload" imageSrcSet>.
Live result on Google PageSpeed Insights API v5: 100/100 Mobile Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices & SEO on our Low-Spec PC Game Repacks Hub (1.1s LCP, 0 CLS).
We also shipped an edge SVG badge generator (Free SVG Verification Badges) and an open GitHub Pages PC Compression & MD5 Reference.

articles.title: 2 self-hosted apps for Indian businesses: CA Vault for CA firms and Toran for weddings
articles.description:
Most business software today is a monthly subscription, and your data lives on someone else's cloud. For some Indian businesses that's a real problem:
A CA firm holds the PAN, Aadhaar, bank details and Income Tax / GST portal passwords of hundreds of clients.
A wedding family or planner holds the phone numbers of 300+ relatives and an exact record of who gave how much shagun.
CA Vault and Toran take a different approach. You pay once, install the app on your own hosting (ordinary cPanel shared hosting works), and your data never leaves your server. Neither app has telemetry, and neither needs to "phone home" to keep working.
Here's what each one does.

CA Vault runs the whole CA office in one place: clients, compliance deadlines, documents, passwords, DSC tokens, notices and billing.
37 statutory compliances built in:



GST: GSTR-1, GSTR-3B (including QRMP), CMP-08, GSTR-9/9C
TDS/TCS: payments and returns (24Q, 26Q, 27Q, 27EQ), Form 16/16A
Income Tax: advance tax, ITR, tax audit
ROC and LLP: AOC-4, MGT-7, DIR-3 KYC, LLP Form 8/11
PF/ESI
Tasks are created automatically for every client and period, about 45 days before each due date, with step-by-step checklists.
Government extensions are entered once and move every open task.
Each staff member gets a morning email listing what's due.
PAN, GSTIN, TAN, CIN and Aadhaar are validated as you type. For example, the PAN's 4th character must match the entity type, and an Aadhaar number must pass its check digit.
PAN, Aadhaar, bank details, portal passwords, DSC PINs, documents and backups are all encrypted.
Two-step login, staff who see only their own clients, and a tamper-evident audit trail.
Password vault for Income Tax, GST, TRACES and MCA logins. Every reveal is logged.
DSC register with expiry alerts and an in/out log.
Notice tracker for Income Tax, TDS, GST and ROC notices, with suggested reply dates and appeal deadlines.
GST billing: invoices, receipts with TDS, retainers, credit notes, and a UPI QR on every invoice.
Client portal where clients upload documents, see filings and pay by UPI, on your own domain.
Excel / Tally import, plus optional modules for timesheets, leads and office registers.



CA Vault screenshots














Price: one-time, from ₹7,999 (GST included), with unlimited users and clients. 12 months of updates are included, and after that the software keeps working.
👉 cavault.rsflowhub.com · GitHub page with screenshots & docs

Toran puts a whole Indian wedding (Sagai, Mehndi, Haldi, Sangeet, Lagna, Reception) in one app. All modules share one guest list: an RSVP updates the seating, the seating shows at the gate, and the shagun shows on the family.
Guests are grouped into families, with bride/groom side, relation, city, Jain diet and tags.
Excel import of up to 5,000 rows, with column headings recognised in English, Hindi, Gujarati and Marathi.
Each family gets a private RSVP link: no app and no login. They answer per function, with headcount and food choice.
Sends only through official routes: the Meta WhatsApp Cloud API, Twilio, or free click-to-chat links.
Built-in throttling, retries and duplicate protection.
Guests can opt out by replying STOP, बंद or બંધ.
An invitation designer creates a personalised image for every family, with Gujarati and Devanagari fonts that render correctly.
Shagun / chandlo ledger: type a name and an amount and press Enter. You get a running total and totals by function, side and payment mode (cash, UPI, cheque, gift), with Excel/PDF export.
Drag-and-drop seating plan with auto-seating that keeps families together.
Vendors and budget: advances, instalments, planned vs spent, and payment reminders.
QR check-in at the gate on any phone. It keeps working offline and syncs when the network returns, because wedding venue Wi-Fi is rarely good.



Toran screenshots














Languages: English, हिन्दी, ગુજરાતી and मराठी, chosen per user.
Price: one-time, from ₹9,999 (GST included), with every module and no per-guest or per-event fees. Wedding planners get white-label plans: your name, your logo, and use for your clients' weddings.
👉 Try the live demo: a sample wedding with 300 guests, no sign-up needed · toran.rsflowhub.com · GitHub page
