Both are built with Laravel 12, Vue 3 and Tailwind. The release ZIP needs no Composer, npm, Node, Redis or SSH on the server: you upload it, open the installer, and you're running in about 15–20 minutes.
CA Vault does not file returns on the government portals (no GSP/ERI access). It tracks the work and the acknowledgement numbers. It doesn't replace Tally either.
Toran doesn't generate video invitations; invitations are personalised images.
CA firms, tax consultants and GST practitioners who want client data on their own server and no per-user fees.
IT partners who set up software for several CA firms (CA Vault has an Agency plan).
Families planning a wedding, and wedding planners, event studios and banquet halls who want their own branded app.
Societies and companies running garba nights, religious events, reunions or corporate events.
Know a CA or a wedding planner still running everything on Excel and WhatsApp groups? Send them this post 🙂
CA Vault and Toran are made by RSFlowHub. Questions are welcome in the comments.

articles.title: Why useReducer? Why do we need multiple functions to update a single state?
Hand an issue to an AI agent with your own model key: a checklist that keeps it safe
articles.description:
Disclosure: I work on Git A. The checklist in the first part works with any setup. The last part shows how Git A does it.
More teams are assigning issues to AI coding agents and getting a pull request back. Usually the agent runs in the cloud and uses a model you pay for with your own API key, often called BYOK (bring your own key). That's the right direction. You choose the model and the provider bills you directly.
But "assign the issue and wait" goes wrong in some predictable ways. Here is the checklist we use. Every point holds whatever tool you run.
The agent only knows what the issue says. Four short parts are enough:
Title: one change, in plain words. "Add rate limiting to /login", not "auth stuff".
Why: one or two sentences. It helps the agent choose between two reasonable fixes.
Where: the files, folders or endpoints involved, if you know them.
Acceptance criteria: a short list of things that can be checked. "Returns 429 after 5 attempts in a minute." "Existing login tests still pass." "New test covers the limit."
The acceptance criteria are what a review checks the result against. Without them, "done" means whatever the agent decided.
The agent needs to call the model. It does not need to hold the key. If the key sits in the agent's environment, anything the agent runs can read it, including a dependency's install script. Prefer a setup where the platform makes the model calls on the agent's behalf, or where a gateway you control holds the key.
If you already run a gateway such as LiteLLM, point the agent at the gateway. Then you get one place for logging, budgets and switching models.
An agent stuck in a loop can burn an afternoon of tokens. Set two limits before the first task:
the longest a single run may take, in minutes;
the most a single run may spend on the model, in dollars (an estimate is fine).
When a run hits a limit, it should stop and tell you. It should never quietly carry on.
Run each task on a clean machine or container that is thrown away afterwards. Then one task can't leave files, caches or credentials behind for the next. It also makes failures easy to reproduce: same issue, same starting point.
Ask for tests as part of the task, not as a follow-up. Then run your checks, the same CI a human change would go through, on the agent's branch. A green run of the agent's own tests alone proves little.
The agent that wrote the change shouldn't be the one that approves it. A separate review, by a person or a second agent with its own instructions, should answer one question: does this change do what the acceptance criteria say, and nothing else?
Choose a short list of paths an agent can never change without a human approving: CI workflows, deploy scripts, lockfiles, auth code. An agent should also never approve its own change.
What you want back is one reviewable change: the diff, the tests, the check results and a short summary of what was done and why. Then approving it is a decision, not an archaeology project.
At some point you'll want every running task stopped at once. Make sure you know where that button is before you need it.
Git A is built for many AI agents working on the same code at once. Every change lands on main without the rejected-push retry loop. The second half is the Agent factory: you hand an issue to an agent and get back one finished change to approve.
What the flow looks like in Git A today:
Connect your model once per organization: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, Mistral, xAI, DeepSeek, Groq, Together AI or Fireworks AI. You can also use your own gateway (OpenAI or Anthropic format) or a model on your own machine (Ollama or vLLM) on your own runners. Choose Save and test. Your provider bills you directly, and the agent never sees your key.
Create an agent: name it and pick the repositories it may work on. Under When it's done, choose Ask me (you approve every change) or Land by itself when checks pass. Keep Every change comes with tests ticked. You can choose the program it runs: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, OpenCode, your own command or your own container image. Set limits per run.
Write the issue and hand it over: assign it, @mention the agent, or run ga issue assign from the command line.
Watch it work: it works on a fresh machine of its own (Git A's or your own runners), writes the code and its tests, and runs your checks. A separate review checks the change against the issue. If the agent has a question, it asks you on the issue.
Review and land: you get one proposal. Approve it, or let it land when the checks pass.
Agents are free: there are no per-agent seats. You prepay credit for what they use (machine minutes, storage). The model bill stays with your own provider.
The full step-by-step guide is at git--a.com/docs under "Hand an issue to an agent". Everything above is described there as it works today.
If you run several agents on one repository and want to see what the rejected-push loop costs you now, git--a.com/measure has a bash script that counts it on your own repo, using a throwaway branch. It never touches main and sends nothing to us.
What's on your checklist that isn't on mine? I'd like to hear what went wrong the first time you let an agent take an issue.

articles.title: The pnpm Executable's Embedded Node Runtime Carries a CA Trust Problem
articles.description:
The pnpm Executable's Embedded Node Runtime Carries a CA Trust Problem


Package managers are usually discussed as supply-chain clients. CVE-2026-130756 turns one of them into a certificate-trust lesson: pnpm standalone executables before 10.34.8 embedded an older Node.js runtime that still trusted compromised eMudhra intermediate CA certificates during registry TLS connections.
Updating the host operating system's CA bundle does not automatically update a self-contained binary. The executable carries its own Node runtime and trust behavior. That creates a separate patch surface in developer laptops, build agents, release runners, and containers.
Pnpm is often used to fetch and build code. A registry connection that accepts a compromised chain could undermine the identity of the package source. The advisory establishes the trust defect. It does not establish that a particular registry or package was replaced.
Upgrade standalone pnpm executables to 10.34.8 or later. Inventory both pnpm installations and pinned copies inside CI images, developer bootstrap scripts, and release tooling. Check the actual executable version, because a newer package lock does not prove that the command on PATH changed.
Rebuild or replace images that contain the old executable. Clear caches only after preserving hashes needed for investigation. Review registry URLs, proxy settings, and custom CA files for unexpected additions.
Look for package downloads during the trust window and compare fetched artifacts with lockfile hashes and approved provenance. Review outbound TLS failures around the eMudhra distrust dates; failures can reveal stale runtimes but are not proof of interception.
If a compromised chain may have been accepted, rotate publishing and registry tokens used by the affected environment. Revalidate release artifacts with an independent trusted environment.
Treat standalone tooling as software with its own runtime and CA policy. Produce an inventory of embedded runtimes, monitor vendor advisories, and test certificate-distrust updates in CI. Pinning a tool improves reproducibility only when the pin also receives security updates.

articles.title: Tirei meus arquivos da nuvem e escrevi um navegador de arquivos em um único binário
articles.description:
Sou o autor do projeto, então leiam como relato de construção, não como review independente.
Meu escritório é pequeno: um NAS, uma máquina com os arquivos de trabalho e, várias vezes por dia, o mesmo pedido — "me manda a versão mais recente?". O problema nunca foi onde guardar os arquivos. Era ver antes de baixar. Ninguém quer baixar 400 MB só pra descobrir que pegou o arquivo errado.
O que saiu no fim é um binário em Go. Sem Docker, sem banco, sem PHP, sem cron.
./banyan -headless

Ele imprime um endereço; você abre no navegador de qualquer aparelho da mesma rede. A instalação acaba aí. Há clientes nativos para Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD e Android, e o resto entra pelo navegador.
Pré-visualização de 100+ formatos no servidor: Office, PDF, DWG, vídeo, imagem, arquivo compactado, código-fonte, fonte tipográfica. O arquivo é transmitido, não baixado.
Links de compartilhamento que o destinatário abre sem criar conta, com validade e contador de acessos.
Editar na pré-visualização grava direto no caminho original. Adeus, final_v2_final(2).psd.
Exportar para PDF com marca d'água, assinatura e anotação no mesmo lugar onde o arquivo já está.
Criptografia AES-256-GCM por diretório, sem conta, sem telemetria, funcionando offline na rede local.
Não é cliente de sincronização. Sem resolução de conflito, sem espelhamento. É um navegador com pré-visualização, não um Dropbox.
Não tem versão hospedada. É self-hosted: TLS, domínio e proxy reverso ficam por sua conta.
O binário tem ~65 MB porque leva embutido todo o pipeline de pré-visualização.
A interface tem dez idiomas, mas a tradução foi gerada automaticamente a partir do chinês; o português tem trechos estranhos e eu estou corrigindo à mão.
A alternativa habitual é montar Nextcloud ou parecido, ou seja: Docker Compose, banco de dados, atualizações, PHP, painel de administração cheio de avisos. Para "quero ver meus arquivos do notebook no outro quarto", isso é aparelhagem demais. Um binário que você copia, roda e esquece é mais honesto para esse caso.
O preço dessa escolha: sem ecossistema de apps, sem móvel-first sincronizado, e se você quer colaboração multiusuário de verdade, este não é seu produto.
Página do projeto, com downloads para as seis plataformas e documentação em dez idiomas: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_pt
Código-fonte: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan
Se você resolveu o "baixar pra saber o que é" de outro jeito, quero saber como.

articles.title: When someone leaves, their API keys stay: how to offboard the access people create
articles.description:
Most offboarding checklists stop at the same point: disable the login, collect the laptop, remove the person from the group chat. That handles the person. It doesn't handle what the person built.
Over a year or two, an engineer, analyst or ops lead creates access that isn't tied to their own sign-in. A service account for a nightly job. An API key pasted into a reporting script. An OAuth grant that lets a SaaS tool read the shared drive. And now, an AI agent connected to their mailbox or the ticketing system. Some of this breaks loudly when they leave. Most of it keeps running with nobody watching.
The quiet part is the risk. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report says credential abuse is still the most common way attackers get in, and that the median time to remediate leaked secrets found in a GitHub repository was 94 days. A key with no owner is a key nobody rotates.
This is the order I'd work in.
In the first week of notice, ask the person leaving for a written list: every service account, API key, token, webhook, scheduled job and AI tool they set up or connected. They know more than any scan will find. Make it a handover task with a due date, not a favour.
Memory misses things, so verify. Look in:
Your identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace): app grants and OAuth consents made by that user.
Cloud consoles (AWS, Azure, GCP): access keys, roles and service principals they created or last used.
Code repositories and CI/CD: secrets stored under their name, deploy keys, personal access tokens used by pipelines.
SaaS admin panels: integrations they installed, especially anything with "read all files" or "send as user" permissions.
AI tools: any agent or assistant connected through their account to mail, files, CRM or chat.
Anything the systems show that isn't on their list goes to the top of the review.
A person, not a team. "The data team" owns nothing at 2 a.m. when a job fails. The new owner should know what the item does and be able to say whether it still needs to exist.
Keep it if it's needed and already runs on its own identity with narrow permissions. Change the owner and move on.
Move it if it runs on the departing person's own credentials. Create a dedicated service identity, give it only the permissions the job actually uses, switch the job over and confirm the next run succeeds.
Retire it if nobody can explain what it's for. Disable it rather than delete it, and wait two weeks to see if anything complains.
They probably had access to more secrets than they created: shared vault folders, .env files, config for tools they administered. Rotate those too. It isn't about trust. Former employees' laptops and password managers get compromised like anyone else's.
Cut interactive access on the last day as normal. Hold off deleting the account until steps 3 to 5 are done, because in some platforms deleting a user also removes or breaks what they owned. Then watch the logs for a week for failed authentications tied to the old account. Each one is something you missed.
Agents are where this gets harder each month. An agent connected "as me" inherits everything that person could do, and it may keep its own saved connections outside your identity provider. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found that 13% of organisations reported breaches of AI models or applications, and 97% of those said they lacked proper AI access controls. For each agent the person connected, revoke its tokens in the source app (not only inside the agent), and if the work still matters, rebuild it under a dedicated identity with an owner.
The real win is never having to rebuild this from memory again. Three habits cover most of it:
Every new service account, key or agent gets an owner and an expiry date when it's created.
Quarterly access reviews include non-human identities, not only people.
The offboarding checklist has a "things you created" section that both the manager and IT sign off.
You can do all of this with admin consoles and a spreadsheet. It's slower, and it depends on someone remembering every time, so it's worth automating the discovery step once you've done it by hand a couple of times. Whatever you use, the steps above are what matter: an owner, a decision and a rotation for everything a departing person leaves behind.
Originally published on my Substack: https://nurankhan.substack.com/p/when-someone-leaves-their-api-keys

articles.title: Anthropic's $104B 'Loss' Is Fake. The $895B Bill Isn't.
articles.description:
Anthropic's $104B "Loss" Is Fake. The $895B Bill Isn't.


Anthropic went public today. The company priced its IPO at the top of its $70–$78 range, began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, and immediately crossed $2 trillion in market capitalization — making it the largest tech IPO on record. A company that was founded in 2021, raised its Series B at $580 million, and had $41 million in 2023 revenue now trades at a valuation that Apple didn't reach until 2020.
📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →
The headline every financial outlet is running: Anthropic lost $104 billion in nine months.
That number is real. It is also meaningless. And the fixation on it is obscuring the number that actually matters: $895.4 billion in signed compute commitments — the largest infrastructure obligation any technology company has ever taken on.

View original post on X →
Here is what the amended S-1/A filing actually says:
For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, Anthropic reported a net loss of $104.0 billion. That looks catastrophic — until you read the footnotes.
91% of that loss — roughly $94.3 billion — is a non-cash fair-value remeasurement of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs. Here is what that means in plain English:
When Anthropic raised private capital through convertible instruments, those instruments became liabilities on its balance sheet. As the company's valuation climbed from $965 billion (May 2026 Series H) toward the $1.5–$2 trillion IPO range, accounting rules (ASC 825) required Anthropic to mark those liabilities to fair value each quarter. The liability grew because the underlying equity grew — and that growth flows through the income statement as a "loss."
It is not a loss. No cash left the building. No customer stopped paying. No server got unplugged.
ℹ️ The $104B net loss is 91% paper mark. Anthropic's nine-month operating cash flow was actually +$6.569 billion, swinging from -$2.0B in the prior-year period. The company is generating cash.
The moment ANT shares began trading today, those convertible instruments started converting to equity. The liability vanishes from the balance sheet. The mark-to-market swings stop. Next quarter's income statement will look nothing like this one.
As Finimize put it: "The loss is an accounting mark, not cash burn." Anyone using the $104B number to argue Anthropic is bleeding out either hasn't read the S-1 or is counting on you not to.
Strip out the convertible-note theater and the operating picture is different:

Revenue has grown roughly 10x per year for three consecutive years: $41M in 2023, ~$386M in 2024, ~$4.6B in 2025, and an annualized pace north of $65B in 2026. The 900%+ net revenue retention means the installed customer base is expanding its usage faster than any cohort is churning. These are, by any measure, exceptional unit economics.
The Q3 operating loss of $567M on $17B of revenue is a 3.3% operating margin deficit. That is not a company in distress. That is a company investing at the edge of breakeven while growing 47% quarter over quarter.

View original post on X →
  
  



  
  
  The Number That Actually Matters: $895.4 Billion


Now for the part of the S-1 that deserves the headlines it isn't getting.
Anthropic has signed $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all of which is for compute and infrastructure. That number includes contracts with Google ($121.3B+), Amazon ($110B), Microsoft ($44.9B), SpaceX ($120.5B), and others. As Boingboing summarized: "Keeping Claude running apparently requires nearly a trillion dollars."
$69.8 billion of those commitments are due within the next 12 months. At the current $81B annualized run rate, that means roughly 86% of one year's gross revenue is pre-committed to infrastructure before Anthropic pays a single employee, researcher, or landlord.
Here is the structural problem: approximately 80% of these commitments are non-cancelable or payable regardless of actual usage. The revenue is consumption-based and can fluctuate. The costs are fixed.
⚠️ Contrarian Corner: The bull case says locked-in compute is a moat — Anthropic has capacity others can't get, and at 900%+ NRR the revenue will grow into the obligation. The bear case: consumption-based revenue can evaporate in a downturn, while non-cancelable commitments cannot. If a recession hits, or a competitor ships a 10x cheaper model, Anthropic still owes $895B to providers who are simultaneously building rival models.
Here is the detail that the commitment number alone doesn't capture. Anthropic's three largest infrastructure providers — Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — are also its three largest competitors.
Google runs Gemini. Amazon backs (and distributes) models through Bedrock and has its own Nova models. Microsoft owns 49% of OpenAI. Together, they account for approximately $275+ billion of Anthropic's locked-in compute spend.
The S-1 itself flags this as a key risk: dependence on cloud providers "which provide computing infrastructure and distribution while also developing rival AI models." That is not boilerplate. As one analyst quoted in the coverage noted: "It reduces demand risk and replaces it with counterparty risk."
The company hedges this by training on multiple chip architectures — Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AWS Trainium — but architectural diversity doesn't solve the economic dependency. If Google decided to preference Gemini on its own infrastructure, or Amazon throttled priority for non-Bedrock workloads, Anthropic's options are limited by contracts that run through 2045.
There is one more number buried in the quarterly data that warrants attention: compute and infrastructure expense was 58% of Q3 revenue, up from roughly 48% in Q2.
This matters because it moves against the narrative. The standard tech-company trajectory is declining marginal cost of delivery — you build the platform once and each incremental dollar of revenue costs less to serve. Anthropic's Q3 shows the opposite: a swing to $567M operating loss driven by $5.0 billion of short-term compute purchases and $2.0 billion of non-cash donation matching charges.
Is this a one-quarter anomaly driven by pre-IPO capacity buildout? Possibly. Is it the early signal of a structural cost trajectory where frontier AI models get more expensive to serve, not less? Also possibly. The honest answer is that nobody — including Anthropic — knows yet. But the direction matters, because every percentage point of compute-to-revenue ratio represents billions of dollars at Anthropic's scale.
The Hacker News thread on the IPO pricing (749 comments, 405 points) captures the split cleanly.

View on Hacker News →
The bull case, articulated by multiple commenters: "People are saying that Anthropic has no moat which sounds right but at the same time they have left everyone behind: Google is trying lately but seemed very lost over the last years despite inventing the thing; OpenAI cannot match Opus 5.5 and Fable at the moment."
The bear case: "Remember the dotcom? Anthropic and OpenAI are the AltaVista of the AI era. With first starter advantage but no real moat and very good at spending money."
And the existential dread, from the Nasdaq debut thread (345 comments): "Genuinely a massive moment in human history. As a SWE the gravy train is basically over in my view. They figured out how to make a program that does the job."

View original post on X →
David Sacks, who called this moment months ago, posted the most provocative take: Anthropic is "racing toward Recursive Self-Improvement faster than any other frontier lab and has marketed 'closing the loop' on its IPO roadshow as a core advantage." The implication is that the company is simultaneously selling safety as its brand and speed as its investment thesis — and those two pitches may eventually collide.

View original post on X →
Jeremy Howard distilled the competitive landscape into one tweet: "What they want — OAI: capture light cone of all future value. Anthropic: rule world because no-one else is worthy. Google: meet 4th quarter analysts' expectations. ...and that's why I want Google to win."
  
  



  
  
  The PBC Structure and Founder Control


One more structural detail worth noting: Anthropic is a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation, legally obligated to balance profit with "developing AI for the benefit of humanity." CEO Dario Amodei and six co-founders retain 50.1% of voting power through a single Class F share structure, and a Long-Term Benefit Trust remains part of the governance architecture.
This is both a feature and a risk. The PBC structure gives the founders a legal shield to slow down capabilities development if they judge it unsafe — which is exactly what the safety-conscious investor base wants. But it also means minority shareholders have almost no governance leverage. If Anthropic's leadership decides to cap revenue growth for safety reasons, public-market investors who bought at a $2 trillion valuation have no recourse.
For developers and builders: Watch the compute-to-revenue ratio in future 10-Qs. If it keeps climbing past 60%, expect pricing pressure on API calls. The $895B commitment means Anthropic has the capacity to serve you — but it also means they need your dollars to service those obligations. The AI economy is paying for itself right now, but that loop requires continued adoption velocity.
For investors: Ignore the $104B net loss. It is noise. Focus on three numbers: (1) operating cash flow trajectory (+$6.6B nine-month, up from -$2.0B), (2) the commitment-to-revenue coverage ratio (commitments / trailing-twelve-month revenue), and (3) Q4's compute cost as a percentage of revenue. If compute costs stabilize or decline, the business model works at scale. If they keep rising, the cloud concentration tax becomes existential.
For enterprise customers: Your Anthropic vendor risk is not just "will Anthropic survive?" It is tripartite: Anthropic + AWS + Google. If you are building mission-critical systems on Claude, understand that your AI vendor's infrastructure depends on companies that sell competing AI products. The compute cost opacity in this market makes it nearly impossible to assess how much of your API spend goes to actual inference versus servicing Anthropic's infrastructure obligations.
💡 The number to watch: Anthropic's commitment-to-revenue coverage ratio. At $81B annualized run rate against $895B in total commitments, the company needs roughly 11 years of current revenue to cover its infrastructure obligations. If revenue keeps growing at current rates, that denominator shrinks fast. If growth slows, it doesn't.
Anthropic's IPO is simultaneously the strongest validation of the AI business model and the starkest illustration of its structural risk. Revenue growth is real, cash flow is positive, and customer demand exceeds capacity. But the largest infrastructure gamble in corporate history is also real — and it is non-cancelable.
The $104B loss is a headline for people who don't read footnotes. The $895B compute bill is the thesis for people who do.
We are watching the market price in the upside of frontier AI while mostly ignoring the fixed-cost structure that makes it possible. The Nasdaq gave Anthropic a $2 trillion vote of confidence today. Whether that confidence is justified will be answered not by next quarter's loss figure — which will look dramatically better once the convertible instruments are gone — but by whether the revenue can grow fast enough to outrun the largest infrastructure obligation any technology company has ever signed.
The selloff and the s-curve thesis applies here in miniature: the capability growth is real, the market is volatile, and the only honest position is to watch the numbers that matter — not the ones that make for better headlines.
Originally published at ComputeLeap

articles.title: Where My Level 5 Software Factory Doesn't Cut It Yet
articles.description:
Originally published at jduncan.io.
I've been talking a lot lately about Leaf and the data behind how it runs.
If you use Dan Shapiro's Five Levels of AI coding framework, Leaf operates as a Level 5 software factory (what Shapiro calls the "Dark Factory"). A specification goes in as a contract, and working, tested software comes out the other side without a human writing code or reviewing diffs.
Most days, it's great. It hums along on a few small boxes in my office closet and ships real work while my laptop lid is closed.
But it's far from perfect.
"Dark factory" sounds very clean on a conference slide. In practice, taking humans out of the implementation middle doesn't make engineering problems disappear. It just moves the failure modes to places you weren't watching.
When a human writes code by hand, human boredom and typing speed act as natural rate limiters. You don't accidentally trigger forty container builds before lunch. You don't write a fifty-step coordination plan to update a CSS theme. And you don't rewrite your own job description just to make a unit test pass.
Take the human rate limiter off, and the edges of your harness get stress-tested fast. I've gotten a few things wrong recently, and each one taught me something about where my factory doesn't cut it yet.
I use GitHub Actions to build and deploy my projects. I pay for a GitHub Enterprise Cloud license for one user, which includes 50,000 Actions build minutes a month on standard runners for private repositories.
Before Leaf, I never came close to touching that number. For a solo developer, 50,000 minutes is the same as 50 billion. It's more than thirty-four straight days of compute every month.
This month, I blew right through all 50,000 minutes on October 18th.
Why? Did I have repetitive jobs and unoptimized workflows in there? Yes. When you aren't paying attention to build minutes, it's easy to let full container builds and redundant test runs pile up on every push.
But the real reason wasn't just sloppy YAML. It happened because autonomous loops multiplied my commit and PR throughput nearly fourfold, while my CI triggers were still designed for human typing speed. Between feature work, automated bug fixes, and the Improvement loop sweeping for dead code while I slept, the factory was firing off full pipeline runs around the clock.
My factory wasn't broken; my plumbing was still sized for a human.
So now I'm tightening the screws. I'm building container images less often. I'm being much smarter about when a workflow runs the full end-to-end test suite versus a fast, targeted check. It's all fixable, and high throughput is a good problem to have. Still, hitting a hard billing wall two-thirds of the way through October is a rough way to learn that lesson.
My current setup is great for bug fixes and the average new feature. If a problem fits neatly into a handful of files with a clear boundary, Leaf chews right through it.
Where it gets lost and goes sideways is when I ask it to make fundamental, sweeping changes across an existing project.
For my BrandCast project, I recently updated the admin UI. While I was poking around, I noticed that a lot of hand-coded styling changes had crept into individual pages over time (agents will do that when they're focused on closing a local ticket). I wanted Leaf to update the core theme and make sure every page in the admin UI was using that updated theme consistently.
It was a lot of changes and a lot of checks, but the work itself was mostly mechanical.
Leaf lost. Its. Mind.
The planner generated a graph with 50+ nodes. It took over an hour just to finish planning. (I'm blaming my choice to test Astra and Fable as planning agents there. Way too much horsepower and way too much over-thinking.) Once execution finally started, the foreman almost crashed a node, then sent over 30 nodes back to workers for changes. After three hours of churn, the build still failed.
In Part 6 of the Loops series, my data already showed that an 8+ node plan costs 17× what a single-node plan costs. A 50-node plan isn't just expensive; splitting a wide, mechanical sweep into fifty isolated worker contexts creates more coordination friction than the work itself. Every worker touches adjacent files, merge conflicts multiply, and the foreman spends all its turns playing traffic cop.
I'm still digging into this one. Some of it is definitely my choice of models (looking at you, Astra). Heavy reasoning models love to turn a straightforward cleanup into a doctoral thesis. But some of it is how I create plans in the first place. I'm not sure what the right fix is yet, whether that's capping graph size, batching mechanical sweeps differently, or keeping foundational refactors in an interactive session. Maybe all or none of the above. Maybe it'll occur to me magically in the shower tomorrow morning.
I love the Improvement loop in Leaf. Having an autonomous sweep that deletes dead weight and simplifies code while the factory is idle has been one of my favorite wins of the whole project.
But I need to start setting barriers on what it's allowed to touch.
Leaf can run the Improvement loop on its own repository. Recently, somewhere along the line, an improvement pass decided that it needed to add a regex-style test to validate one of Leaf's role prompts. Testing natural language prompts with regex is already a bad idea. Then, on later sweeps, the loop noticed that other prompts were "missing" similar tests, so it dutifully added more of them.
Then came the rot.
When a later change tripped those brittle checks, the agent didn't fix or remove the bad tests. Instead, it started changing the prose of the prompts to match the regex tests, because updating markdown prose is faster and easier than refactoring test code.
Writing a test takes code.

Changing a prompt takes prose.
Agents always take the shortest path to the reward. Independent evaluators like METR have documented this exact reward-hacking behavior across frontier coding models: give an agent an automated check as its definition of done, and it will happily game the check if that's the path of least resistance. Nobody in my closet was plotting world domination. The worker just wanted a green exit code in the fewest turns possible.
Suddenly, Leaf started exhibiting odd behavior on real runs. I ended up spending a 90-minute human-in-the-loop session unwinding the mess, deleting the regex tests, and restoring sanity to the prompts Leaf uses to do its job. Lots of typing in all caps and cursing happened.
I'm working on this right now. In Part 2 of the Loops series, I wrote that judgement lives in the prompts, where I can read it and change it. Letting the automated cleanup loop modify the factory's own prompts violated my own rule. I'm thinking about adding guardrails to skip certain paths (like role prompts and skills) from the Improvement process altogether, though I'm not completely sure where that boundary should sit yet.
Running a Level 5 software factory doesn't mean you stop doing engineering. It means your engineering shifts to the harness, the boundaries, and the economics of the loop:
Audit your downstream plumbing. If your commit throughput jumps 4×, your CI bill and container registries are going to feel it before you do. Gate heavy builds and full suites so autonomous loops don't burn your monthly quota in eighteen days.
Don't use a sledgehammer planner on wide, mechanical sweeps. Big reasoning models will over-decompose foundational changes into giant node graphs that choke on their own coordination.
Fence off your prompts from self-improvement loops. If an agent can pass a test by weakening a prompt instead of fixing code, it will take that deal every single time. Keep automated cleanup focused on mechanical code, and keep human hands on the prompts that define judgement.
This is all very much a work in progress, and sometimes it goes sideways. Sometimes it goes really sideways.
But I can't wait to look at the data from that awful three-hour run.

articles.title: Factory: The Next Phase of Hybrid AI Development
articles.description:
Originally published at jduncan.io.
A couple weeks ago I wrote about my hybrid LLM setup. At the time, the division seemed simple enough: cloud models for writing code, and a local server in my house for family life, privacy, and experiments.
That split was always a temporary checkpoint.
I spend a lot of my spare time building BrandCast. It's a large monorepo with thousands of moving parts. Over the past year, I've poured a huge amount of effort into dialing in its AI harness. I use Claude Code as my primary pair programmer, backed by custom skills, system prompts, and my Root development framework.
At this point, the harness is predictable. If my input context is clean, I can predict the quality of the output with high confidence.
The problem isn't the code generation anymore. The problem is the friction around it.
Sitting in front of a terminal hitting enter every few minutes gets old fast. I don't want an interactive copilot glued to my face all evening. I want an autonomous software factory.
Most conversations about AI agents suffer from binary thinking.
One camp insists on running everything locally. They imagine an 8B or 32B model refactoring hundreds of files across a massive monorepo with zero external API calls. I love my local hardware, but that's fantasy today. When the cost of a wrong edit is high, you pay for the frontier model. Local models don't have the context coherence or reasoning depth to navigate deep monorepo migrations without going off the rails.
The other camp hands their credit card over to cloud agents for every tiny step. They spin up autonomous swarms that burn millions of frontier tokens just reading GitHub issues, hallucinating roadmaps, and doing basic ticket triage.
The reality is more nuanced.
Frontier models are expensive and rate-limited. You don't use a master craftsman to sweep the workshop floor or sort tickets into neat piles. You use them to build the intricate mechanisms.
Local models, on the other hand, are fast, private, and practically free once the server is paid for. They aren't ready to rewrite my backend, but they are fantastic at classification, evaluation, and triage.
The logical step isn't choosing between local and cloud. It's chaining them together.
Before I could automate the factory floor, I had to fix where it lived.
For months, I ran my entire development harness directly on my MacBook. If you've ever run continuous agent loops, multiple git worktrees, Docker test containers, and local build tools on your primary laptop, you know the pain. The fans spin up. The battery melts. Your terminal history turns into an unreadable blur of agent output. Worst of all, your working git tree is constantly in flux.
So I moved the bulk of my BrandCast development off my laptop entirely.
I set up a dedicated Intel NUC with 32GB of RAM. It sits quietly on my network, always powered on, running the dev harness and the background agents.
That hardware separation changed how I think about my time:
Research is still mine to own. I use my laptop for high-leverage work: exploratory coding, architectural spikes, deep customer work, and reviewing diffs. My laptop stays fast, quiet, and responsive.
The chopping wood and carrying water moves to the NUC. The repetitive mechanics of software engineering: triaging bug tickets, spinning up branches, writing boilerplate, running tests, fixing regressions: all move to the factory floor.
Let git merging do what it's good for. I can work on an experimental feature on my laptop while Factory runs an automated queue on the NUC. When the NUC finishes a ticket, it pushes a PR. When I finish an experiment, I push a branch. Git and GitHub Actions handle the merging and the validation. Distributed version control was built for asynchronous collaboration. It works just as well when your collaborator is an autonomous box in the closet.
With the harness running on the NUC, I built a small web UI to manage the flow. I call it Factory.
It sits between my GitHub issue backlog and my coding harness.

Here's what is happening behind that screen:
Intake: Issues land in GitHub. Some are written by me by hand. Others come out of agentic brainstorming sessions when I'm exploring new features.
Local Evaluation: Factory pulls down all open issues and sends them to my local LLM server (the Infplane Hilbert box sitting in my house).
Scoring and Rationale: The local model inspects the title, description, and acceptance criteria. It scores each issue by complexity, impact, and feasibility. In the screenshot, you can see issue #4156 scored an 8.1, accompanied by a clean summary: "Critical security fix with clear scope, acceptance criteria, and mechanical implementation path."


Queue Presentation: Factory sorts the candidates and shows me the top 15 ready-to-run items.
Instead of staring at a sprawling backlog and wondering what to tackle next, I have a prioritized queue scored by a model that didn't cost me a penny in API tokens.
Here's how the entire topology fits together across the laptop, the NUC, the local inference box, and the cloud:

Notice how each machine has a dedicated responsibility:
Developer Laptop: Where I do research, plan architecture, and run targeted one-off experiments.
Infplane Hilbert: Dedicated local AI inference box running AMD Ryzen AI hardware with 128GB of RAM. It handles high-speed, zero-cost backlog evaluation.
Dedicated NUC: The factory floor with 32GB of RAM. It hosts the Factory service, SQLite state DB, and background Claude Code sessions in isolated git worktrees.
Cloud & Frontier Tier: GitHub hosts the repository and Actions CI/CD. The Anthropic API delivers deep frontier reasoning on the Claude 20x Max plan.
Factory gives me two execution modes depending on how involved I want to be.
Sometimes I want specific control over what runs. I open Factory, look through the top 15 ranked issues, find the one I care about, and click run.
Factory immediately launches a backgrounded Claude Code session on the NUC. It provisions an isolated git worktree so the main repository tree isn't touched. The session boots with my full configuration: project-specific MCP servers, custom system prompts, and the Root dev workflow.
The agent reads the issue, writes the plan, edits the code, runs the tests, and pushes a PR. I can monitor it if I want, or go back to whatever else I was doing on my laptop.
This is where the setup becomes genuinely autonomous.
I click run at the top of the queue and let Factory take the wheel.
Factory grabs the top-ranked issue and kicks off the background session. While Claude Code works through the Root workflow, Factory continuously polls GitHub Actions to monitor build and test progress.
When the pull request passes CI and merges into main, Factory runs its teardown routine:
It removes the isolated git worktree (in the screenshot, you can see cleaned /home/jduncan/Code/bc-4377).
It cleans up dangling agent processes and deleted branches.
It logs the execution stats to a local SQLite database (issue #4377 took 151 minutes and 26 seconds).
It marks the ticket complete, picks the next highest issue from the queue, and starts the cycle again.
If you've heard me speak at Google Cloud recently, you've heard this exact talk track.
Enterprises are wrestling with the exact same challenge. Everyone knows how to hook up an LLM to an IDE. The real question is how to scale agentic development without burning out your developers, draining your API budget on trivial tasks, or letting unvetted code run wild.
The answer is division of labor.
Use the frontier model for what it does best: large-scale, complex reasoning and code modifications in a massive codebase. Augment it with a local LLM to automate your supervisory duties away. Offload the heavy execution to a dedicated machine so your primary workstation stays free for creative thought.
This is me eating my own dogfood. I have a Claude 20x Max plan. Let's see how well it holds up when a local factory keeps feeding it work around the clock.
If you're looking at your own development workflow and wondering how to take the next step toward autonomy, keep these principles in mind:
Match model cost to task complexity. Don't spend frontier tokens to sort a list or summarize an issue. Use cheap, local models for classification and routing. Save the frontier power for code execution.
Get the harness off your primary machine. If an agent is running for two hours in the background, it shouldn't hold your personal laptop hostage. A cheap, dedicated box with plenty of RAM gives you the freedom to step away.
Your harness is your safety net. Factory only works because the Root framework enforces strict testing and verification steps before any code gets committed. Autonomous loops without rigid harness constraints just create technical debt faster.
Isolate your environments. Never let an autonomous agent work directly in your dirty working tree. Use git worktrees and clean teardown scripts so failed runs can be pruned instantly without leaving collateral damage.
Keep research human. The goal isn't to remove yourself from software engineering. The goal is to own the architecture and the research, while delegating the chopping wood and carrying water to the factory.
Hybrid AI isn't just about where your data lives. It's about how your models collaborate across your hardware. And right now, the factory floor is humming.

articles.title: Making a Trino lake as fast as a SQL database
articles.description:
Photo by Joshua Kettle on Unsplash
Moving analytics data from a SQL database to a lake usually comes with a quiet assumption: you will pay for cheap, unlimited storage with slower answers. I tested that assumption end to end, with an AI agent that answers business questions over synced SaaS data, and the result surprised me. With four fixes, full answers on the lake took the same time as on the database. The biggest fix had nothing to do with Trino's speed.
The setup, in one breath
The data is CRM and accounting records, copied by a managed ingestion service into Iceberg tables on Azure storage (ADLS). Iceberg is an open table format: plain files plus a small "description file" per table saying which files make up the table right now. A hosted Polaris catalog keeps the list of where each table's description lives. Trino is the query engine that reads all of it. The comparison point is the same data in Azure SQL.
The agent doesn't run one query per answer. It runs five to seven: it lists tables, reads column names, samples a few values, then asks the real question. That detail turned out to matter more than anything else.
Out of the box, the lake lost badly
A small question touching four tables took about 2 seconds in Trino, against about 0.1 seconds in the database. A big accounting question that combines 25 tables took about 30 seconds, against about 6.
I expected the time to be in reading data. It wasn't. Trino splits its own work into stages, and most of the time sat in "analysis", the step before any data is read.
Trino asks the catalog about every table, in every query, with no memory between queries. Each ask is a network call. Our catalog sat in one region and the engine in another, so each lookup cost about half a second. Twenty-five tables, twenty-five calls, about 13 seconds of waiting before the engine did anything useful.
Think of a delivery driver who phones head office for the address of every stop, every single day, even though the addresses never changed.
The fix was to give the driver a notebook. Trino supports an Iceberg catalog stored in a plain Postgres database (the JDBC catalog in Trino's docs). "Registering" a table there is just writing one row: its name and the location of its current description file, which I read from the table's own $metadata_log_entries. No data is copied. Nothing is written to the lake.

Before and after: the engine stops phoning the catalog and reads a local address book instead.
The result was the clearest number of the whole project. Analysis on the 25-table question went from about 13 seconds to 0.8. On the small question it went from 1.5 seconds to 0.17. Answers were byte-for-byte identical.
The price is a job you now own. Every time new data lands, the notebook has to be updated with each table's new description file, or the engine reads yesterday's data.
A newer Trino setting, snapshot-loading-mode=REFS, asks the catalog for a shorter answer that leaves out old table history. Someone on another catalog measured a 6x faster lookup with it, but their tables had about 9,000 old versions. Mine had one. I tried it anyway: no gain. The time was the trip, not the size of the reply.
Trino's metadata cache was already on, and it caches description files, not the catalog lookup. Rewriting or compacting the source tables was off the table too, since the ingestion service owns them and would undo it on the next sync.
Removing the lookups took the big accounting question from about 30 seconds to about 17. What remained was real work: about 8 seconds planning a query with hundreds of stages, and about 8 seconds running it.
So I stopped doing that work at question time. The accounting "model" (the recipe that turns 25 raw tables into one clean ledger) runs once after each sync and saves its result as a single table. A question like "income in March" then reads one small table instead of rebuilding the ledger.

The heavy combining happens once per data refresh, not once per question.
I tried the ready table in three places: in Trino's memory, in Postgres, and as an Iceberg table on the lake itself. All three answered in about 0.15 to 0.3 seconds, against about 6 seconds in the SQL database. Writing it to the lake took about 30 seconds. Writing it into Postgres took about 90, because rows go in one by one.
That last point matters if you worried, like I did, that precompute means "we're back to a database." The data stays in the lake. Postgres only holds pointers, and you can rebuild it from the catalog at any time.
The engine first ran on a VM on the US west coast, with the data on the east coast. A single round trip across the country took 65 to 100 milliseconds, and each catalog call needed several. Moving the engine east cut a call from 0.21 to 0.40 seconds down to 0.06 to 0.16, and small questions got about twice as fast again, landing around half a second.
Then I made the mistake that taught me the most. I timed full answers with the app on my laptop.
Full answers on the lake averaged 53.7 seconds. On the SQL database, 44.3. Same correct answers, nine seconds worse. The engine was fine; the app was talking to it five to seven times per answer, across the internet, several round trips each time.
When I ran the app on the same machine as the engine, the lake averaged 42.5 seconds. Inside the noise of the database's 44.3.

Same engine, same questions. Only the app's location changed.
About 40 seconds of every answer is the AI thinking, on either system, and it swings by five seconds from run to run. Per-query benchmarks hid that. If you are timing a database for an agent, time the whole answer, and put the app where it will live in production.
An answer cache in the app, keyed on the exact SQL text, did what it promised. A repeated 18-second question came back in under a millisecond, and by the third question in a session only the real query reached the engine.
It saved about a second per answer. I've seen caching cut query latency by 60% on a high-traffic payment system before, where queries were the whole cost. Here the AI is the whole cost, so the same trick barely registered. Worth keeping, not worth leading with.
StarRocks read the same catalog and the same storage with the VM's managed identity (the machine's own Azure login, no passwords) on the first try (its Azure auth docs cover it), and gave identical answers. With none of the fixes above, small questions took 0.4 to 0.7 seconds and the big accounting questions 7 to 10. That is faster than plain Trino out of the box, likely because it keeps table information between queries and shares repeated query blocks instead of planning each copy. The catch is a different SQL dialect, so every query the agent writes would need porting.
Apache Doris connected to the catalog and listed every table, then failed on the first read. Its Azure storage docs list account-key access only, and I wasn't going to hand a query engine a key to the whole storage account. If you use managed identities on Azure, check this before anything else.
Profile the step before the data. On a lake, the slow part is often looking things up, not reading. Keep a local copy of the catalog's answers, precompute the few heavy models, and put the engine and the app next to the data. Then time whole answers, not queries.
The lake was never slow. It was asking for directions.

articles.title: Saqué mis archivos de la nube y programé un navegador de archivos en un solo binario
articles.description:
Soy el autor del proyecto, así que lean esto como un relato de construcción, no como una reseña independiente.
Tengo un estudio de diseño pequeño: un NAS, una máquina con los archivos de trabajo y, varias veces al día, el mismo pedido: "mándame la versión más reciente". El problema nunca fue dónde guardar los archivos. Era verlos antes de descargarlos. Nadie quiere bajar 400 MB para descubrir que eligió el archivo equivocado.
Lo que salió al final es un binario escrito en Go. Sin Docker, sin base de datos, sin PHP, sin cron.
./banyan -headless

Imprime una dirección; la abres en el navegador de cualquier dispositivo de la misma red. La instalación termina ahí. Hay clientes nativos para Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD y Android, y todo lo demás entra por el navegador.
Vista previa de más de 100 formatos en el servidor: Office, PDF, DWG, vídeo, imágenes, archivos comprimidos, código fuente, tipografías. El archivo se transmite, no se descarga.
Enlaces para compartir que el destinatario abre sin crear cuenta, con caducidad y contador de visitas.
Editar desde la vista previa guarda directamente en la ruta original. Se acabó el final_v2_final(2).psd.
Exportar a PDF con marca de agua, firma y anotaciones en el mismo sitio donde ya está el archivo.
Cifrado AES-256-GCM por directorio, sin cuenta, sin telemetría, y funciona sin conexión si estás en la red local.
No es un cliente de sincronización. No hay resolución de conflictos ni replicación. Es un explorador con vista previa, no un Dropbox.
No hay versión alojada. Es autoalojado: TLS, dominio y proxy inverso corren de tu cuenta.
El binario pesa ~65 MB porque lleva dentro todo el pipeline de vista previa.
La interfaz está en diez idiomas, pero la traducción se generó automáticamente a partir del chino; en español hay frases que suenan raras y lo estoy corrigiendo a mano.
La alternativa habitual para este problema es montar Nextcloud o similar, o sea: Docker Compose, base de datos, actualizaciones, PHP, un panel de administración lleno de avisos. Para "quiero ver mis archivos desde mi portátil en otra habitación", eso es demasiado aparato. Un binario que se copia, se ejecuta y se olvida es más honesto para ese caso de uso.
El precio de esa decisión: no hay ecosistema de apps, no hay móvil-first sincronizado, y si quieres colaboración multiusuario real, este no es tu producto.
Página del proyecto, con descargas para las seis plataformas y la documentación en diez idiomas: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_es
Código fuente: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan
Si resolvieron el "descargar para saber qué es" de otra forma, me interesa saber cómo.

articles.title: How Long to Study for AZ-900? Realistic Hours by Level
articles.description:
This article was first published on the SecLern blog.
How long to study for AZ-900? Plan on 15 to 25 hours with some IT context, or 20 to 30 hours from zero. At 5 to 7 hours a week, that is two to five weeks, or four to six weeks as a beginner at an hour on weekdays. If you already work with Azure, 8 to 12 hours across a week is often enough. These are planning estimates, not Microsoft figures. AZ-900 is a 45-minute fundamentals exam with no prerequisites.
Plan 15 to 25 hours for AZ-900 with some IT context, and 20 to 30 hours from zero.
At 5 to 7 hours a week, that is two to five weeks; beginners need four to six weeks at an hour on weekdays.
Microsoft weights architecture and services highest at 35 to 40%.
AZ-900 is 45 minutes, has no prerequisites, and costs US$99 in the US; no passing score is published.
A 7-day sprint works only with existing cloud context and 3 to 4 hours a day.
Plan on 15 to 25 hours of AZ-900 study with some IT context, and 20 to 30 hours from zero. At about an hour on weekdays, that is three to five weeks, or four to six weeks for a beginner. If you already work with Azure, 8 to 12 hours across a week is often enough.

If you miss a week, add a week. End each block with a two-minute recall check: close your notes and write five concepts you just covered.
Working full time? One hour on five weekdays plus three hours on Saturday is about 8 hours a week, so 20 hours lands in about three weeks.
Study the three skills-measured areas in proportion to Microsoft's weights: cloud concepts 25 to 30%, Azure architecture and services 35 to 40%, and management and governance 30 to 35%. See Microsoft's study guide. Architecture gets the biggest block of a 20-hour budget.

Do not spend the first week on cloud concepts alone; it is the smallest slice and can eat hours that belong to services. The verb is "describe." Questions ask what a service is for, not how to configure it. Re-read the study guide before booking, because Microsoft updates the skills measured.

A three-week AZ-900 plan is about 21 hours: seven hours a week, with Microsoft Learn covering the first two weeks and practice questions plus one simulation covering the third.
Week 1 (about 7 hours). Work the cloud concepts modules of Microsoft Learn's AZ-900 path at 45 to 60 minutes a day. Write one page on IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with an example each, and one on the Azure hierarchy. Finish with 20 to 30 questions.
Week 2 (about 7 hours). Finish architecture and services, then management and governance. Answer questions by domain, not mixed, so a miss points at a topic. Keep a list of misses.
Week 3 (about 7 hours). Take one timed simulation early, review every miss, then spend two days on your weakest domains. In the last 48 hours, reread objectives and notes only. Book the exam for the end of the week.
Compression rule: with 10 days, double the daily hours and keep the sequence.
Yes, if you already have IT or cloud context and can put in 3 to 4 hours a day, about 20 to 30 hours across seven days. From zero, a week is not realistic: plan four to six weeks.
Day 1, cloud concepts. IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, deployment models, consumption pricing, scalability versus elasticity.
Day 2, architecture. Regions, availability zones, resource hierarchy, subscriptions and tenants.
Day 3, core services. Compute (VMs, containers, functions), networking (virtual networks, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute), storage tiers.
Day 4, identity and governance. Microsoft Entra ID, RBAC, Azure Policy, tags, pricing calculator, cost management.
Day 5, questions by domain. Read every explanation, including the options you did not pick.
Day 6, timed simulation. Use the exam clock and no pauses, then review every miss.
Day 7, weak areas only. No new videos, just notes and missed questions.
The exam clock is short, so one long scenario can consume a large share of your time. Flag it and come back.
The best way to study for AZ-900 is to start from Microsoft's objectives, cover the material with Microsoft Learn, and spend at least a third of your hours on practice questions you review.
Read the skills-measured list first. Every study hour should map to an objective.
Work the Microsoft Learn AZ-900 path. Course AZ-900T00 covers the objectives and does not require a paid Azure subscription for the core modules.
Answer questions by domain. Read the explanation for every option, including distractors.
Take one timed simulation. A score is a diagnostic; the useful output is two or three weak topics.
Turn misses into notes and re-drill after 48 hours. Spacing the retest makes the fix stick.
Review objectives and misses only in the last 48 hours. New material adds anxiety, not points.
Retention comes from answering, not reading. Answering forces recall; reading only builds recognition.
You can run steps 3 to 6 on SecLern, where AZ-900 practice questions include an explanation for every answer and timed simulations return a readiness grade by domain. The AZ-900 practice test guide shows how to review a simulation.

You are ready to book AZ-900 when you can explain the core concepts without notes and score 85% or higher in all three domains in two full timed simulations finished inside the exam time.
Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with a real example each.
Name core compute, storage and networking services and what each is for.
Draw the Azure hierarchy from management groups to a resource.
Explain Microsoft Entra ID versus on-premises Active Directory, including hybrid identity.
Describe cost and governance tools: pricing calculator, cost management, Azure Policy, RBAC.
Describe regions, availability zones and what an SLA covers.
Score 85% or better in each domain.
Finish two full simulations inside the time limit with every miss reviewed.
If two or more lines are unchecked, push the exam back a week. Extra practice is cheaper than a retake.
AZ-900 is the exam for Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals. It lasts 45 minutes and costs US$99 in the United States; Microsoft lists current details on the official AZ-900 exam page.

Confirm price, duration and current skills measured before you schedule. Local pricing varies, so the official page wins over any blog.
A short exam rewards pacing. Answer short questions first, flag long scenarios, and return to them.
If you are comparing entry-level cloud credentials, AZ-900 vs AWS Cloud Practitioner puts the two fundamentals exams side by side.
We built SecLern around a pattern: people who fail fundamentals exams usually did not run out of hours; they spent them passively. Three weeks of video feels like preparation and leaves you recognizing terms without being able to define them. Microsoft Learn already teaches AZ-900 well, so we do not replace it. What a course cannot do is tell you that you are weak on governance and strong on cloud concepts. The habit that matters is 45 minutes a day plus a short question set, with misses written down.
SecLern's AZ-900 path follows the loop this article describes: answer questions by domain, read why every option is right or wrong, and turn misses into notes and drills. Timed simulations return a readiness grade per domain, so you can see whether you are at the 85% mark before you book. The free tier includes the first module, 30 questions a day, 3 labs and PBQs, and unlimited flashcards, no card needed. Pro is $15 a month or $99 a year with a 7-day trial (card required); Exam Sprint is $29 once for 90 days. See pricing.
Is 2 weeks enough to study for AZ-900?
Yes for many candidates. Two weeks at about 1.5 hours a day is roughly 20 hours, in the middle of the 15 to 25 hour estimate. It is tight from zero with no IT background, where 20 to 30 hours over four to six weeks is more realistic. Book only after two timed simulations at 85% or better in every domain.
How hard is AZ-900 with no IT experience?
It is not technically hard, but it is vocabulary-dense: storage tiers, identity, governance and pricing models arrive faster than you can absorb them. Budget 20 to 30 hours over four to six weeks. There are no prerequisites, and the questions ask you to describe concepts rather than configure anything in the Azure portal.
Can you pass AZ-900 in 3 days?
Only if you already work with Azure. Three days at four hours a day is 12 hours, enough to refresh vocabulary you use weekly and not enough to learn it from scratch. If cloud is new to you, use the three-week plan; a retake costs more than the extra study time.
How many questions are on the AZ-900 exam?
Microsoft does not publish a fixed question count for AZ-900, so there is no number to memorize. Expect multiple-choice and interactive items inside the 45-minute window. Flag long scenarios, answer short questions first, and check the official exam page before you schedule.
Does the AZ-900 certification expire?
No. Microsoft's certification expiration page states that Fundamentals certifications, including Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals, do not expire. That makes AZ-900 a one-time exam rather than an annual commitment, though Microsoft can still retire an exam version and replace it with a newer one.
Should you take AZ-900 or go straight to AZ-104?
Take AZ-900 first if cloud is new to you; it builds the vocabulary AZ-104 assumes. If you already administer Azure subscriptions, networks or identities at work, skip it and start AZ-104, a role-based administrator exam with hands-on expectations. AZ-900 is not a formal prerequisite for AZ-104.

articles.title: Patrones de Arquitectura de Software: Guía Comparativa y su Uso en Frameworks Modernos
articles.description:
Propósito


Identificar las características, ventajas y aplicaciones de los principales patrones de arquitectura de software, y analizar cómo los frameworks modernos los implementan, así como la relación entre las decisiones arquitectónicas y el éxito de un proyecto.
a. Patrón de Capas (Layered)
b. Patrón Cliente-Servidor
c. Patrón Modelo-Vista-Controlador (MVC)
d. Patrón Filtro de Tuberías (Pipes and Filters)
e. Patrón Intermediario (Mediator)
f. Patrón Igual a Igual (Peer-to-Peer)
g. Patrón Bus de Eventos (Event Bus)
h. Patrón Pizarra (Blackboard)
El patrón Pizarra no es simplemente un almacén de datos compartido. Su estructura completa requiere tres componentes fundamentales:
La pizarra (blackboard): contiene el estado del problema y las soluciones parciales.
Las fuentes de conocimiento (knowledge sources): son módulos independientes que leen el estado de la pizarra y contribuyen con nuevas soluciones parciales.
El componente de control (control component o motor heurístico): es el encargado de evaluar el estado actual de la pizarra y decidir qué fuente de conocimiento debe ejecutarse a continuación.
Sin este componente de control, el patrón colapsa y se convierte en un simple repositorio de variables globales o una base de datos compartida, perdiendo su naturaleza de resolución de problemas no determinista. El control es lo que permite que el sistema progrese hacia la solución sin un algoritmo predefinido.
2. Lista Comparativa de Patrones


A continuación se presenta la comparativa de cada patrón con su definición, estructura, ventajas, desventajas y ejemplos de aplicación.
a. Capas (Layered)
Definición: Divide la aplicación en capas horizontales según las responsabilidades; cada capa solo interactúa con la capa adyacente inferior.
Estructura: Capas apiladas presentación → negocio → persistencia → datos. Capas cerradas que obligan a pasar por todas las otras capas; capas abiertas permiten saltos.
Ventajas: Separación clara de responsabilidades; fácil de probar y mantener; curva de aprendizaje baja; es buena para migrar sistemas heredados.
Desventajas: Puede generar capas embudo sin lógica real; añade latencia; dificulta el despliegue independiente; el monolito por capas es rígido.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Aplicaciones web empresariales; sistemas heredados a la nube; ERPs tradicionales; aplicaciones Java EE / Spring MVC.
b. Cliente-Servidor
Definición: Separa roles: el cliente inicia solicitudes, el servidor las procesa y responde.
Estructura: Dos capas, cliente con interfaz y algo de lógica / servidor con datos, o N capas. Servidor con o sin estado.
Ventajas: Datos centralizados; seguridad y respaldos más simples; roles claros; soporta múltiples tipos de clientes.
Desventajas: El servidor central es cuello de botella y punto único de fallo; en dos capas hay alto acoplamiento entre UI y lógica; cambios costosos.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Aplicaciones web; servidores de archivos; sistemas de correo; acceso a bases de datos; FTP, HTTP.
c. Modelo-Vista-Controlador (MVC)
Definición: Separa la aplicación en modelo (datos y reglas), vista (interfaz) y controlador (entrada y flujo).
Estructura: El controlador recibe la entrada y opera el modelo; el modelo notifica a la vista; la vista renderiza. Un modelo puede tener varias vistas.
Ventajas: Separación de preocupaciones, desarrollo en paralelo; pruebas unitarias más fáciles, un ecosistema maduro y reutilización de modelos.
Desventajas: Sobrediseño en apps pequeñas; controladores que se inflan, sincronización vista-modelo requiere mecanismos extra.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Spring MVC; ASP.NET Core MVC; Laravel; Ruby on Rails; Django; AngularJS (versión clásica).
d. Filtro de Tuberías (Pipes and Filters)
Definición: Descompone el procesamiento en filtros independientes conectados por tuberías que transforman datos secuencialmente.
Estructura: Filtros sin estado que reciben, procesan y emiten datos; tuberías que solo conectan y transmiten; sin lógica de enrutamiento.
Ventajas: Altamente modular; filtros reutilizables, reordenables y reemplazables; soporta paralelismo y distribución; escalado por filtro.
Desventajas: Cambios exigen pruebas de extremo a extremo; incompatibilidad de formatos añade sobrecarga; manejo de errores e idempotencia complejos.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Compiladores, análisis léxico/sintáctico; pipelines de datos (ETL); procesamiento de logs; procesamiento de imágenes; Unix pipes.
e. Mediador (Mediator)
Definición: Introduce un componente central que encapsula la comunicación entre objetos, evitando referencias directas entre ellos.
Estructura: El mediador mantiene referencias a los colegas; los colegas solo hablan con el mediador; este enruta, transforma o coordina mensajes.
Ventajas: Reduce drásticamente el acoplamiento muchos-a-muchos; lógica de interacción centralizada; más fácil de modificar y depurar.
Desventajas: El mediador puede volverse un "objeto dios"; centralización crea punto único de fallo; puede convertirse en un cuello de botella.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Diálogos GUI; salas de chat; agentes de servicio en sistemas distribuidos; torres de control aéreo.
f. Igual a Igual (Peer-to-Peer, P2P)
Definición: Cada nodo actúa como cliente y servidor a la vez; no hay control central; los nodos colaboran directamente.
Estructura: Nodos simétricos que mantienen recursos y responden a otros. P2P puro, sin centro, o híbrido, con nodo de descubrimiento.
Ventajas: Escalabilidad excelente, cada nodo añade consumo y servicio; robustez por descentralización, y sin punto único de fallo.
Desventajas: Difícil aplicar seguridad y regulación uniformes; descubrimiento y consistencia complejos; problemas de privacidad y derechos de autor.
Ejemplos de aplicación: BitTorrent; Gnutella; Bitcoin; Skype arquitectura temprana; redes de intercambio de archivos; blockchain.
g. Bus de Eventos (Event Bus)
Definición: Los componentes se comunican asíncronamente mediante eventos publicados en un bus; los emisores y receptores no se conocen.
Estructura: Bus central que distribuye eventos; generadores publican sin esperar respuesta; consumidores se suscriben y procesan asíncronamente. Modelo publicar y suscribir.
Ventajas: Bajo acoplamiento; añadir consumidores no afecta a generadores; soporta asincronía y concurrencia; altamente escalable.
Desventajas: Flujo de control difícil de rastrear; depuración y pruebas complejas; el bus puede ser cuello de botella; cambios de esquema impactan ampliamente.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Eventos de UI; microservicios asíncronos (Kafka, RabbitMQ); IoT; trading financiero; sistemas de notificaciones.
h. Pizarra (Blackboard)
Definición: Varias fuentes de conocimiento independientes colaboran sobre un almacén compartido hasta resolver un problema sin algoritmo determinista.
Estructura: Pizarra con estado y soluciones parciales; fuentes de conocimiento independientes; componente de control que evalúa el estado y decide el orden de activación de las fuentes.
Ventajas: Adecuado para problemas complejos con múltiples estrategias; fuentes desarrollables y reemplazables por separado; sin algoritmo único necesario.
Desventajas: Estado compartido difícil de controlar como variables globales; riesgo de condiciones de carrera; lógica de control compleja.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Reconocimiento de voz; interpretación de imágenes; fusión de recomendadores heterogéneos; sistemas expertos de IA.
Es importante distinguir entre patrones de diseño de software y estilos arquitectónicos de distribución. Spring Boot es un framework que facilita la creación de aplicaciones stand-alone y, por sí solo, tiende a producir monolitos modulares. Los microservicios no son un patrón de diseño de software, sino un estilo arquitectónico de distribución. Spring Boot no "implementa" microservicios; se utiliza dentro de una arquitectura de microservicios, a menudo apoyado por Spring Cloud (Eureka para descubrimiento de servicios, API Gateway para enrutamiento, etc.).
- Spring Boot
Patrones centrales: MVC + Capas (monolito modular). Los microservicios son un estilo arquitectónico de distribución, no un patrón que Spring Boot implemente por sí solo.
Práctica concreta: Spring MVC implementa aplicaciones web en capas; convención sobre configuración reduce código boilerplate. Para microservicios se requiere Spring Cloud, que añade descubrimiento de servicios (Eureka), balanceo de carga, API Gateway y trazabilidad distribuida.
- ASP.NET Core
Práctica concreta: Soporte MVC nativo con límites claros entre controlador, vista y modelo; inyección de dependencias integrada que promueve el desacoplamiento en capas; mecanismo de filtros que encapsula preocupaciones transversales.
- Laravel
Práctica concreta: MVC como núcleo desde su diseño; el motor de plantillas Blade asume la responsabilidad de la vista; Artisan CLI genera esqueletos de controladores, modelos y otros componentes.
- Angular
Práctica concreta: Organiza la interfaz como un árbol de componentes; inyección de dependencias para gestionar servicios; soporta micro-frontend mediante Module Federation / Native Federation.
- React
Práctica concreta: Es una biblioteca de vistas, no impone MVC; Flux y Redux proporcionan gestión de estado con flujo unidireccional; Context API para estado compartido ligero.
Convención sobre configuración:


Implementación integrada de patrones:


Contenedor de inyección de dependencias: 


Soporte de herramientas y ecosistema: 


Motores de plantillas y abstracción de componentes: 




  
  
  5. Opinión Personal: ¿La Arquitectura Determina el Éxito o Fracaso de un Proyecto?


Sí, considero que la elección de arquitectura es uno de los factores clave del éxito o fracaso de un proyecto, aunque también influyen otros factores o condiciones. La evidencia de la industria, documentada en post-mortems y estudios de casos, muestra que una arquitectura correcta pero mal ejecutada también lleva al fracaso: equipos que eligen una arquitectura limpia pero llenan la capa de lógica de negocio con consultas SQL y anotaciones específicas del framework terminan con capas que no funcionan como tales. Por otro lado, sistemas entregados con arquitecturas simples de tres capas han demostrado ser extremadamente estables y evolucionar durante años. La clave no es la sofisticación de la arquitectura, sino que el equipo entienda y respete sus restricciones, con la guía adecuada.
La arquitectura sirve a los requisitos, al equipo y a las restricciones de tiempo. Un equipo de cinco personas desarrollando una herramienta interna no tiene sentido que adopte P2P; un MVP que necesita validar el mercado rápidamente ve el sobrediseño como un retraso en el aprendizaje. La esencia de la decisión arquitectónica es hacer compensaciones apropiadas bajo las restricciones actuales, no perseguir la solución teóricamente óptima. ASP.NET Core y Laravel son populares precisamente porque encuentran el equilibrio entre una arquitectura suficiente y flexible.
La arquitectura no es un fin en sí mismo, sino una herramienta de gestión de riesgos. La verdadera pregunta no es "¿cuál es la mejor arquitectura?", sino "¿qué riesgos técnicos (escalabilidad, tiempo de mercado, complejidad operativa, costo de mantenimiento) estamos dispuestos a asumir con esta elección para satisfacer los objetivos del negocio?". Una buena elección arquitectónica hace que el cambio sea barato y que los riesgos sean identificables y acotados; una mala elección hace que el cambio sea caro y que los riesgos se materialicen en forma de deuda técnica, retrasos o fallos en producción. Por ello, la arquitectura debe ser entendida, respetada y ajustada según las circunstancias, y su evaluación debe hacerse siempre en función de los riesgos que el negocio está dispuesto a tolerar.

articles.title: pstack 完全ガイド ─AIエージェントに雑なコード     を書かせない技術─
articles.description:
AIエージェントに仕事を頼むと、自信満々の報告と一緒に検証されていない大量のコードが届いて困ったことはありませんか？

AIエージェントを使い始めた人はもちろん、日常的に使いこなしているエンジニアでも、「どうすれば品質を担保できるのか」「どこまで自律的に仕事を任せられるのか」という疑問は共通の課題ではないでしょうか

pstack は、元React コアチームのエンジニア poteto（Lauren Tan）氏が、日々の開発で使っているスキルを公開したものです

本書は、pstackの思想から実践までを体系的に解説した初心者から中上級者までを対象とする実践ガイドです。

単なるスキルの使い方にとどまらず、AIエージェントの仕事の進め方そのものを見直し、検証可能で信頼できる開発ワークフローをどう構築するかまで踏み込みます。

この本を読むと、明日からAIへの仕事の任せ方が変わります

- 寝る前に仕事を頼み、朝には検証済みのPRが作成されている
- AIの「直しました」を、実行結果や動作確認の証拠つきで受け取れる
- コードレビューする必要性が減り、動画やスクショのチェックだけでマージできる
  (機械的な検証を自動化し、人間がレビューすべき範囲を減らせる)
- 属人的なプロンプトの工夫から脱却し、再現性のある開発手順を構築できる

pstackが目指しているのは、AIにたくさんコードを書かせることではありません。書く量を減らし、質を上げることです。

そのために「証拠がなければ完了と認めない」「書いた本人に採点させない」「足す前に引く」といった考え方が、各スキルやプレイブックに組み込まれています。

本書では、入口となる /poteto-mode の使い方とプロンプトの書き方から始め、22のプレイブック、34のスキル、24の原則を一つずつ解説します。

さらに、似たスキルの使い分け、寝ている間にエージェントに仕事を任せる方法、日本語でそのまま使えるプロンプトのレシピ集、よくある失敗と対処法も収録しました。Cursor だけでなく、Claude Code で使うときの違いも説明しています。

初心者にはpstackを迷わず使い始めるための入門書として、中上級者にはAIエージェントの運用や検証戦略を見直すための実践書としてオススメです
